#6313. The Best Hotels Near Disneyland Paris With Cinderella Suites, 'Toy Story'–Themed Rooms, and Quaint Cottages

Located just 40 minutes from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, Disneyland Paris is the ideal place to begin a Parisian vacation or say au revoir before returning home. Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World, pair timeless charm with an ease you'll never find stateside. Here, you can sip Champagne in front of Sleeping Beauty's castle—or visit a dragon beneath it—while filling your days with delightful architecture, unprecedented thrills, and the wildest wilderness ride Disney's ever built (Big Thunder Mountain!).

There's also never been a better time to visit. Walt Disney Studios Park's March 2026 transformation into the new Disney Adventure World brought a drone-filled nighttime show, Avengers coaster, and even a Frozen-themed land featuring a lifelike Olaf robot to its once-faltering second gate. Now, between Fantasyland classics and futuristic favorites, there's something new and thrilling for the entire family to experience.

Of course, you'll need somewhere to rest your head at night, and that's where the best hotels near Disneyland Paris come into play. Staying at a Disney-branded property typically affords guests special amenities including ticket packages, exclusive character meet-and-greets, and Extra Magic Time, which provides bonus time in the parks prior to opening. These hotels are great options, but can also be pricey—luckily, there are also a few non-branded properties in the area that make for great alternatives. There's something here for everyone and every budget.

Unsure of whether you want to add something so Américain to your Paris vacation? As a theme park journalist who has visited all Disney parks worldwide, trust me: It's worth the visit. Even with so many cultural monuments in Paris, nothing is more delightfully uncanny than witnessing the United States section of It's a Small World. So, whether you're looking for glamour or simply a good location, read on for the very best hotels near Disneyland Paris.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Three-minute walk

As the crown jewel of France's Disney resort, this 487-room property is Disney's best hotel overseas—and, quite possibly, in the entire world. After undergoing an extensive three-year overhaul, the iconic pink palace reopened in 2024 with princess suites and luxurious amenities worthy of its five-star ranking. Great for couples or families, guests can anticipate the ultimate royal treatment thanks to rooms with romantic castle views just steps from the park. With kids treatments at the Spa by Clarins and two complimentary hours of childcare each day, parents can unwind at the Fleur de Lys bar, enjoy a prix fixe meal at chef Jean Imbert's on-site restaurant, or perhaps even sneak back into the parks themselves. (We won't tell.)

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Eight-minute drive

Rustic-chic in the best of ways, Marriott's Village d'Île-de-France offers cozy abodes that sleep up to eight with full kitchens, washing machines, and plenty of space to stretch out, all a short shuttle ride from the theme parks. Designed to emulate the charms of a small Parisian village, these quaint studios and multi-bedroom town houses feel more like cottages than traditional vacation rentals. Surroundings like these may sound quotidien to someone like Princess Belle, but the resort is as sweet as the rooms are spacious, making it an ideal choice for a hotel near Disneyland Paris as well as extended trips to nearby towns.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute walk, 10-minute drive

Considering it's the only hotel in the world dedicated to Marvel's famed comic book characters, it's no surprise the Infinity Stone–colored beverages and slick, silver rooms at Disney Hotel New York - The Art of Marvel are somewhat out of this world. Family-friendly amenities like superhero meet-and-greets and a design studio with character drawing experiences make it the ultimate getaway for any comic book–obsessed fan in your family. Yet, even with hundreds of unique pieces of artwork, it won't feel like you're living through an Infinity War. Delicately executed details, like Manhattan Restaurant's Asgard-inspired chandelier and Spider-Man swinging across the panel screens at Skyline Bar, provide simple city elegance with the lightest touch of Marvel magic.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 17-minute walk, 8-minute drive

If this hotel reminds you of Walt Disney World's Yacht & Beach Club resorts, you're not mistaken—this 1,098-room Disneyland Paris hotel was inspired by its Florida counterpart. The nautical theming is strong, and it's that seaside charm that keeps parkgoers returning to this waterfront escape. Just a 15-minute walk from the park gates, guests can meet maritime Mickey & Minnie Mouse (who don delightful cruisewear) or indulge in a seafood buffet at the aptly named Cape Cod restaurant. It's modeled after a familiar location back in the States, sure, but after spending the day with princesses, dragons, and superheroes, you may find yourself overjoyed to return to those country club comforts.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 13-minute walk, 8-minute drive

Craving a bit more theming on your Disneyland Paris trip? Look no further than this national park–inspired escape. It offers lodge-style living perfect for a wintertime trip. Cozy up to the Redwood Bar & Lounge hearth, or in one of the newly renovated rooms with nods to Bambi and Pocahontas, and take in the charms of what Disney does best. Multiple on-site buffets allow you to feast like you've been on the move all day because, well, you likely have.

Note that this Disney-operated hotel is currently undergoing a phased refurbishment. For stays in late 2026 and early 2027, I recommend selecting a refurbished room in The Lodges. Starting in February 2027, construction will move to general hotel spaces, and certain facilities will be temporarily unavailable.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 30-minute walk, 10-minute drive

Rooms at the boutique Hôtel l’Elysée Val d’Europe are modern and minimal, offering the perfect escape from any theme park chaos. Though it's just a 30-minute walk or a short, free shuttle ride away from the gates, the real perk of being a bit removed is its proximity to the Val d’Europe shopping complex and the designer outlet mall La Vallée Village. With a bounty of discounted prices on luxury brands like Prada, Saint Laurent, and Gucci, you're sure to find a Parisian souvenir that'll rival the array of Mickey Mouse goods sold within the parks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: Nine-minute drive

If the City of Lights appeals to you for its style and romance, consider this your ideal hotel. Design-forward rooms with concrete walls, sleek bathrooms, and an open, plant-walled lobby offer reliable value without sacrificing taste, making it a perfect choice for travelers seeking something a little less Disney. While families will benefit from select rooms offering full kitchens and stovetops, the upgraded amenities—which include a heated indoor pool, sauna, and hammam—offer a little something for everyone, just beyond the parks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 16-minute walk, 10-minute drive

Step right up to this quirky hotel that feels like a Western film set and is jam-packed with Toy Story details. Small touches, like cowprint bedspreads and appearances by Woody and Jessie, make Disney Hotel Cheyenne a hidden gem that's nearly as themed as Disneyland Paris's own Frontierland. Given that it's significantly more affordable than the majority of its Disneyland-owned counterparts yet retains perks like Extra Magic Time, this property offers a best-of-both-worlds approach for those who want to live a full Disney-fied day from first rides to fireworks.

Distance from Disneyland Paris: 10-minute drive

Multi-room cabins at this expansive, woodsy resort are the perfect way to experience a taste of the outdoors between trips on Big Thunder Mountain. Sadly, there are no theme park shuttle services, so parks must be reached by car, rideshare, or taxi. But that's not to say it's worth skipping—here, nature abounds in both form and function. There's an on-site aviary, comfort food at the Crockett's Tavern buffet, and plenty of rustic charm, so the comforts of home are never too far away. Consider this Disneyland Paris hotel as close as you can get to camping at Disneyland's theme parks—if camping also included unfettered access to Mickey waffles.

What area is the best to stay in when visiting Disneyland Paris?

Any hotel near Disney Village, the entertainment and dining district at the entrance to Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, is going to be the most convenient choice. This not only offers more ease and access, but affords you the option to shop and dine after the parks close each night. Still, booking nearly any Disney-operated hotel will give you benefits like Extra Magic Time and exclusive character encounters, which help get you even more out of your Disneyland Paris vacation.

Are there any hotels that are walking distance to Disneyland Paris?

Yes—but you might want to bring your sneakers. Disneyland Hotel is located directly at the entrance to Disneyland Paris, while Disney Hotel New York - The Art of Marvel, Disney Newport Bay Club, and Disney Sequoia Lodge are all a 10- to 15-minute walk through Disney Village to reach both parks. Disney Hotel Cheyenne is a further trek, about 15 to 20 minutes away, but absolutely doable. Shuttle buses are available as well.

What is the 3-2-1 rule at Disneyland Paris?

The 3-2-1 rule is essentially shorthand for how to streamline your Disneyland Paris experience. Experts recommend selecting three rides, two entertainment offerings, and one dining option for an easy, straightforward approach to planning a day at any Disney theme park. It works as well at Walt Disney World and Disneyland as it does here at Disneyland Paris, but I recommend you still do a little research before you go. Be sure you don't skip Phantom Manor, which can only be found in Paris, secure your dining reservations early, and don't miss the nighttime shows offered at both parks—they're among the best in the world.

It is best to stay within the park at Disneyland Paris, or outside of it?

It goes without saying that the closer you are to the castle, the “better” your hotel will be, but it shouldn't be a deal-breaker. Convenience is always a factor, but Disney-operated hotels at Disneyland Paris tend to be much pricier than their American counterparts, so staying a bus ride away might be necessary. Still, the perks are plenty across most of Disneyland's own hotels, including extra time in the parks, which is why I recommended so many of them.

#6312. A Guide to NYC’s Little Italy—and the Culinary Gems Hidden Among the Tourist Traps

Contrary to other tourist-focused neighborhoods in New York (looking at you, Times Square), Little Italy boasts an innate charm that resonates with visitors and locals alike. Sandwiched between SoHo and the Lower East Side, this jewel box area is home to long-standing, family-owned restaurants and authentic Italian bakeries, the majority of which have been neighborhood staples for decades. Yet despite its touristy atmosphere, a unique feeling of old school New York magic hangs in the air; beyond the personality-less stands and souvenir shops, framed family photos on restaurant walls and structural imperfections of tenement buildings speak to a bygone area of the city’s past, evoking a sense of nostalgia that so many neighborhoods lack. Pop down to Mulberry Street and see for yourself—though be sure you know which spots are actually legit (that’s where we come in).

A note on how we’re defining the area: Over the years, Little Italy’s boundaries have shrunk to focus on the touristic area of Mulberry Street and its immediate surroundings. While the southern and western boundaries of Canal Street and Lafayette Streets remain unchanged, the historic easterly Bowery boundary has arguably shifted to Elizabeth Street; similarly, the northerly boundary of Kenmare has also condensed down, according to many, to Broome Street. For the sake of this piece, we’re using the boundaries of Lafayette Street, Canal Street, Elizabeth Street, and Broome Street as a happy medium.

Located in the heart of Little Italy, Umberto’s Clam House is best known for its—you guessed it, all things clams. The restaurant quickly garnered attention shortly after opening in 1972, when mobster Joe "Crazy Joe" Gallo was shot in the restaurant’s dining room. Like its mafia-related history, the food at Umberto’s is as Italian-American as it gets. Baked clams and fried calamari are the appetizer list’s biggest show-stoppers, while superbly chilled clams on the half-shell pair exquisitely with equally cold (and generously sized) cocktails from the bar. Seafood-focused mains are the name of the game here, including the garlicky linguini and clam sauce and recently resurfaced scungilli with pasta served with piping hot red sauce.

Address: 132 Mulberry Street, New York, NY 10013

For Italian-American eats in a less stereotypically Little Italy ambiance, Il Cortile is the way to go. Contrary to the old school Italian vibes found in the majority of the neighborhood’s restaurants, Il Cortile’s atrium-style glass ceiling and plant-filled room feel more like dining al fresco in Trastevere than the heart of Mulberry Street. The family-owned restaurant’s neighborhood roots date back to 1975, with a solid focus on Northern Italian cuisine. The homemade cheese ravioli and wood-fired pizzas are always a safe bet, though for meat lovers, springing for the Fettuccine di Parma made with sweet sausage and wild mushrooms won’t disappoint—and be sure to save room for the pillowy soft tiramisu made with creamy mascarpone and imported Italian ladyfingers drenched in espresso.

Address: 125 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013

Original Vincent’s, often called The Original Vincent’s Clam Bar, is home to one of the richest restaurant success stories in Little Italy. Founded in 1904 by Giuseppe and Carmela Siano, the business began as a sidewalk street cart serving up fresh seafood and jars of homemade red sauce, available in mild, medium, and hot. Today, the restaurant sits on the corner of Mott and Hester Streets, and is still known for its signature gravies, baked clams, and linguini-based pasta dishes (don’t skip the frutti di mare). As in its earliest days, Original Vincent’s still sells jars of their red sauce to-go, making replicating the restaurant’s pasta dishes at home a breeze—simply grab a bottle of Chianti, cue up your Louis Primo playlist and voila.

Paesano of Mulberry Street is home to one of the coziest interiors in Little Italy, offering a peaceful refuge from the neighborhood bustle. Rustic twig bunches and leafy plants strung with twinkle lights hang from the ceiling, while traditional Italian frescos and framed family photographs adorn the whitewashed brick walls. Originally opened in 1961, the restaurant remains owned by the same family and continues to be known for their Southern Italian recipes, including linguini with clam sauce, wood-fired pizzas, and savory chicken marsala drenched in sautéed mushrooms. Meat lovers, don’t skip the restaurant’s signature Veal A La Paesano, featuring a juicy and tender veal base layered with thin slices of prosciutto, steamed broccoli, and gooey mozzarella cheese finished with succulent brown gravy.

Address: 136 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013

For serious pizza lovers, a trip to Lombardi’s is a no-brainer. Tucked on the corner of Mott and Spring, this neighborhood institution is credited as America’s first pizzeria, originally founded by Gennaro Lombardi in 1905. Lombardi quickly rose to fame for his large, heavily-topped pies, which he baked in an on-site, coal-and-gas oven. The result? Smoky crusts topped with perfectly balanced tomato sauce and gobs of whole milk mozzarella—along with sweet Italian sausage and various other accoutrements. The interior oozes with classic New York charm, featuring tables clad in red-and-white checkered cloths and framed family photographs strung along the red-hued walls. Head’s up, the spot is cash only, and while there’s an ATM on site, we recommend coming prepared to avoid the withdrawal fee.

Address: 30 Spring St, New York, NY 10012

Pasquale Jones-12_2. Brussels Sprout Pizza with Red Onion, Smoked Mozzarella & Lemon

In a sea of mediocre neighborhood wine lists, Pasqule Jones offers a breath of fresh air for Little Italy exploring wine lovers. Situated on the cusp of the neighborhood’s boundaries (and easily identifiable by its rainbow neon lights), this Italian-American pizzeria first opened its doors in 2016 and quickly became a staple for industry folks and visiting oenophiles alike. Beloved for its wood-fired New York style pizzas (don’t miss the signature clam pie) and thick, homemade pastas, the restaurant’s warm-yet-casual ambiance is ideal for posting up with a pie and a bottle—especially if you’re after great Burgundy, Champagne, or Italian reds. Expect classic picks from Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey, Domaine de l’Arlot, and Vietti, as well ample fun and fresh selections from Sandlands, Chacra, and Domaine Gramenon.

Address: 187 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10012

Address: 195 Grand St, New York, NY 10013

Although less famous than nearby Ferrara, Caffé Palermo features the innate Italian charm one looks for when wandering the neighborhood. Owned and operated by Baby John DeLutro (the self-proclaimed “Cannoli King”) since 1973, the establishment lives up to its owner’s moniker, offering flavored iterations—including pistachio and hazelnut made with sweet ricotta cream, the former of which is one of the joint’s standouts—in perfectly crisp shells. What Palermo does have over Ferrara is a solid amount of outdoor seating, ideal for posting up with a cappuccino and people watching on Mulberry.

Address: 148 Mulberry St, New York, NY 10013

If you’re looking for a wine break between pizza and pastries, this is just the ticket. Located on Little Italy's western limits (Centre Street between Broome and Grand), this French-inspired wine bar offers extensive by-the-glass options and shareable bites, including cheese and charcuterie boards to larger main courses, including beef tartare and lemon spaghetti. The comprehensive wine list, which features anywhere from 750 to 1,000+ references at all times, leans unsurprisingly French, though ample selections from Italy, Spain, and the USA are also available. Our suggestion? Post up with a bottle of Grower Champagne and relish in the perfectly executed Parisian bar à vin ambiance.

Address: 249 Centre St, New York, NY 10013

Address: 409 Broome St, New York, NY 10013

Technically located on the cusp of Little Italy’s historic boundaries (Kenmare and Broome Streets), La Esquina offers a flavor-packed reprieve from the classic red-sauce joints synonymous with the neighborhood. Situated in a former counter deli, this multi-level Mexican hotspot is best known for its casual taqueria (located in ‘The Corner Deli’ space) serving tacos, tortas, and ceviche. However, for those looking for something a bit stronger, head through the secret door and down the stairs to find the restaurant’s underground speakeasy. Lit by candle and adorned with Lucha Libre posters, the bar’s high-energy ambiance is prime for enjoying queso fundido and smoky Mexican street corn (elotes callejeros) washed down with expertly crafted agave-based cocktails.

Address: 114 Kenmare St, New York, NY 10012

#6310. Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

The airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

The redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

#6309. 2 Virgin Australia Pilots Admit They’re Too Tired To Continue Flying, Immediately Offloaded

Two Virgin Australia pilots declared themselves unfit to continue flying after fatigue set in during a domestic flight from Melbourne Airport (MEL) to Adelaide Airport (ADL) on Wednesday. Both crew members requested to be stood down upon reaching their destination. The aircraft landed safely at Adelaide Airport, after which the pilots were immediately removed from further flying duties.

The incident highlights the importance of fatigue management in commercial aviation, where pilots must recognize when tiredness could compromise their ability to operate an aircraft safely. Although the flight itself was completed without incident, the decision to remove both pilots raises broader questions about crew scheduling, rest periods, and the challenges of managing fatigue across Australia's airline industry. Virgin Australia's response also shows why self-reporting remains essential to aviation safety.

According to AIRLIVE, the incident occurred aboard VA219 on Wednesday morning. The Boeing 737-800, registered VH-VUX, was operating a domestic service between Melbourne and Adelaide when both pilots reported fatigue. Rather than continue their planned duties, the flight crew requested to be stood down at their next destination.

The aircraft continued to Adelaide and completed its journey safely, touching down at 11:05 local time. The flight had departed Melbourne about an hour earlier, following the aircraft's previous operation of flight VA814 from Sydney to Melbourne earlier that morning. Once in Adelaide, both pilots were immediately offloaded, preventing them from operating any subsequent flight sectors until they were considered fit to return to duty.

The decision followed Virgin Australia's fatigue risk management procedures, which allow pilots to report when tiredness affects their ability to perform their responsibilities safely. Importantly, declaring oneself unfit to fly is not an admission of wrongdoing. It is a safety measure designed to prevent potentially impaired crew members from continuing operations.

This is not the first time fatigue management has attracted attention at Virgin Australia. In May 2024, The Guardian reported that senior pilots had raised concerns about the airline's rostering arrangements, arguing that demanding schedules were contributing to fatigue across the pilot workforce. Correspondence reviewed by the newspaper highlighted concerns about consecutive long duty days, sometimes lasting 11–12 hours, followed by the minimum 12-hour rest period permitted under the applicable rules.

The pilots also questioned the airline's rostering software and its ability to accommodate operational realities, particularly when flights were delayed. Virgin Australia responded at the time by saying it operated under a robust fatigue management system approved by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA). The airline also highlighted that its pilots received 156 rostered days off annually. Although those earlier concerns do not establish the cause of the November 2026 report, they illustrate how crew scheduling and fatigue have remained important topics within the airline.

Fatigue is also a concern beyond the flight deck. Last month, ABC News reported on an Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) investigation into a taxiway incident at Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) involving Virgin Australia flight 1589 and Qantas flight 420. An air traffic controller working during the incident had a high predicted fatigue risk after being rostered to finish at 8:50 PM and return to duty at 5:30 AM the following morning. The ATSB stressed that a high predicted fatigue level does not necessarily mean an individual is actually fatigued. Nevertheless, the case demonstrates how demanding schedules can affect safety-critical aviation personnel across different operational environments.

While the aircraft involved landed safely at its planned destination, it is yet to return to service.

Fatigue can significantly affect a pilot's concentration, reaction time, memory, and decision-making under pressure. According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), tiredness can reduce the ability to perform tasks requiring manual coordination, vigilance, and higher-level cognitive processing. These effects can develop after a single demanding period or accumulate over several days of insufficient rest.

The consequences can be particularly serious in commercial aviation, where pilots must continuously monitor aircraft systems, communicate with air traffic control, assess changing weather conditions, and respond to unexpected situations. Even experienced flight crew members are not immune to these effects. The FAA also notes that coffee, medication, motivation, and willpower cannot overcome fatigue; adequate sleep remains the most effective solution.

Virgin Australia's decision to remove both pilots from further duties should be viewed positively. Allowing fatigued crew members to keep flying just to avoid disruption would create an unnecessary safety risk for passengers, other crew members, and everyone involved in the operation. While replacing pilots can create scheduling complications and potentially delay subsequent services, those considerations must remain secondary to operational safety.

This incident demonstrates an important principle of commercial aviation: a flight is only safe when its crew members are fit to perform their duties. By allowing both pilots to report their condition and immediately standing them down after arrival, Virgin Australia followed the appropriate safety-first approach.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

At least they reported it, which is always better to do in aviation

#6307. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

Cruises can be truly affordable vacations — but that doesn’t mean you won’t run up a significant bill booking your sailing or spending during your trip. It’s also easy to overspend on certain travel costs when you don’t know all the best money-saving tricks.

As someone who cruises often, I don’t have a huge budget to spend on onboard purchases for each sailing, so I’ve had to get wise on how to save money on a cruise.

Some of my strategies are obvious and others I’ve learned from trial and error over more than 80 sailings. I’m happy to share the wealth, so to speak, so you can avoid money mistakes and stretch your travel budget as far as it can possibly go. Here are my 35 top tips on how to save on a cruise.

Book early. Most cruise lines increase prices as ships sell out. Book early to get the lowest prices, as well as the widest choice of cabin types and locations, plus dining times.

Book at the last minute. The corollary advice is that cruise lines will sometimes drop prices or offer value-added promotions on cruises that have too many available cabins left a few months before their scheduled departures. You can find cheap deals on last-minute sailings, especially if you’re not picky about which cabin you get. Start looking about 90 days out for most big-ship sailings.

Related: When is the best time to book a cruise?

Book a shoulder-season sailing. Spring and fall tend to be less busy travel times, and cruises during these shoulder-season months are priced accordingly. Pick a cruise at the beginning or end of the Alaska or Mediterranean season when the weather isn’t as optimal, and you’ll save big over the peak midseason voyages. Sailings departing after Thanksgiving but before Christmas are also less popular and, therefore, cheaper.

Book an inside cabin. The cheapest room on the ship is an inside cabin, so choose one of those rooms if you want to spend less on your next sailing. You’ll get access to the same pools, restaurants, shows and activities as the folks in the balcony cabins; all you’re missing out on is a window and some more floor space. Some people actually prefer inside cabins for amazing sleep in the pitch dark or because they spend all their time out and about on the ship and are never in their room.

Be flexible on dates. Many unpredictable factors combine to make one sailing more expensive than the identical itinerary the week before or after. If you can be flexible on which week you cruise, you can save money by choosing whichever sail date is cheaper.

Book an older ship. Newer ships with their one-of-a-kind attractions and up-to-date everything get all the attention — and can command the highest prices. Seek out older ships to get a better cruise deal. Cruise lines maintain their older ships and often give them massive makeovers to add the latest restaurants and top-deck attractions, so you’ll hardly notice you’re on a 20-year-old ship. But your budget will notice the more affordable rates, leaving money in your pocket to spend on splurges like spa treatments and specialty dining.

Look for sales and promotions. Cruise lines run sales so often that you’re wasting money if you book when there isn’t a deal. Some promotions are all about lower fares, while others save you money with included perks, like free Wi-Fi or a complimentary beverage package. Solo travelers should look out for sales that waive the single supplement, saving you up to 50% of the normal single cabin price. Families should watch out for kids-cruise-free sales or other discounted third- and fourth-guest offers.

How do you find out about your favorite cruise line’s latest sales? Sign up for the brand’s email list or a large online travel agent’s deal alert newsletter, and they’ll send info on promos straight to your inbox.

Check for price drops. If you book a cruise and discover that the price has decreased down the road, your cruise line or travel agent will often be able to issue you a price adjustment. Some passengers have even reported receiving more than one adjustment if the prices fall repeatedly. The key is to make sure you spot the lower prices before the final payment deadline passes. After that, the best a cruise line can usually do for your is to offer a cabin upgrade.

Related: The best cruise booking perks — and which ones are actually free

Leverage your casino play. Cruise lines love casino players because they spend money on board. Once you’ve established yourself as a member of a cruise line’s players club, you might find yourself the recipient of cruise discounts and complimentary casino cruise offers. You can definitely save on a cruise when all you have to pay are taxes and fees.

Be loyal to one cruise line. Sail once with a cruise line, and you’re eligible to join its loyalty program. All members are eligible for select past-passenger cruise fare discounts, but the most loyal members can access free upgrades or even free cruises.

Request your shareholder credit. Cruisers who own 100 shares or more of the big three publicly traded cruise corporations — Carnival Corp., Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings and Royal Caribbean Group — can request onboard credit as a perk of being a shareholder. You can request it via an online form on each cruise line's website; the amount you'll receive, if approved, depends on the type of cruise you book. Credit can only be requested on full-fare voyages, and only one shareholder credit is permitted per stateroom.

Choose a drive-to port. Parking a car for a week is almost guaranteed to be cheaper than airport transfers, flights and a precruise hotel for a family of four. Cruise ships depart from ports all along the U.S. and Canada coastlines; consider choosing a cruise that departs from a port within driving distance of your home to save money on your next cruise.

Use a credit card that gives you perks. Even if your cruise fare isn't dirt cheap, you can still get more value from your vacation dollars when you pay for that vacation at sea with the right card. For example, book with The Platinum Card® from American Express, and its Cruise Privileges Program will get you double Membership Rewards points, onboard credit and cruise line-specific perks. Book a Carnival cruise with the Carnival Rewards™ Mastercard®, and you can earn extra Carnival Rewards points that you can redeem for cruise-related purchases and Loyalty Status stars that will fast track your elite status.

Or, perhaps you can use your cruise final payment to make the minimum spending requirement on a new credit card and get a slew of points or miles you can use for a free trip down the road.

Related: Should you get a cruise line credit card? Here’s a closer look

Bid for an upgrade. Several major cruise lines, like Norwegian Cruise Line and MSC Cruises, offer select guests the option to bid for an upgraded cabin. Bid less than the difference between your cabin cost and the price of the nicer room, and if your bid is approved, you’ll get upgraded onboard digs at a discount.

Use a travel agent. Most travel agents won’t charge you to use their cruise-booking services, but they can help you find the best deal on the best sailing for you, and they might even throw in a free bottle of Champagne or some onboard credit. If nothing else, these knowledgeable advisers can save you from making costly mistakes on the wrong cruise purchases, and that is a value in and of itself.

Book your next cruise on board. Most cruise lines run a future cruise sales desk on board ships. If you put a deposit down on a future cruise while sailing on the current one, you can be eligible for discounts and onboard credit (i.e., free spending money for you).

Related: Mistakes to avoid when booking your cruise

Get first-day discounts. Embarkation day can be chaotic. You’re getting familiar with the ship’s layout, signing up for all the things and likely going to the main dining room for dinner to meet your waiters. You might not even realize that the spa and specialty restaurants are open that evening. To lure passengers through their doors, onboard spas might offer first-day discounts and specialty restaurants might throw in a free bottle of wine.

Book activities and packages in advance. Many cruise lines offer discounts for booking drink packages, Wi-Fi plans and shore excursions online before your cruise. It will save you money on your next cruise if you do some precruise planning instead of being spontaneous once on board.

Go to the spa on port days. Most passengers get off the ship when it’s docked in port, so they prefer to book spa treatments on sea days. (The salon is especially busy on formal nights.) Cruise ship spas will often run specials or discounts to entice passengers to book treatments on port days, saving you money on the pricey massages and body treatments.

Enjoy specialty restaurants at lunch. You can rack up quite the cruise bill dining at specialty restaurants each night of your cruise. To save money, look for extra-charge eateries that are open for lunch. The food is usually just as good, but the menu is smaller, and the prices are reduced from the dinnertime fee.

Look for daily or happy hour drink specials. Your ship’s daily activity schedule (found in a printed newsletter or the cruise line's app) is your guide to saving money. Look for daily drink specials or happy hour deals that will save you money on those tropical drinks that are the hallmark of a Caribbean vacation. Or ask at your favorite onboard bar if they ever run drink deals, and plan your visits around those times.

Book a drink or dinner package. If eating and drinking are how you spend your money on a cruise, you could save by bundling your purchases. Look for all-you-can-drink packages that will save you money if you plan to drink a lot each day or specialty dining packages that offer a discounted total price for booking multiple reservations in advance.

Know when to skip the drink package. If you’re a casual drinker who doesn’t order more than a few drinks a day (including coffee and soda), or you don’t think you can drink enough to break even on the beverage package price every day, you will save more by skipping the package and ordering drinks a la carte, especially if you can utilize happy hour specials or loyalty perks to cut costs.

Also note that NCL’s Unlimited Open Bar package that’s part of its Free at Sea booking promotion is not a truly complimentary perk; you’ll need to pay $28.50 to $32 per person, per day. If you typically don’t spend that much on cruise drinks, you’ll save more by going a la carte.

Related: Are cruise line drink packages worth the price? What to know before you buy

Skip the souvenir glass. Step onto a cruise ship pool deck or atrium on the first day of your cruise, and you’re likely to be approached by a waiter offering you a drink in a souvenir glass. You want the cocktail, but do you really need to bring home a cup shaped like Carnival’s funnel? Say yes to the drink and no to the souvenir glass, and you will save a few bucks on the cost of the drink (not to mention the extra bag fees when you realize you can’t carry all those souvenirs home).

Seek out free alcohol. If you pay attention, you can find several opportunities to get drinks for free on a cruise ship. Many of the onboard art auctions pass out Champagne or sparkling wine to attendees, and sometimes the ship’s shops will offer liquor tastings in an attempt to convince you to buy a bottle. If you’re a suite guest or loyalty member, you might be eligible for free drink vouchers, happy hours or events with comped drinks.

Shop the sales for souvenirs. Cruise line boutiques often run BOGO sales or “everything for $10” hours on items like T-shirts, evening purses and sunglasses. If you’re thinking of purchasing some souvenirs, look for promotional events listed in your daily schedule. If you want to splurge on high-end jewelry or other expensive gifts, wait for those onboard shops to announce specials. These purchases won’t be cheap, but you might be able to save a bit or get an extra bauble thrown in for free.

Check out the seminars. Your cruise ship’s spa or boutiques will often host seminars about wellness practices or understanding gemstones. These events are really marketing ploys to get you to sign up for spa treatments or buy shoe insoles or jewelry. However, they often convince people to attend by giving away spa credit or jewelry in a raffle. If you’ve got nothing better to do on a sea day, you might show up in the hopes of winning something. Spa tours and port shopping lectures also run raffles (plus, you might get a free massage for a minute).

Look for midcruise specials. Cruise ships will discount paid attractions on the fly if they need to drum up more revenue in a certain area or if restaurants are not full. If you keep your schedule flexible, you can jump on midcruise specials, advertised in your daily schedule, and save on specialty dining, arcade games, spa treatments and more.

Evaluate laundry costs. Doing laundry on board is a smart way to avoid checked bag fees by packing light. In some cases, sending a bag of laundry to be washed on board (especially if you take advantage of a midcruise laundry special) can be more economical than paying to check a bag. However, you can save even more if you take advantage of a ship’s self-serve launderette or hand wash small items in your cabin’s bathroom sink. Some top suites come with free or discounted laundry, and top-tier frequent cruisers might also get comped laundry as a loyalty perk, so check the options before packing as part of your savings strategy.

Book your own tours. Cruise lines mark up shore excursions because they have to pay the provider and turn a profit. You can often save money by going to the source and booking a tour directly with a provider. Alternatively, a private tour guide for a group might not always save you money, but you will usually get more value out of a small-group tour that you can customize to your preference.

Skip the tour and explore independently. You don’t need to shell out big bucks for an organized tour in every port. To keep costs down, skip the beach break tour and walk or take a bus or taxi to the beach. Do your own walking tour with a guidebook or app. Go on a hike or take yourself to a cathedral or museum. If you tour independently, you won’t have to pay for a guide or cruise line overhead.

Look for less inclusive beach breaks. Sometimes a cruise line will offer several versions of the same resort day pass or beach break excursion — one that just covers your entrance and another that includes lunch and drinks and water toy use. If you don’t plan to eat or drink that much, or at all, you can save by booking the least expensive version of the tour and just paying for the amenities you use a la carte.

Use local transportation. Taxi rides can add up quickly. Consider using less expensive forms of transportation to explore a city during your port stop. Local buses and subways can be more affordable ways to get around, plus offer a glimpse into local life.

Use Wi-Fi in port. Cruise ship internet access is pricey; you might pay more for a week on board than you do for a month at home! If you don’t have to be connected at all hours, skip the cruise ship Wi-Fi plan and seek out free or cheap Wi-Fi in port. Many port terminals have free Wi-Fi, or you can grab a cup of coffee or a drink at an establishment in town with complimentary Wi-Fi for customers.

Negotiate prices. Know when prices aren’t set in stone and negotiate a lower fee to save on your in-port purchases. You can often barter over the price of crafts, food or souvenirs in open-air markets, or negotiate rates for taxi tours or rides. Always be friendly and polite when haggling, and be prepared to walk if the vendor does not accept your offer.

Bring your own beach gear. Most beaches you’ll visit on a cruise, including the cruise lines’ private islands, will rent you snorkel gear, umbrellas and beach floats, or sell you beach toys. Save money by purchasing and bringing your own snorkel gear, beach shade, inflatable beach toys and floats. The upfront cost might be higher than a single rental, but you can use the gear in multiple ports and on multiple cruises. Look for inflatables or collapsible gear that can pack down small or come in convenient carrying cases.

Don’t eat lunch or dinner in port. I always recommend trying the local cuisine in port, both because it’s a fun way to experience a new culture and to support the local economy. But if you’re on a budget and need to cut costs, skip the meals in port and head back to the ship for meals in the many included eateries on board. Don’t forget to fill up on breakfast, so you can spend more time in port before hunger drives you back to the ship.

If nothing else, avoid the overpriced and often inauthentic waterside tourist restaurants and ask around for where locals eat on the cheap — or skip the lunch and treat yourself to a cheaper gelato or pastry instead.

You don’t have to employ every one of these tips to save money on your next sailing, but keep them in mind to make smart decisions as you plan your next vacation and once you’re on board. It’s always OK to splurge a little on vacation, but you want to make sure you’re not spending unnecessarily. What matters is that you’re getting the biggest benefit from your vacation buck.

#6305. Flexibility: How Flight Attendants Can Be Displaced From Their Schedule With Little Notice

Flight attendants' schedules in the US can change at short notice in several ways, but union contracts set limits on how it happens and what they're paid when it does. This guide will take a closer look at how it all works, when things change at the last minute, and what can happen to a flight attendant's schedule.

In the rest of the world, it's a little bit different, and unions rarely have much input. It's all down to the airlines' operations teams and aviation regulators when it comes to how our schedules can change. Of course, flexibility is key, and things can happen unexpectedly, but that's all part of the fun of being a flight attendant or cabin crew.

When a trip or part of a trip is canceled, crew scheduling can move the affected flight attendant to another trip, put them on reserve/standby, or release them from duty entirely. One older contract, filed with the SEC, pays them for whichever is greater: the original assignment or the new one. Many US airline contracts call this "pay protection." This is a contractual rule that keeps a flight attendant's scheduled pay credit safe when flights change, get canceled, or get delayed through no fault of their own.

If the trip or a leg of the sequence is canceled, union collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) typically guarantee that they still get paid for the original scheduled value or the new assigned trip, whichever is greater. If crew scheduling alters the route or equipment after a disruption, pay protection ensures that they do not lose money if the new assignment ends up paying less than what was originally on the line.

Alaska Airlines' current agreement, for example, can remove a flight attendant from an assignment with pay protection and fly them home as a passenger; this is called deadheading. Under the 2025-2028 Collective Bargaining Agreement between Alaska Airlines and the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, line-holding flight attendants receive 150% pay on top of strong base trip protection when crew scheduling reassigns or reroutes a sequence. If a crew member is assigned to four or more legs over the original sequence, pay is 200%.

Trip displacement occurs when a crew member is involuntarily removed from a scheduled flight pairing or stranded away from their planned itinerary. This could be due to operational needs, regulatory limits, or personnel bumps; it is not a personal absence from duty. It can vary from airline to airline in the US, and union contracts may vary. At carriers without union contracts, such as Delta Air Lines, displaced flight attendants often do not receive automatic pay protection and must choose between sitting on-call availability or taking a lesser payment.

A flight attendant can also be bumped from a trip that they bid for. They can be displaced from trips to make room for training or for new hires' supervised flights, which are called operating experience. A flight attendant can be pulled from a trip so a supervisor, for example, can occupy that position for qualification or observation. In those cases, the displaced flight attendant gets a similar trip or is released from duty for the rest of the trip.

Frontier Airlines' 2019 contract requires at least 24 hours' notice before a flight attendant is displaced, and pays them for the trip they lost. Depending on the contract, crew scheduling may have a specific window (often matching the original trip's footprint) to assign replacement flights. If the airline does not reassign the flight attendant within those rules, the crew member is released with pay.

There is no such thing as 9 to 5 work here.

The one thing that most often catches US flight attendants off guard is the junior assignment, sometimes called junior availability or JA. This is a last-resort scheduling measure where an airline forces the most junior legal flight attendant to work a flight during their scheduled day off or open time because all reserve crews have been exhausted. This prevents cancellations or other disruptions when the reserve pool runs out, and it typically falls on the most junior available flight attendant.

This is used in cases such as major weather disruptions, holiday travel spikes, or high sick-call volume, after all on-call reserve flight attendants have already been assigned. Airlines assign these open trips starting from the absolute bottom of the seniority list at that base and working upward until the flight is covered. However, the new trip cannot violate mandatory rest requirements or maximum duty limits. This will also attract a premium payment, and the airline has to restore any lost days off.

Contracts usually limit how often junior assignments can happen. PSA Airlines' contract caps it at three days a month and bars assignments that are more than 24 hours in advance, while Silver Airways' contract limits it to twice a month. They also usually pay at a premium rate of 150% at Silver Airways and PSA Airlines, and 2.5 times the trip rate under Alaska Airlines' 2025–2028 contract. Silver Airways closed down in June 2025.

At some airlines, flight attendants who are already on duty at the airport, such as those arriving, checking in, or waiting in between flights, can be drafted onto another flight when time is critical, or the reserve pool is empty. Therefore, their entire schedule can change if a new trip is added or removed. Usually, crew scheduling tries not to disrupt the schedule too much and swaps them with a trip with similar timing, but of course, this is not always possible.

Flight attendants on reserve or standby are usually more junior crew with low seniority, are on call, and can be given trips with little notice. Many US-based crew start out on reserve and may do so for the first few years. At American Airlines, for example, flight attendants are on reserve for the first year and then move to one month on reserve, one month off reserve until year five, when it moves to one month on reserve and three months off according to their APFA contract.

At Delta Air Lines, junior flight attendants bid on a line and do not have to complete a full month on reserve. Instead, they have six 'A' days a month, where they are on call. If a Delta flight attendant's trip is canceled or removed, they only keep their pay if they convert to availability. Delta's order of assignment places displaced lineholders on availability ahead of A-Day reserves, and management holds broader discretion to modify trips during irregular operations.

United Airlines has reportedly terminated several senior flight attendants following an internal investigation into trip trading.

Airlines in the rest of the world rarely have union agreements, and schedules are set by the operations or crew scheduling department. Rosters are scheduled four to six weeks in advance in accordance with duty time regulations, so you know what your trips will be and your days off, if all goes to plan. Long-haul rosters don't change much, but short-haul rosters are more likely to change. There is no bidding for trips, although crew can sometimes request one or two trips a month; it is rare that they are given. Part-time work is very rare.

In addition, every crew member has some standby days, usually three or four per month, when you are on call to cover a trip at short notice because a flight attendant calls in sick or misses a trip. These are periods of around six to eight hours, and you would hope to be called at the beginning, not the end, of the shift. This can be at base, at the airport, or home standby; it varies by airline. Standby isn't just given to junior cabin crew; everyone has to do it, although seniority remains important throughout your career.

Some airlines also have available days that are filled 12 to 24 hours in advance; you could get a trip, standby duty, or be stood down, and then it becomes a day off. If a change is made to your schedule by operations, it shows up on your roster, and that's it; you do the trip. There is no payment protection pay, sit pay, or any extra payments for schedule changes. Rosters are more likely to change at the last minute due to being called out on standby duty or if a flight is delayed and doesn't allow enough rest, but it is more likely on a short-haul or mixed-fleet roster.

Every contract is different, so the rules, limits, and premium pay vary widely by airline and by where you are working. Large international airlines in Europe and the UK are not heavily unionized like those in the US, and they have no influence on your schedule or what you actually earn; that is up to the airline itself. In the Middle East, there are no unions.

The contracts noted here are for comparison to show how contracts have changed in recent years and are for reference only; not all the airlines still exist, and some may have merged. American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and Southwest Airlines contracts have all changed significantly in recent years, affecting how flight attendants are scheduled and paid. Delta's flight attendants are not unionized, so their scheduling rules come from company policy rather than a contract.

Terminology used by airlines can also be different. In the UK, Europe, and the Middle East, instead of reserve, we have standby, and instead of operating experience for junior flight attendants, we have supernumerary flights. We do not have "junior assignment," "junior availability," "drafting," "reassignment," and "displacement," which can all mean slightly different things depending on the contract. Although it's the same job with the same rules, the terminology, scheduling system, and pay are very different.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6304. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card is a solid option for travelers who want to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

And with two welcome offers available, prospective cardholders have a choice to make.

The standard VentureOne currently offers 20,000 bonus miles, earned after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Meanwhile, the Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card - Miles Boost has a new offer: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The other key difference is the introductory APR. The standard VentureOne offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers (followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74%; a balance transfer fee applies). The Miles Boost version, on the other hand, doesn't offer an introductory 0% APR period.

Here's a closer look at both offers and how to decide which one makes the most sense for you.

There are currently two welcome offers available on the VentureOne:

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, the standard VentureOne Rewards offer is worth $370, while the VentureOne Rewards - Miles Boost offer is worth $740.

That's an additional $370 in potential value with the Miles Boost offer, provided you can meet the higher spending requirement and maximize your miles through Capital One's transfer partners.

Alternatively, you can redeem Capital One miles at a fixed rate of 1 cent apiece to cover eligible travel purchases. That would make the standard 20,000-mile offer worth $200 and the 40,000-mile Miles Boost offer worth $400.

Of course, the larger welcome bonus isn't the only factor worth considering. Here's how to decide which version of the VentureOne is right for you.

Related: The easy route: How to redeem Capital One miles at a fixed value

The biggest difference between the two VentureOne offers comes down to whether you value a larger welcome bonus or an introductory APR period.

If your goal is to maximize travel rewards and you can comfortably meet the $1,000 spending requirement, the VentureOne - Miles Boost is likely the better choice. You'll earn twice as many bonus miles as the standard VentureOne after meeting the higher spending requirement.

However, this version doesn't offer an introductory 0% APR period, making it a better fit for those who plan to pay their balance in full each month — something I'd recommend regardless of which card you choose.

On the other hand, the standard VentureOne Rewards may make more sense if you're planning a large purchase and want extra time to pay it off. It offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers, followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74% (a balance transfer fee applies). You'll earn fewer bonus miles, but you'll just need to spend just $500 to earn the welcome bonus.

Ultimately, both versions offer the same ongoing rewards and benefits, so the right choice depends on your financial priorities.

Related: This month's best credit card welcome bonuses

Regardless of which welcome offer you choose, both versions of the VentureOne have the same ongoing rewards structure.

That means if you meet the minimum spending requirement entirely through purchases earning the base rate, you'll earn at least 20,625 miles with the standard VentureOne or 41,250 miles with the VentureOne - Miles Boost, including the respective welcome bonuses.

One of the VentureOne's biggest selling points is that it provides access to Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel transfer partners without an annual fee.

Both versions of the card also have no foreign transaction fees, making them useful options for international travel.

Related: Capital One miles: How to earn, redeem and transfer rewards

Before applying for either VentureOne offer, you'll want to understand Capital One's application restrictions.

Capital One has a 48-month welcome bonus restriction across its Venture card family. According to the issuer's current terms, you aren't eligible for a new VentureOne bonus if you've received a new cardmember bonus on the VentureOne, Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card within the past 48 months.

Capital One may also consider other factors when reviewing your application, so approval isn't guaranteed even if you meet the bonus eligibility requirements.

Be sure to review the terms of the specific offer you're considering before applying.

Related: The ultimate guide to credit card application restrictions

The two versions of the VentureOne give prospective cardholders a choice between earning more miles upfront and taking advantage of an introductory APR period.

For travelers who can comfortably meet the $1,000 spending requirement and don't need an introductory APR offer, the new VentureOne - Miles Boost offer is the more rewarding option. Its 40,000-mile bonus is worth $740 at TPG's valuations, twice the value of the standard offer.

However, the standard VentureOne may be a better fit if you want an introductory 0% APR period on purchases and balance transfers (for 15 months, then 18.74%-28.74% variable APR; a balance transfer fee applies) or prefer a lower spending requirement.

Whichever offer you choose, you'll get the same ongoing earning rates, redemption options and card benefits without paying an annual fee.

#6301. Private Pilot Disputes Trump’s Claim That He Used Non-US ATC To Fly In US Airspace Before Office

President Trump has revived a claim that his private pilot previously relied on another country's air traffic control (ATC) system while flying in the US, prompting a public rebuttal from a private pilot. Speaking during a White House press conference on Friday, Trump criticized America's aviation infrastructure while discussing recent disruptions affecting the country's airspace, according to National Public Radio (NPR).

The comments came one week after a nationwide FAA ground stop disrupted thousands of flights and just days after the administration requested another $50.1 billion for aviation modernization. However, Trump's account of using foreign controllers has raised questions about whether he meant air traffic control or the navigation technology installed aboard his aircraft.

According to the Daily Beast, Trump made the remarks during a "bonkers appearance" at a White House press conference addressing recent disruptions involving aviation, banking and communications networks. Asked about the incidents, the president maintained that they were unrelated, before discussing his personal experiences with private aviation.

Trump described US ATC infrastructure as "ancient", and said that his pilot had used foreign air traffic control before he entered office.

“It's ancient! In fact, you know, before I was here, I had a plane. I had a very nice life. And my pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country. This was years ago, before I was in office. I don't want to say the country, but he found one country better than ours.”

The assertion prompted a response from journalist Brian Karem, who identified himself as a private pilot. In a post on X, Karem disputed the suggestion that pilots operating in US airspace could bypass domestic controllers by seeking assistance from another country. His objection centered on the distinction between the authorities controlling airspace and the equipment pilots use to navigate.

"You cannot call up ATC in Europe and say, 'Hey give me a hand. I'm flying over US airspace.'"

Trump's remarks were not entirely new. During the National Prayer Breakfast in February last year, he similarly claimed to use equipment or services from another country when landing his private aircraft in New York, according to Anadolu Ajansı. The comments attracted scrutiny from aviation experts at the time, Forbes reported.

President Trump likely confused air traffic control systems with onboard navigation technology, according to Forbes. Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox explained that pilots operating under ATC supervision must comply with the applicable rules of that country, regardless of their navigation equipment's country of origin.

Air traffic control and aircraft navigation perform very different functions. Controllers issue clearances, instructions and traffic information, while onboard navigation systems help pilots determine their position and follow flight plans. An aircraft operating under instrument flight rules in controlled US airspace cannot simply select a foreign ATC provider. The differences are summarized below:

Provides clearances, traffic separation and instructions

Provides satellite-based positioning and navigation

Calculates and manages the aircraft's flight path

Tracks aircraft position and movement using onboard sensors

Provide route, waypoint and procedure information

Provide navigation, communication or flight management capabilities

A plausible explanation is that Trump's aircraft used internationally manufactured avionics, navigation databases, or satellite-based positioning technology. As the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Aeronautical Information Manual explains, these technologies provide navigation guidance but do not replace ATC services. Without confirmation from Trump's former pilots, the precise technology he was describing remains unknown.

The White House wants Congress to approve $30.1 billion for aviation upgrades as nationwide flight disruptions renew safety concerns.

The dispute comes amid growing pressure to modernize the FAA's aging infrastructure. On November 13, a telecommunications failure triggered a nationwide ground stop lasting nearly five hours. According to the FAA's subsequent investigation, excessive network traffic destabilized legacy equipment, affecting communications and radar feeds at 17 of the country's 22 enroute control centers. Approximately 12,500 flights were canceled that day, and hundreds more over the days that followed.

On November 17, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, and Budget Director Russell Vought formally requested $50.1 billion from Congress. The proposal follows $12.5 billion approved in July 2025 and would finance technology upgrades, replacement facilities, and airport infrastructure. The administration's request is broken down as follows:

Five consolidated enroute control centers

Construction and upgrades of up to 140 ATC towers

The FAA aims to complete the first phase of its Brand New Air Traffic Control System by December 2028. However, in September, the Government Accountability Office warned that incomplete cost estimates and scheduling would undermine progress. Although the need for modernization is well documented, it does not establish that foreign controllers previously managed Trump's flights within US airspace. The president's renewed remarks therefore leave the original technical question unresolved.

#6300. American Grows Maintenance Footprint in Miami

A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

The airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

“Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”

American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.
