#6299. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6297. Why The Flying Wing Never Became A Commercial Airliner

Jack Northrop envisioned a sleek, tailless future when he sent the YB-49 aloft on October 21, 1947, stretching a 172-foot (52.4 meters) wing across the desert sky without a conventional fuselage or vertical stabilizer. Promising lower drag and greater efficiency than traditional layouts, the experimental jet bomber nevertheless battled stability challenges before the second prototype crashed on June 5, 1948, killing all five crew members aboard and leading to the program winding down between 1949 and 1950.

Despite the allure of an all-wing silhouette, commercial aviation stuck with cylindrical fuselages and tailed configurations that offered predictable handling, straightforward cabin pressurization, and familiar airport compatibility. Now that digital flight controls and blended-wing concepts are bringing tailless aerodynamics back into the spotlight, what technical, operational, and commercial hurdles still stand between a flying wing concept and a viable passenger airliner?

Converted from two piston-engined YB-35 airframes, the YB-49 stretched to a 172-foot (52.4-meter) wingspan and measured 53 feet, 1 inch (16.2 meters) in length, trading propeller drives for eight Allison J35 turbojets buried inside the wing, according to The Little Aviation Museum. Removing a conventional fuselage and tail assembly allowed almost the entire planform to contribute to lift with reduced parasite drag, helping the prototype reach roughly 493 mph (793 km/h). At the same time, early turbojet fuel burn and internal volume tradeoffs tempered its range and payload flexibility relative to piston-powered designs.

Flying without a tall vertical tail meant the YB-49 had less natural stability in yaw and had delicate pitch and roll-yaw coupling, including dutch roll, during turbulent air, maneuvers, and simulated bombing runs. As noted by MiGFlug, four small vertical fins were fitted to aid directional damping, though in the late 1940s crews relied on mechanical linkages and human coordination rather than high-speed digital flight control computers to manage continuous stability corrections.

After its maiden flight on October 21, 1947, the program flew only two converted airframes before the second prototype crashed on June 5, 1948, claiming the lives of all five crew members on board. Production orders were canceled in 1949 as Air Force leadership shifted toward competing bomber programs, and formal flight testing concluded in March 1950 before the surviving airframes were scrapped.

For an aerodynamically unstable tailless wing to become a dependable aircraft and actually work, it requires replacing purely mechanical linkages with high-speed digital fly-by-wire flight-control computers. Motion sensors can continuously measure aircraft attitude and rate changes, feeding real-time data to flight computers that command rapid, micro-adjusted deflections across trailing-edge control surfaces. That closed-loop automation damps pitch, yaw, and dutch roll oscillations far faster and more consistently than manual pilot inputs alone could achieve in earlier eras.

Digital flight control design made the Northrop B-2 Spirit possible by allowing a pure flying wing to achieve low-observable radar signatures without needing a conventional vertical tail. Instead of using a large fin that would compromise stealth, the B-2 uses computer-coordinated elevons and split drag rudders to generate controlled yawing moments and maintain crisp handling across varying weights and flight regimes. Computing redundancy and sensor voting became foundational to keeping a naturally neutral or unstable wing profile predictable from takeoff through landing.

Decades later, the Northrop B-21 Raider extends that digital control lineage into a modern low-observable bomber program built on newer avionics and computing architectures. The B-2 and B-21 demonstrate that computerized flight controls conquered the core stability and control challenges of tailless military aircraft, but solving stability in a combat airframe did not automatically translate into an airline cabin, and how to make it a reality.

Flying wing bombers nearly entered service during WWII and soon after, however, they would become reality until the B-2 in the 1990s.

The pure flying wing has not necessarily been revived, but JetZero is advancing the Z4 as a blended wing body (BWB) concept designed to carry roughly 230 to 250 passengers by smoothly merging a wide, lifting center body into outer wings. The program has gained traction through a $235 million US Air Force award supporting full-scale demonstrator development alongside plans to establish manufacturing operations in North Carolina. With a full-scale demonstrator targeted to fly in late 2027, the roadmap aims for commercial entry into service in the early 2030s if technical and regulatory hurdles are cleared on schedule.

Commercial interest in the Z4 is very real, and carriers such as Japan Airlines and United Airlines have made agreements to support the development of the aircraft. For airlines evaluating next-generation single-aisle and midsize replacements, a BWB promises lower drag and reduced fuel burn per seat compared with conventional tube-and-wing layouts. Making those conditional fleet commitments become firm deliveries, however, depends on proving that the airframe can meet strict safety, manufacturing, and operational standards at scale.

Propulsion integration sits near the center of that verification effort, including a November 2026 report from Leeham News noting that the FAA is funding a study into top-mounted engine airflow for JetZero's design. Placing engines above the aft airframe can help shield noise, but maintaining clean airflow and stable engine operation across flight conditions remains a critical engineering focus ahead of commercial certification.

A cylindrical tube naturally resists internal cabin pressure by distributing hoop stress evenly around a circular cross-section, whereas a wide, flattened wing-body hull faces far higher bending and pressure-loading demands. A non-cylindrical cabin shell tends to bow outward when pressurized at cruise altitude, so to compensate, designers need to add structural reinforcement, internal bulkheads, or load-bearing frames that add mass and complexity.

Emergency evacuation rules further add to cabin design complexity, particularly the regulatory requirement to evacuate a full aircraft within 90 seconds using half of the available exits, covered in Simple Flying analysis. Unlike a narrow single- or twin-aisle tube where passengers move linearly toward well-marked doors, a wide blended-wing cabin needs carefully engineered pathways, clear signage, and balanced exit placement, so travelers seated deep inside the layout can reach exits without bottlenecks. Cabin tiering across premium and economy zones also needs to align with aisle geometry and exit capacity rather than treating interior floor space as an open hall.

On the ground, widebody wingspans around 213 feet (65 meters) must fit within existing terminal gate envelopes, taxiway clearances, and apron stand markings without forcing costly airport rebuilds. Even when a wide airframe clears wingspan limits at a standard widebody gate, its broader center section and altered fuselage contour can complicate jetbridge docking reach, de-icing access, and ground support vehicle positioning. Smooth ramp operations really depend on proving that turnaround tasks load and unload cleanly alongside conventional airliners.

Several companies, including Airbus, JetZero, and Boeing, are actively developing prototypes.

Within a wide, open cabin, the sensory rhythm of a flight changes compared with walking down a narrow, low-ceilinged aisle. Designers can shape the atmosphere through layered ambient lighting, tactile fabrics, and warmer material palettes that soften the industrial feel of long-haul travel and create distinct zones for rest, work, or socializing. When the interior feels less like a corridor and more like a curated living space, passenger stress often eases.

Sightlines and motion perception play a major role in whether that spaciousness feels inviting or disorienting. Travelers seated further outboard from the centerline can notice more pronounced vertical movement when the aircraft banks or hits chop, making smooth cabin damping and calm visual anchors especially valuable. At the same time, passengers placed in central rows away from outer walls miss natural views of the horizon, requiring thoughtful lighting cues or digital view panels to keep the cabin feeling open and grounded.

For airlines, an unconventional cabin layout offers a rare canvas for brand differentiation in a crowded market. Carriers can build an identity around quiet acoustics, signature color schemes, and tailored service rituals that signal innovation without feeling gimmicky. If passengers connect emotionally with the warmth and poise of the space, the cabin itself becomes part of the airline's promise, not something that needs to be explained to customers.

Pure flying wings remained absent from passenger service because winning aerodynamic efficiency on paper is only half the battle when weighed against structural pressure loads, emergency evacuation rules, airport compatibility, and airline economics. Digital flight controls solved the stability hurdles that haunted the YB-49 and paved the way for stealth bombers, but turning a wide, wing-shaped cabin into a profitable, certified airliner is no easy task.

Any manufacturer brave enough to try and make something like this has to solve practical constraints that circular fuselages and conventional tails handle with far less friction. Whether a blended wing body can actually fill that divide comes down to proving real-world reliability, passenger acceptance, and unit economics without turning every airport gate or cabin layout into a costly exception.

The next major checkpoints arrive with full-scale demonstrator flight testing targeted for late 2027 and potential commercial entry into service in the early 2030s. If JetZero or other ventures like Nautilus can validate aerodynamic performance, propulsion integration, and regulatory certification along that timeline, blended-wing designs could finally move from aviation curiosity to active airline fleets.

#6295. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#6294. Aviation Gems: The Airbus A380 Is The Largest, But The Boeing 747-8 Actually Holds 2 Worldwide Titles

Markus Mainka | Shutterstock, Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying

The introduction of the Airbus A380 historically dethroned Boeing as the reigning champion of big jet builders. However, that statement comes with a couple of caveats. It is true that the A380 beats the classic Boeing 747 in wingspan, height, weight, and passenger capacity, but the long-reigning 'queen of the skies' was not made irrelevant overnight.

Boeing responded not with a brand-new double-decker, but by stretching its classic 747 design into the 747-8 Intercontinental. With two full passenger decks running from nose to tail, the European superjumbo dwarfed every competitor in wingspan, tail height, weight, and seating capacity. On paper, it looked as though Airbus had swept every major size and performance record in commercial flying.

However, while the Boeing jet carried fewer passengers and weighed hundreds of thousands of pounds less, it quietly held onto two major world records that the massive A380 could never take away. First, by extending the fuselage, Boeing made the 747-8 the longest airliner in service, measuring 250 feet 2 inches (76.25 meters) from nose to tail.

This made it over 11 feet longer than the A380. Second, thanks to its sharply swept wings and modern engines, the 747-8 cruises at Mach 0.855 (about 567 mph), edging out the A380’s Mach 0.85 pace to claim the title of the fastest commercial jetliner flying today.

For one pragmatic reason, airport gates, Boeing decided to make the 747-8 longer rather than wider. Because the A380 has such an enormous wingspan, major airports had to widen taxiways and build special two-story boarding bridges just to handle it. Boeing kept the 747-8’s wingspan narrower at 224 feet 5 inches, allowing it to pull into standard international gates with minimal airport upgrades.

Boeing extended the earlier 747-400 body by 18.3 feet (5.6 meters) to create the 747-8, the longest aircraft in the sky. Two extra fuselage sections were added by engineers, one in front of and one behind the wings, increasing the overall length to 250 feet 2 inches (76.25 meters).

The 747-8 surpassed the Airbus A380 by about 11.5 feet (3.5 meters) in terms of its additional length, surpassing the previous record set by the 75.36-meter Airbus A340-600. While a four-engine Boeing remained expensive to fly, the 747-8's gate compatibility still gave airlines a practical edge over the A380.

Because the superjumbo required costly terminal upgrades and triggered higher size-based airport fees, its route map was limited to a small group of mega-hubs. By staying within standard widebody gate limits and weighing far less, the 747-8 carried over 400 passengers into a wider range of international airports with slightly lower ground costs.

Boeing’s second trump card over the Airbus colossus comes down to its cruising speed world title. Rated at Mach 0.855, or roughly 567 mph at 35,000 feet, the 747-8 is the fastest commercial airliner flying today, edging out the Airbus A380, A350, and Boeing 787 at Mach 0.85, as well as the 777 at Mach 0.84.

While a speed advantage of under 1% only trims a few minutes off a long flight, it gives pilots helpful schedule padding against headwinds and arrival delays. That speed advantage comes straight from a 1960s design decision. When Boeing engineers first shaped the 747, they expected supersonic jets like Concorde to take over passenger travel.

As such, they angled the 747's wings sharply backward to help it cruise faster and keep up with high-speed air traffic. Four General Electric GEnx engines provide the power needed to take full advantage of that high-speed wing. Adapted from the Boeing 787 Dreamliner program, these modern engines produce strong thrust while burning less fuel than older 747 powerplants.

While straight wings work best at lower speeds, swept-back wings slice through high-altitude air with far less wind resistance, a shape Boeing kept on the 747-8 alongside modern, fuel-saving raked wingtips. Paired with the wing, the powerplants allow the 747-8 to cruise comfortably at Mach 0.855 without hitting the drag penalties that slow down wider, less aggressively swept airliners.

How carriers around the world are filling the jumbo-sized void left by an icon of aviation.

Stretching a classic fuselage to over 250 feet in length created unexpected engineering headaches during early test flights. When pilots pushed the prototype 747-8 to high speeds, the longer body and redesigned wings experienced troublesome vibrations along the wingtips. Fixing that flexing forced Boeing to reinforce internal structures and rewrite flight-control software.

This pushed deliveries more than two years behind schedule and added over $2 billion in program costs. Once flight-test results were in, fuel economy turned out to be an even greater problem. The promised fuel-burn targets were not met by the new GEnx engines by 2.7%. That seemingly small miss wiped out the narrow cost advantage Boeing needed to convince airlines to buy a 747 instead of twinjets like the 777.

The tension exploded in September 2011, when launch customer Cargolux abruptly walked out of delivery ceremonies and refused to accept its first two jets until Boeing and General Electric offered financial discounts. Watching from the sidelines, passenger airlines grew wary of four-engine fuel and maintenance bills, choosing twinjets or the A380 instead and leaving the passenger 747-8 with very few orders.

The compromise on the factory floor that stopped the 747's 21st Century evolution.

The two biggest passenger flagships in the world have different design philosophies, which can be seen by comparing them side by side. Airbus's A380 can accommodate about 525 seats in conventional layouts thanks to its enormous maximum takeoff weight of 1,268,000 lb (575,155 kg) and two full passenger decks.

The Boeing 747-8, on the other hand, trades raw capacity for cheaper airport fees and easier ground logistics throughout a 410-seat cabin by capping its takeoff weight at 987,000 lb (447,700 kg). Depending on how their wings fit actual airport gates, airlines use the two aircraft in different ways.

Lufthansa, the only carrier flying both types in significant numbers, keeps all 17 of its 747-8s in Frankfurt for routes to cities like Newark, Tokyo, and Johannesburg, where the jet slips into standard gates without special infrastructure. Meanwhile, Lufthansa flies its eight A380s out of Munich to massive hubs like Los Angeles and Delhi, where airports have widened taxiways and dual-level jet bridges built for the superjumbo's wider wingspan.

The 747-8’s slight speed edge also shapes daily flight planning across winter jet streams. Cruising at Mach 0.855 allows dispatchers to trim a few valuable minutes off twelve-hour westbound flights compared to the A380, helping protect passenger connections when departures face ground delays. However, even that operational flexibility could not shield the four-engine jet from brutal economic headwinds whenever cabins flew with empty seats.

The contest between titans of aerospace to be the widebody king of tomorrow.

In order to build the longest airliner in history, a challenging engineering conundrum had to be resolved: how to extend length without increasing debilitating weight? In response, Boeing developed aluminum-lithium skin panels that stiffened the stretched fuselage against repeated cabin pressurization while reducing metal density by 10%.

Across the Atlantic, Airbus used GLARE, a composite laminate of glass and aluminum fibers that stops minuscule cracks throughout its massive double-deck hull, to address weight and durability on the A380. Equally different priorities are reflected in their wing designs.

In order to reduce drag during long-haul cruise, Boeing replaced the upright winglets of the 747-400 with sweeping composite raked wingtips. By contrast, Airbus fitted the A380 with small vertical wingtip fences, leaning on an enormous 9,100-square-foot wing area to lift up to 575 tons into the sky.

To protect those long wings in flight, Boeing paired traditional mechanical cables with new computer-controlled actuators on the outer wing surfaces. During turbulence, the system automatically deploys wing spoilers to absorb bending forces, and at high cruising speeds it locks outer control surfaces in place to stop the wing vibrations seen in early testing.

Both quadjets are massive and serve several high-capacity routes.

For both aircraft manufacturers, producing the largest aircraft in commercial history came at an incredible financial cost. Before completing more than 50 years of 747 manufacturing in January 2023 and delivering its last cargo to Atlas Air after producing 155 of the stretched aircraft, Boeing had to endure nearly $4.2 billion in accounting losses on the 747-8.

As airlines switched from four-engine behemoths to fuel-efficient twinjets, Airbus suffered an even worse blow after investing more than $30 billion in the A380 and closing its manufacturing line in December 2021 after just 251 deliveries. With both assembly lines closed, the 747-8 stands alone as the fastest and longest commercial airliner flying today, marking the final peak of four-engine design.

Still, its length record has an expiration date. Stretching 251 feet 9 inches (76.7 meters), about 19 inches longer than the 747-8, Boeing’s upcoming twin-engine 777-9 packs massive GE9X engines and folding wingtips to carry over 400 passengers at a fraction of the fuel cost.

Rove has grown quickly since launching in 2025, expanding to 22 airline and hotel transfer partners. Now, just in time for the holiday shopping season, Rove has launched personalized shopping offers that let members earn up to 25 Rove miles per dollar on select purchases. The program has also expanded its in-store shopping offers.

Online shopping portals and card-linked merchant offers are some of the best ways to earn additional rewards on top of what you earn from your credit card. TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Rove miles at 2.05 cents apiece, so earning 25 Rove miles per dollar could yield rewards of up to 51.25 cents per dollar spent.

Here's what you should know about Rove's new offerings.

Not a Rove member yet? The program is free to join, and you can score 1,500 bonus miles when you sign up through TPG's link.

Rove members already know they can navigate to the shopping tab on the Rove website or app and see featured offers or search for a specific merchant.

Now, Rove members who link and connect an eligible payment card can access personalized offers in the For You section of Rove's website and app.

When a personalized offer has a higher earning rate than Rove's standard offer, you'll see both rates displayed. Since these offers are personalized, the available merchants and earning rates may vary by member. Plus, a Rove spokesperson told TPG that Rove refreshes its offers each week, so you may see new or different offers the next time you check.

You'll need to activate each offer before making a qualifying purchase. Click the plus button to activate, and then check the circle that replaces the plus after activation to see how long you have to use the offer.

Be sure to review each offer's terms before purchasing, including where the offer is valid, when it expires and whether any spending limits or purchase exclusions apply.

By reviewing the Hyatt House and Hyatt Studios offer I enrolled in, I found it is only valid for stays within the U.S. This is too bad, as I was excited to use it for an upcoming Hyatt House stay in Canada until I read its terms.

Finally, it's worth noting that neither TPG's Lyndsey Matthews nor I saw any offers in our For You sections for 25 miles per dollar spent. Instead, 15 miles per dollar spent on a new Sam's Club membership purchase is the best offer either of us found in our accounts.

Related: Why the holiday season is the best time to start earning points and miles

Rove initially introduced in-store card-linked offers in August. It now says members can earn miles on qualifying purchases at hundreds of participating physical retailers.

To earn Rove miles on an in-store purchase, link an eligible card to Rove and review the merchant's offer before making a purchase. Activate the offer first if required, then use your linked card to make a qualifying purchase. Rove says transactions are automatically tracked after the charge clears and that miles typically post within seven days.

Rove's personalized offers could be a lucrative way to earn transferable rewards on purchases you already planned to make, especially when targeted rates reach 25 miles per dollar.

However, offers and earning rates will vary by member, so check the For You section and review the activation and purchase requirements before shopping. You should also compare Rove's rate with other shopping portals and check for card-linked merchant offers you may be able to stack with your purchase.

#6291. Here's How Much The 787 Dreamliner Heavily Influenced Boeing's 747-8 Development

Feri_Davat & InsectWorld | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

When Boeing launched the 747-8 in November 2005, it presented the airplane as a stretched, re-winged, and re-engined update of the 747-400 that would use technology borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner. The Dreamliner program had been launched only a year earlier, and its work on lightweight composites, efficient engines, and electronically managed systems gave Boeing a supply of proven solutions at the moment the aging jumbo needed them.

Rather than commissioning an all-new quadjet for a limited market, Boeing chose to graft selected Dreamliner innovations onto a familiar airframe, which kept development costs manageable and preserved the operating familiarity that long-time 747 customers valued. The resulting aircraft differs from its predecessor in several visible ways, yet it remains a 747 in its structure and in the way it is flown, so a fair assessment of the Dreamliner’s influence requires examining each major system in turn. That review shows a program that borrowed boldly where performance was at stake and conservatively wherever certification, cost, or pilot familiarity argued for restraint.

The most substantial transfer from the 787 program came through the powerplants. The 747-8 uses four General Electric GEnx-2B67 engines, a smaller-diameter relative of the GEnx developed for the Dreamliner. The design emphasizes a high bypass ratio, sending most of the air around the core to generate thrust more efficiently than the lower-bypass engines of earlier generations.

Engineers modified the design so that each engine could supply bleed air, the compressed air tapped from the engine to run onboard systems, because the 747 still depends on a conventional pneumatic architecture that the 787 largely abandoned in favor of electrical power. Each engine generates 66,500 pounds (30,164 kg) of thrust and carries a 105-inch (267 cm) composite fan, a material choice that cuts weight relative to metallic blades.

Sawtooth-shaped edges called chevrons line the rear of the engine housing, borrowing a noise-reduction device from the 787 that encourages exhaust and bypass air to blend more gradually. Noise also carries financial weight, since many airports levy charges tied to certified noise levels, and Boeing has said the 747-8 produces a considerably smaller noise footprint than the 747-400.

Sharing a design lineage with the 787 engine allowed Boeing and GE to spread development effort across two programs rather than funding a bespoke powerplant for a model expected to sell in modest numbers. Unlike the Dreamliner, which Boeing offers with a choice between GE and Rolls-Royce engines, the 747-8 is offered only with the GEnx-2B, which spared Boeing the cost of certifying a second powerplant for a modest order book. For operators, the engine change translated into lower fuel burn and emissions per seat than the 747-400, which formed the core of the airplane’s commercial pitch to airlines and cargo carriers.

Boeing designed a new wing for the 747-8 with fresh airfoil shapes intended to improve aerodynamic efficiency at cruise. Designing a wing for a derivative airplane also imposes constraints that a clean-sheet program avoids, because the new surface had to mate with the existing fuselage architecture, which limited how far the planform could depart from the 747-400’s.

At the tips, the upright winglets of the 747-400 gave way to raked wingtips, the same approach used on the 777 and the 787. Sweeping the tip aft reduces drag generated by wingtip vortices while adding less weight than a taller vertical surface would. The configuration debuted on the 767-400ER, which means the 747-8 inherited it from a lineage broader than the Dreamliner alone.

Boeing attributes the 747-8’s higher cruising speed relative to the 747-400 to the combined effect of the wing, wingtips, and engines. The gain matters to passenger carriers flying long routes, where minutes accumulate into meaningful time savings. The aerodynamic gains in cruise efficiency also translate directly into range or payload, which matters especially for the freighter, where operators trade fuel against cargo on long sectors.

The larger wing extends the span to roughly 224 feet (68.27 meters), compared with about 211 feet (64.31 meters) on the 747-400, a growth that supports the airplane’s higher maximum takeoff weight. Aerodynamic refinement of this kind typically yields incremental gains, yet on an airplane that burns many tons of fuel on every long flight, even small improvements compound into sizable savings over a fleet’s life.

Discover the surprising design differences between the engines of the Boeing 747-8 and 787 Dreamliner, and how they impact performance.

The 747-8 also adopted elements of the 787’s fly-by-wire philosophy, in which pilot inputs travel as electrical signals to flight control computers rather than moving surfaces through mechanical cables and pulleys. Electronic signaling reduces weight, since cable runs and associated hardware can be shortened, and it allows computers to modulate surface movements for smoother handling and greater structural efficiency.

The shift follows a broader pattern within the company, since the 777 was Boeing’s first fly-by-wire airliner and the 787 extended that approach more thoroughly. Boeing applied the technology selectively because it wanted qualified pilots on the 747-400 to move to the new model easily. The flight deck therefore keeps a layout and control feel close to its predecessor’s.

Training pilots on an unfamiliar type requires simulator time, instructor capacity, and revenue flying hours that airlines would rather devote to scheduled service, so commonality functions as a quiet but substantial financial benefit for operators already flying the 747-400, whose crews can serve both types. The Dreamliner, by contrast, was free to adopt an entirely new flight deck, a freedom the 747-8 deliberately did not exercise.

The passenger version of the 747-8 received an interior inspired by the Dreamliner’s. Curved, upswept ceiling panels give the cabin a more spacious feel, and LED lighting that runs the length of the cabin can shift color to suggest different times of day. Airlines adopt such lighting and ceiling cues largely because they believe the surroundings can ease fatigue on long sectors, though the benefit is difficult to measure objectively. Windows are larger than those on the 747-400, which improves natural light and passenger views, although they remain smaller than the Dreamliner’s distinctive dimmable windows.

The most visible change for many travelers is the staircase to the upper deck. The classic 747’s narrow spiral staircase has been replaced by a wide, curved staircase that is easier to use and gives the entry area a more open, premium character. The interior upgrades arrived alongside an 18-foot-4-inch (5.5 meters) fuselage stretch, which lets Boeing quote a typical three-class capacity of 467 passengers. The stretch also lengthened the upper deck, giving airlines additional space for premium seating.

Modern, streamlined and elegant, the new cabin architecture could change the passenger experience forever.

Despite the heavy borrowing, the 747-8 does not share the Dreamliner’s defining structural feature. The 787 builds its fuselage from carbon fiber composites, whereas the 747-8 remains an aluminum airframe, consistent with the metallic construction of every earlier 747. The decision carries consequences that passengers can feel. Because composite structures resist corrosion and fatigue better than aluminum, the Dreamliner can maintain a lower cabin altitude and higher humidity than conventional metal airplanes, benefits the 747-8 does not offer.

Retaining aluminum made commercial sense. A composite fuselage would have required a new manufacturing process, new tooling, and a fresh certification effort for a program that was never expected to reach the volumes of a mainstream twin-aisle jet. Boeing instead reused the structure and production methods established over decades at its Everett factory, where the 747 had been built since the late 1960s.

Boeing also preserved many systems in common with the 747-400, a choice that simplifies maintenance, spares provisioning, and mechanic training for airlines operating both models. The freighter, which accounts for the majority of 747-8 deliveries, retains the hinged nose door that lets long loads enter straight along the main deck.

The 747-8 shows that technology transfer, when applied with discipline and clear commercial goals, can extend an airframe’s commercial life without the expense of starting over. The final aircraft left the production line in early 2023 after 155 had been built. Its more durable influence may appear in cargo operations, where the freighters seem likely to remain in service for decades. Few alternatives offer comparable volume, and the Dreamliner-derived engines should keep operating costs competitive as fleets age in the years ahead.

Sustainable aviation fuel offers a further lever for extending service lives, because engines of the GEnx generation are approved for blends with conventional jet fuel, which lets operators reduce lifecycle emissions without modifying the airplane. Market pressure shapes what comes next, since fuel efficiency and emissions goals increasingly favor twin-engine aircraft, so the quadjet is unlikely to return as a clean-sheet design, and the 747-8’s lasting contribution may be as the final demonstration of how far a four-engine airliner could be pushed with the technology of its time.

The 747-8 program also previews how Boeing is likely to modernize mature designs in the future. The 777X, for example, pairs a new composite wing with new engines on a fuselage descended from the 777, a pattern that mirrors the 747-8’s selective borrowing but moves much further toward composite structure. For engineers, the more transferable lesson concerns what to share and what to withhold.

Components that improve efficiency without altering certification basis or pilot procedures, such as engines, aerodynamic surfaces, and lighting, moved across freely, while anything that would have disrupted commonality with the 747-400 stayed behind. Future derivatives are likely to follow the same filter, with the cost of recertification acting as the main gatekeeper, and the 747-8 supplies the clearest template of that logic.

I use ChatGPT most days and am just getting started with using Instinct AI via WhatsApp. And I'm increasingly using AI to plan and improve my travels. For example, I frequently ask ChatGPT to plan walking tours in new destinations, use Instinct to find stores selling specific items and even tried connecting Gondola to ChatGPT for more personalized travel advice.

But as AI tools become increasingly capable of booking trips and managing accounts on your behalf, airlines and banks are becoming increasingly concerned about how consumers use them. For example, United Airlines recently announced restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents, while Bank of America warned customers against sharing their banking passwords with AI assistants.

These developments don't mean you should stop using AI to plan your travels. But they highlight why it's important to understand — and thoughtfully consider — what information you're sharing, what you're allowing AI to do and when you should verify its recommendations.

Before we dive into the dos and don'ts, let's discuss how consumers are using AI for travel. Most usage falls into one of three categories:

Each of these types of AI usage carries different risks. So, especially as AI agents become more capable, it's important to understand the risks you're taking when using them.

Related: How AI is transforming the future of travel

One way travelers can use AI is to help them research and plan trips. I've used AI to research and plan trips with extended family to both Iceland and Venice. And I use AI most days to help me plan walking routes in new cities, decipher restaurant menus and figure out how to operate appliances in Airbnbs.

While researching and planning travel, you can also use AI to:

Besides the time you can save and the experiences you can discover, the best part of using AI to research and plan your travels is that you can often provide enough context to help the AI improve its recommendations without sharing unnecessary personal information. As such, using AI to plan and research your travels is often relatively low-risk.

Related: Can Hilton’s new AI planning tool help you find the perfect hotel? We put it to the test

You can also use AI to help you with your points and miles. For example, AI can suggest ways to stack earnings and help you decide the best card to use before you make a purchase. However, you have to provide the AI with the proper context, such as the merchant you want to buy from, whether you want to prioritize having extended warranty protection, whether you're working toward any minimum spending requirements and which cards you currently have in your wallet.

AI could also help you compare cards when you're ready to open a new card. And it can also help you with many of the calculations travelers often struggle with, such as comparing cash versus points bookings (you can also use TPG's calculator for this), calculating redemption values, evaluating whether transferring points makes sense and assessing elite status benefits.

Best of all, it can do all these tasks without needing access to your accounts. Sure, the more information you give the AI agent, the more accurate and relevant its responses may be. But you don't need to give an AI agent access to your accounts for it to compare properties at your desired destination, calculate whether it's better to redeem 25,000 Hyatt points or pay $600, or compare the perks of using two different cards for a purchase.

Related: The 9 best rewards credit cards to add to your wallet

Even as many travelers start to use AI for more travel decisions and planning, it's important to fact-check or verify anything an AI agent tells you that you plan to rely on.

Sure, it doesn't really matter if ChatGPT gets a few details about landmarks incorrect during a walking tour I asked it to plan. And it's only a minor inconvenience if it sends me to a closed restaurant or suggests I get off at a slightly farther away bus stop.

But many travel decisions do matter and should be verified. For example, verify driving routes and travel times, entry requirements and whether a hotel offers the amenities you need. I also recommend ensuring that any redemption rates or other calculations pass the "sniff test" and appear correct. And if you ask an AI agent to find sweet spots in a specific loyalty program, be sure to fact-check that the sweet spots still exist at the stated rates and that you can find availability on at least some dates.

Also keep in mind that AI may give you overly conservative advice. For example, it will often recommend arriving at the airport three to four hours before your flight even when the bag drop counter doesn't open until two hours before departure. So, double-check any information that you'd be upset if it were incorrect.

Although sharing information with AI can help you get more personalized advice, you should carefully consider what to share. In particular, avoid sharing passwords, security codes, full credit card numbers and other sensitive information with AI tools.

Bank of America recently warned customers not to share their banking usernames or passwords with AI assistants, noting that customers could be responsible for certain activity resulting from that access. This is good advice for your loyalty accounts, too.

However, you don't necessarily need to avoid sharing any personal information with AI agents. For example, uploading a flight itinerary or hotel reservation could help an AI assistant plan your travels. Consider removing unnecessary details, such as confirmation numbers, account numbers and other identifying information, before uploading documents.

If you've already shared a password with an AI tool, change it immediately and review your account for unauthorized activity.

Related: Why one of the best tools for maximizing rewards is ... a password manager?

As AI agents become more capable, you may be tempted to let them access your loyalty and banking accounts to search for award availability, manage reservations or even book travel on your behalf. But just because an AI agent can access an account doesn't mean the account's provider allows it.

For example, United Airlines recently announced restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents accessing its systems, citing concerns about unauthorized purchases, MileagePlus redemptions and automated check-in. Meanwhile, American Airlines explicitly prohibits "automated re-shopping," and Marriott prohibits automated tools from monitoring or retrieving website information without written permission.

Likewise, some financial institutions restrict how third-party tools can access customer accounts. For example, Chase updated its digital services agreement last month to prohibit third parties, including AI agents, from using customers' login credentials to access accounts.

However, this doesn't mean all AI integrations are prohibited. Some companies allow customers to connect their accounts to approved third-party services through secure connections that don't require sharing passwords.

So, before connecting an AI agent to your travel or financial accounts, check whether the company permits the integration. And even if an integration is authorized, understand what information the AI tool can access, what actions it can take and how to revoke access if you change your mind.

As I was using Instinct AI to research clothing I needed to buy during a trip, its responses kept saying "Nothing has been ordered." This was reassuring on one hand, but I also found myself thinking, "I definitely don't want it ordering anything without my approval."

In the travel realm, actions an AI agent might take without your approval could include:

In short, it's a good idea to keep yourself in the loop. Even if you decide to use an AI agent or connection to make purchases or change reservations, you should require it to explicitly get approval from you each time.

That said, I generally prefer that the AI agent flag potential price drops or award availability for me. Then I verify the information it has told me, and consider whether to act on it.

Related: These new tools will track your flights and get you refunds if the price drops

For each AI tool you use, take the time to understand how the company collects, stores and uses your data. After all, you may be sharing more information than you realize, especially if you're uploading documents or connecting third-party accounts.

For example, some AI services may use your conversations to train or improve their models. Others may retain information even after you delete a conversation. And if you're using an AI tool through another platform, such as WhatsApp, or connecting a third-party service, multiple companies may have access to your information.

AI tools can be incredibly useful for planning trips, maximizing points and miles, and making travel easier. I use them frequently and expect I'll continue finding more ways to incorporate them into my travels.

But as AI tools become more capable, it's increasingly important to understand their limitations and the risks of sharing information or granting them access to your accounts.

My advice is to start with relatively low-risk tasks, such as researching destinations and comparing redemption options. Then, as you become more comfortable with AI tools, consider whether you're willing to share more information or allow them to take actions on your behalf. Just be sure to understand what you're authorizing and maintain control over your accounts and reservations.

#6289. Dear Tunisair: How About A Refund For My Downgrade, Please?

I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

At the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story…

Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

The email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only showed as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

There was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

After the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

But anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

As I said above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

We’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

It just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

I'm extremely well-traveled and Tunisair is by far one of the worst airlines I'm had the misfortune of traveling with.

On the other hand, Tunisair's Contract of Carriage (is it in French, Arabic, or both) might state that when the booked class is not available, the passenger is entitled to a refund if the reservation is canceled, or can apply the fare to the next flight with that class available. Why not?

i would also dispute the charge rather than chase the airline

#6288. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

#6287. Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?

It is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine. However, each of these aircraft uses a different variation of that same turbofan that is tailored to its unique needs and engineering qualities.

The 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B. Boeing chose the GEnx for the 747-8 primarily to modernize the aging jumbo jet with next-generation technology. Both aircraft feature distinctive serrated chevrons on the engine nacelles, which mix hot exhaust with cool air to significantly reduce noise.

For airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training. The GEnx-1B is a larger, more powerful, and more-electric engine designed for a modern twin-engine jet. The GEnx-2B is a smaller, simplified variant that incorporates traditional pneumatics to breathe life into the older 747 systems while providing modern fuel efficiency.

While the GEnx-1B (787) and GEnx-2B (747-8) share a common high-pressure core and 80% of their Line Replaceable Units, they are distinct engines optimized for different aircraft architectures. The most fundamental difference is how the engines interact with the aircraft's internal systems. The GEnx family is designed to stay on wing 20% longer than previous generations, with some fleet leaders exceeding 30,000 hours without a major overhaul.

Both engines offer approximately 15% better fuel efficiency than the older CF6 engines they replaced. Tom Levin, General Manager of the GEnx/CF6 engine product line at GE Aviation, commented on the engine's success when the 1,000th GEnx engine was developed in 2015.

“The GEnx was the fastest selling engine in GE’s history, and now it is the fastest production ramp up of a GE widebody engine program. The GEnx engine has proven itself with outstanding performance and reliability."

The 787 uses a bleedless architecture where most systems are powered electrically. The 747-8 uses a traditional bleed-air system to power environmental controls and start the engines, requiring the GEnx-2B to include bleed-air ports. The GEnx-2B has fewer stages in the booster and low-pressure turbine, optimizing it for a four-engine configuration.

The Boeing 747-8, on the other hand, uses a traditional bleed air system. It must bleed high-pressure air from the compressor to power the 747’s pneumatic systems, including cabin pressurization and thermal anti-icing.

To fit the 747’s wing and ground clearance, the GEnx-2B has a smaller fan diameter, 105 inches, compared to the 787’s 111 inches. Because the 747-8 has four engines while the 787 has only two, the -2B is simplified internally to be lighter and more optimized for its lower per-engine thrust requirement. The -2B produces roughly 66,500 lbs of thrust, whereas the 787 variants can reach up to 76,100 lbs.

The GEnx-1B has more power because it is intended for a twin-engine aircraft (787) that must maintain performance in the event of an engine failure during takeoff. Because the GEnx-2B's power is distributed across four engines on the 747-8, its thrust rating is 66,500 lbf lower. Compared with older engines like the CF6, the GEnx-2B's technology improves fuel efficiency and cuts emissions by 15%.

In contrast to the 1B, the GEnx-2B has de-staged components to maximize weight and performance for a four-engine setup. In contrast to the 1B's four stages, the 2B's low-pressure compressor has three stages. In the low-pressure turbine, the 1B has seven stages, whereas the 2B has six.

The Boeing 787 comes with both GE and Rolls-Royce engine options, although GE's engines have become more popular in recent times.

Compared with the 747-8, the 787 Dreamliner delivers bettereconomics and is much more efficient in the widebody market, as it is a lightweight twin-engine composite aircraft. These engineering variations determine their efficiency and commercial success. The 747 uses about 3,800 gallons of fuel per hour, while the 787 uses about 2,900 gallons. The 787-9 is extremely efficient, using approximately 2.31 liters per 100 km per passenger, which is significantly better than the 747-8's 2.82 liters per 100 km per passenger.

Boeing's Dreamliner also costs significantly less to operate, with a lower cost per available seat mile. Airlines typically prefer smaller twin-engine aircraft because they are less dangerous to fill and fly. The 787's design and performance have allowed it to thrive in the modern aviation market, while the 747-8 saw limited passenger orders before production ended in 2017 and the 747 assembly line fully shut down in 2023.

The Dreamliner has essentially eliminated the conventional hub-and-spoke paradigm that made the 747 necessary. While the 747 required high passenger capacity to be successful, the 787's efficiency lets it cover the same distances with fewer seats, making it a better match for today's point-to-point market.

The 787's efficiency allows airlines to launch new, nonstop point-to-point routes that would not have been economically viable with older, bigger, four-engine planes. Despite being more efficient than previous 747s, the 747-8 is still best suited to high-volume hub-to-hub services. Airlines such as United have made large 787 orders to replace a mix of 747s, 767s, and early 777s with a single, simpler aircraft family, resulting in significant cost savings for pilot training and component inventory.

Unravel the secrets of the massive GE9X, a jet engine that redefines scale and efficiency in the skies.

The 787 incorporates a large amount of carbon composite material, making it lighter, more resistant to fatigue and corrosion, and allowing for higher cabin humidity and lower cabin altitude, which enhances passenger comfort and reduces structural stress. The 747-8 is a development of a traditional aluminum design, with a heavier base structure.

Lufthansa has incorporated the 787-9 to handle flights that need the same range but have about 70–90 fewer people, even though it is still a 747-8 operator. Because of this, even at off-peak times, the airline can maintain high load factors (percentage of seats filled). British Airways switched to the 787-10 for important transatlantic flights to New York and Chicago after retiring its entire 747 fleet. The 787-10 is 25% more fuel-efficient than the 747 while offering comparable cargo capacity and contemporary comforts.

The fastest Boeing found on the flightline today is more than just that, it’s also the last Queen of the Skies to ever take to the air.

Compared to the 747, the 787 Dreamliner offers a better long-haul passenger experience because its composite airframe creates a cabin environment that more closely resembles ground conditions. When compared to older aircraft like the 747, which have a cabin altitude of 8,000 feet, the 787's cabin altitude of 6,000 feet makes a significant difference for passengers. That lower cabin altitude does many things to reduce the effects of fatigue on passengers inflight.

The composite construction of the 787 is not only 50% by weight but 80% by volume. Thanks to that light yet incredibly durable construction, it can do things no previous aircraft could. That includes having larger windows, higher humidity (15% or double that of legacy jets), and a more spacious interior with more natural lighting and better overhead storage.

While the 747 is much loved for its incredibly smooth landing characteristics and gentle handling and flight, the 787 uses a new technology known as 'smooth ride' to counteract turbulence in flight. This is the same technology that the 777X will use when it finally debuts in 2027. Although the 747 was known as the Queen of the Skies, the Dreamliner has become the best-selling widebody in history. It has been the flagship product of the legendary plane maker, as its 737 MAX has flailed in the wake of a disastrous debut.

This is not only a major improvement for the long-haul market, but also for operators that use these aircraft for high-density hub-to-hub transport, and makes a major improvement for the densest routes in the world. A 787 Dreamliner is not only a game-changer for the operators that fly it, but it also marks a paradigm shift in the experience for flyers. While the era of the 747 ushered in a golden age of jet-powered commercial aviation, the 787 and future successors such as the 777X herald the next era in air travel.
