#6286. Park Hyatt Brisbane Opening 2031, As Brand’s Fourth Australia Hotel

Hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia. More Park Hyatt locations are always a good thing, but… well, let’s cover the details first.

Hyatt has announced plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland. The hotel is expected to open in 2031, and will be located on the shores of the Brisbane River, at the western edge of the city’s central business district.

The hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets. For what it’s worth, the two buildings will have 51 floors and 56 floors. The hotel will have 201 guest rooms and suites, offering views of the river and skyline, along with 50 serviced apartments, for extended residence.

There are no additional details about the property yet. I do appreciate that the hotel will at least be at the top of a building, as that should make for some very nice views (I hate when hotels are part of tall buildings, but then take up the bottom floors, as that’s becoming increasingly common).

While a 2031 opening is expected, I would definitely not count on that timeline sticking. Ground hasn’t even broken on this development, and these kinds of mixed-use developments tend to struggle with sticking to their planned timeline.

Here’s how Tamara Lohan, Hyatt’s Global Brand Leader for Luxury, describes this:

“The Park Hyatt calling cards have always been iconic design and extraordinary addresses. Brisbane has the confidence and growing global pull to make it a natural home for the brand. When it opens, Park Hyatt Brisbane will become the fifth Park Hyatt hotel in the Pacific, joining hotels in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Auckland, and a deliberate next step in growing the brand in the right places.”

There are no renderings of the property yet, beyond the below one of the overall 309 North Quay development.

This will be the fourth Park Hyatt property in Australia, and the fifth in the South Pacific, complementing the properties in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney. I don’t have the slightest clue what’s going on with the Canberra property, as my understanding is that it’s not up to Park Hyatt standards, so it’s marketed as “Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel.” So it is a Park Hyatt, or is it not a Park Hyatt?

World of Hyatt is my favorite major hotel loyalty program (though the lead is narrowing as of late), and Park Hyatt is probably my favorite Hyatt brand. 15 years ago, the brand got me really excited, because it had some really spectacular properties. But it just feels like the brand is sort of losing steam, especially when you compare the difference in trajectory between Park Hyatt and Waldorf Astoria. My frustration with Park Hyatt comes down to two things.

First, the brand just seemingly can’t pick up many “flagship” properties, or at least can’t maintain them. Look at the world’s biggest business markets and most iconic cities — we’re talking Hong Kong, London, New York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, etc. There are no Park Hyatts in places like Hong Kong or Singapore, and the ones that have historically been pretty iconic just fall short of actually being the top properties in their cities:

The area where Park Hyatt has been doing well in recent times is in secondary cities, at least in comparison to the above. And this isn’t meant to be shade — I’d much rather hang out in Auckland or Kuala Lumpur than in London or New York (take your pitchforks elsewhere!), but there’s no denying that any true luxury hotel brand wants to have world class properties in those primary cities.

I just feel like as of late, Waldorf Astoria’s trajectory has been way more impressive than Park Hyatt’s, and I’m not sure what exactly is driving that. I feel like owners just aren’t as into developing Park Hyatts as they used to be. Is there a single Park Hyatt in the pipeline where I think “oh, this is going to be a best-in-class property in a major market?” I can’t think of any…

The Park Hyatt brand is coming to Brisbane, Australia, with a hotel expected to open in 2031. The 201-key property will be located on the top floors of a mixed-use development, which will also contain apartments and retail.

It’s cool to see more Park Hyatts in the pipeline, and I don’t want to knock the brand for expanding to more markets. I’m just disappointed that the Park Hyatt brand can’t pick up any steam in the biggest cities, in terms of delivering an actually competitive experience.

What do you make of plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane?

#6284. Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)…

When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.

In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft. For example, if the plane has the registration code N111PG, it would be spoken as “November One One One Papa Golf.”

Meanwhile for commercial aircraft, the callsign consists of a company identifier plus the flight number. In some cases that company identifier is simply the company’s name, while in other cases, a different callsign is used. For example, for American, Delta, and United, the company identifier is simply the airline name, so American flight 100 would be spoken as “American 100.”

In some situations, airlines choose callsigns that are different from the company name, and this can be for a variety of reasons. Callsigns need to be approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with some important considerations:

While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, there are also some airlines that don’t, and there are some names that I find to be particularly fun. In this post, I’d like to share my favorite airline callsigns, with a little backstory on how they were chosen (as I understand it). In no particular order…

Aer Lingus’ callsign is “Shamrock,” and that’s because the shamrock is the national symbol of Ireland. It’s a key part of the airline’s corporate identity, down to the shamrock being featured on the tails of Aer Lingus planes.

British Airways’ callsign is “Speedbird,” and I’d argue it’s perhaps the most iconic callsign out there. The origin of this dates back to British Airways’ predecessor, Imperial Airways, which used the stylized bird logo. British Airways has been using the callsign since it was founded in 1974 (as a combination of predecessors).

While this is of course a creative callsign, it has a practical use as well. “British Airways” would’ve been too long of a callsign, and “British” would’ve likely been too generic. For example, British Midland (which ended up being merged into British Airways) used “Midland” as its callsign, to avoid confusion.

Republic Airways’ callsign is “Brickyard,” and it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The callsign is a tribute to the company’s headquarters in Indianapolis, also home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. The course was initially paved with three million bricks, and nicknamed “The Brickyard.”

For those not familiar, Republic operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is among the most common callsigns you’ll hear on air traffic control frequencies in the US.

PSA Airlines’ callsign is “Blue Streak,” and after Republic, it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The story behind this callsign is definitely a blast from the past. In the 1980s, PSA’s predecessor was Jetstream International Airlines, and it operated commuter flights as a Piedmont Commuter feeder carrier.

The carrier’s planes had a white fuselage with a prominent blue stripe along it, intended to match Piedmont Airlines’ livery, and that’s where it all started.

For those not familiar, PSA operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is also a very common callsign that you’ll hear. Given the lack of blue stripes nowadays, the callsign does tend to cause some confusion!

China Airlines’ callsign is “Dynasty.” It’s my understanding that the Taiwan-based carrier had to choose a non-obvious callsign both to avoid confusion (given the number of airlines with “China” in their name), and also with the intent of differentiating it from mainland China.

So, where did the dynasty term come from? China Airlines uses this branding pretty widely, with its frequent flyer program even being named Dynasty Flyer, and it’s intended to reflect the history of Taiwan.

Starlux Airlines’ callsign is “Starwalker.” The reason is because the “Starlux” callsign was already taken by Comlux Aruba, a tiny charter airline, before the Taiwanese airline was founded. Now, don’t ask me why Comlux Aruba has “Starlux” as its callsign, though!

The reason Starlux ended up with “Starwalker” is presumably because the company’s founder is a huge Star Wars fan, which is why many things about the airline have space branding. He’s also of course a huge aviation geek, and operates flights as a captain!

South African Airways’ callsign is “Springbok.” The reason is because “South African” would be too long of a callsign, so they selected the springbok, which is the national animal of South Africa. The carrier has also used this in its branding over the years. For example, back in the 1950s, the airline used “Springbok Service” to describe its long haul, flagship flights.

Atlas Air’s callsign is “Giant.” Huh, say what? For those not familiar, Atlas Air is a cargo and charter airline, and while it doesn’t operate regularly scheduled commercial flights, it is a big operation.

The callsign is presumably a reflection of the company’s name coming from Greek mythology, where “Atlas” was a titan of great strength, so that may also explain the “giant” callsign. Now, it’s worth mentioning that Atlas also flies some pretty “giant” planes, as the world’s largest Boeing 747 operator, but I don’t think that’s the primary motivation.

Kalitta Air’s callsign is “Connie.” For those not familiar, Kalitta Air is a cargo airline with a few dozen planes (most of which are Boeing 747s!). The callsign is named after the company’s founder, Conrad “Connie” Kalitta, who started the airline back in 1967, as Connie Kalitta Services.

European Air Transport’s callsign is “Postman.” For context, this is one of DHL’s European subsidiaries operating cargo flights, so it’s a pretty fitting callsign, eh?

Airlines have callsigns that they use to communicate with air traffic control. While most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, that’s not always the case. In some situations a different name has to be chosen for practical reasons, while in some cases airlines want to get creative. I love when airlines have some fun with this, so I figured it was worth a post.

It’s the end of an era at American Airlines.

This week, the carrier (officially) bid farewell to Flagship First international service.

We’ve been talking for years about American’s plans to retire its international-style first-class product.

The airline is replacing Flagship First with larger and more modern business-class cabins on its marquee planes — cabins that will feature its next-generation Flagship Suites.

But there’s at least a little nostalgia in bidding farewell to a cabin that, for many years, was billed as American’s most exclusive.

American was the last U.S. airline that claimed to offer a standalone, international first-class product.

Across the global airline industry, many carriers sunset long-haul first-class years ago, choosing to instead offer more — and improved — business-class seats, which take up less space and are considered more profitable.

For years, Delta Air Lines’ Delta One business-class suites have been its premier long-haul offering.

United Airlines bid farewell to international first class in 2018 when it pivoted to Polaris business class.

That left American’s Flagship First as a relic, of sorts, in the U.S. airline industry — and even on its own planes.

In recent years, you could only find the cabin on two fleet types American operated: its Boeing 777-300ER, which offered eight of the pods up front in their own dedicated cabin.

Plus, AA still (for now) offers Flagship First on its three-cabin Airbus A321T, which has been a fixture on lucrative coast-to-coast routes like New York to Los Angeles and San Francisco.

But soon, it will be a thing of the past on both planes.

American is retrofitting its larger 777s, ditching first-class in favor of 70 all-new Flagship Suites in business-class — along with the biggest premium economy cabin it’s ever offered.

Related: This is now American Airlines' most premium plane: Here's what it's like on board

On domestic routes, the A321T will actually keep flying with Flagship First through March 28.

But after that, AA will stop selling the Flagship First cabin on the A321T configuration, which is eventually going away as American flexes in its new A321XLR planes fully onto its top cross-country flights.

In a lot of ways, American ditching Flagship First is a positive (and arguably overdue) transition for flyers.

It’ll give passengers more lie-flat seats to pick from, whether they’re paying cash, using AAdvantage miles or using a systemwide upgrade.

Also — while those Flagship First seats were really spacious and comfortable, many would say that American's new business-class product is a major upgrade from what it previously offered in that cabin.

On some planes, that even includes extra-spacious Flagship Suites Preferred in the front and bulkhead rows of some planes, which offer a lot more space.

Value check: Is it worth buying up to American Airlines' new business-class Flagship Suite Preferred?

Beyond the aircraft, American also plans to still offer many of the same amenities for business-class that first-class passengers historically enjoyed.

For instance, its Flagship business-class tickets get access to its premium lounges. Passengers traveling in Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus on qualifying international, transcontinental and Hawaii routes will also be able to have a meal in its exclusive restaurant-style dining rooms in Dallas, Los Angeles and Miami.

The experience is available on a space-available basis.

So, in some ways, you could argue the end of Flagship First is more symbolic than anything.

But for some AA loyalists, it's still a little bittersweet.

TPG’s Clint Henderson is our resident Flagship First enthusiast, having flown the cabin on dozens of occasions.

"The service in first class wasn't particularly differentiated, but I still liked a few of the special touches," he said, pointing to the additional soup course and appetizer, along with a handful of elevated amenities.

He especially appreciated the “La-Z-Boy-style” seats at the front of American’s 777s, which could lie flat or swivel and turn into an “office in the sky.”

“While these cabins are definitely showing their age,” Henderson added, “I’m sad to see it go.”

While Flagship First is technically going away as an official cabin on international service, the seats themselves won't disappear overnight.

So far, American has only retrofitted one of its 20 Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the seats. That means a handful of jets with the old first-class seats will still be flying around well into 2027.

Going forward, the former Flagship First seats on those planes will be marketed as business-class. They won’t come with the full first-class service, but you’ll still get the elevated seat.

#6281. LATAM Unveils New Airbus A321XLR Business Class Suites, Coming March 2027

LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft. These planes are expected to enter service in the coming months, so we won’t have to wait much longer to fly them!

LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027. The A321XLR is the new long range, narrow body aircraft from Airbus, which stretches the capabilities of the A321 family.

The airline intends to use these planes to open up new long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”

Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been announced.

We can expect LATAM to offer an all-new passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline plans to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:

Throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV shows. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

It also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

The A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

While American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

Admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being said, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”

While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

In early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline plans to use to grow into new markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

Ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is currently offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two new wide body business class products over the past several years.

What do you make of LATAM’s new A321XLR business class?

#6279. Why Are All Pratt & Whitney's GTF Engines Green On The Inside?

Passengers boarding an Airbus A320neo or an A220 who glance at the engine intake from the jet bridge often notice something unusual. Inside the nacelle, ahead of the fan blades, a ring of teal green lines the casing of the Pratt & Whitney Geared Turbofan, whether the aircraft carries the PW1100G of the A320neo family or the PW1500G of the A220. The color is consistent enough across the fleet that spotters and online aviation communities have debated its purpose for years, with explanations ranging from branding to corrosion protection.

The more convincing answers sit in materials science and maintenance practice. Two separate components contribute to the green appearance, each with its own function and its own reason for the shade it carries, and a third factor, the practical needs of the people who inspect the engines, explains why the color has persisted. Examining those components in turn clarifies how a modern geared turbofan manages noise, tip clearance, and inspection, and why a seemingly cosmetic detail reflects engineering decisions made well before the engine reaches an airline.

The broad green band lining the inner surface of the fan case is the engine’s acoustic liner, a panel built from a perforated skin bonded over a honeycomb core. The perforations admit sound waves into the cells of the honeycomb, where each cell behaves like a small resonant chamber that absorbs acoustic energy and converts a portion of it into heat. By sizing the cells and the perforated face sheet for particular frequencies, designers tune the panel to dampen the tones that dominate fan noise.

The geared architecture makes this component especially relevant. Because a reduction gearbox lets the fan turn more slowly than the turbine driving it, the engine produces a different acoustic signature from a direct-drive fan of similar size, with more of the energy at lower frequencies. Low-frequency sound is harder to absorb than high-frequency sound, since longer wavelengths need deeper cavities to dissipate effectively, which is why the liner occupies a generous stretch of the inlet. Pratt & Whitney has promoted the engine’s reduced noise footprint as a headline benefit, and the liner is one of several features that contribute to it alongside the slower fan itself.

Construction follows a sandwich principle common to aerospace structures. A solid backing sheet closes one side of the honeycomb, and the perforated face sheet closes the other. The arrangement delivers acoustic performance with very little weight, a priority in any component carried on an engine hanging from the wing, where added mass raises fuel burn. The panels are also designed to withstand airflow, vibration, temperature swings, and minor debris impacts throughout a long service life.

The teal shade is generally attributed to the composite itself rather than to a decorative coating. According to descriptions of the construction, the resin and epoxy matrix that bind the liner’s layers carry a natural pigmentation that shows through on the finished surface. Engineers have a practical reason to avoid covering it. A thick film of paint would partially fill the microscopic perforations in the face sheet, reducing the open area through which sound enters the cavities and degrading the attenuation the panel was designed to achieve.

However, this explanation should be treated with some caution, because there has not been a published manufacturer statement regarding the color. As a result, the exact origin of the hue remains an informed inference rather than a documented fact. The uniform result across A320neo and A220 installations nonetheless suggests a controlled material choice instead of an incidental one.

As the aviation industry shifts towards composite materials, will the iconic green finish become a relic of the past?

Directly aft of the acoustic ring sits a slightly lighter blue-green band, the abradable rub strip, which technical literature also calls a fan outer air seal. Its job is to control the gap between the fan blade tips and the surrounding case. Any air that leaks across that gap represents lost work, so engine makers want the clearance as small as practical without allowing the blades to strike a hard surface.

The abradable material solves that problem by being softer than the blade tips. During break-in, the tips cut a shallow groove into the strip, producing a seal matched to the actual shape of that particular fan, including any slight growth caused by heat and centrifugal loading. The strip wears while the blades and the case remain intact. A paper from the 2003 NASA Seal/Secondary Air System Workshop, which covers Pratt & Whitney abradable seals, documents the broader engineering approach behind such materials.

The color of this strip carries its own explanation. The compound is supplied as a two-part epoxy and hardener, and the components are mixed to a defined turquoise shade so that a uniform color confirms the two parts were blended properly before application. Streaks or patches of a different tone would signal incomplete mixing, and with it a risk that the cured strip will not abrade predictably. The compound’s behavior over time matters as much as its initial performance. As the engine accumulates cycles, the strip gradually erodes from airflow, particles, and repeated light contact, and clearance grows accordingly. Operators therefore monitor the condition of the strip during scheduled inspections and restore it when wear exceeds published limits, a process that depends on repeating the same mixing and curing steps, and the same color check, each time the material is applied.

Beyond material chemistry, the saturated green interior gives maintenance crews a practical advantage during walk-around checks. The fan case sits in a shadowed cavity, and the blades, the hub, and any dark residue around the casing can blend together in poor light. A bright, uniform background makes departures from normal appearance easier to see.

Ramp inspectors look for several conditions in this region. Foreign object debris, such as fragments of tire, packing material, or bird remains, stands out against the green surface. Erosion of the liner or the rub strip shows as lighter patches or exposed honeycomb, and abnormal wear on the blade tips appears as unusual rub patterns where the strip has been cut. Because these checks often occur between flights under airport lighting and on tight schedules, a background that makes anomalies obvious reduces the chance of a missed finding.

The choice of green also reflects how the human eye distinguishes color. Green sits near the middle of the visible spectrum, where daylight vision is most sensitive, and it contrasts strongly with the reds, browns, and oranges typical of oil, hydraulic fluid, and corrosion products, so a stain or deposit on the liner is easier to notice than it would be on a gray or white surface.

Fuselages appear especially green partly due to a peelable layer and the stage at which they are pictured.

The GTF is far from the first aircraft component to appear in this color. Aerospace suppliers have long finished parts in green, and BMT Aerospace notes that the shade is often traced to protective primers applied to metal surfaces to resist corrosion. Zinc chromate primer, widely used for decades on airframes and components, has a distinctive yellow-green tone, which is why green surfaces are a familiar sight inside wheel wells, wing bays, and equipment racks.

Public discussion has also linked the GTF’s green interior to Pratt & Whitney’s environmental positioning, since the engine is marketed on lower fuel burn, reduced emissions, and quieter operation. This reading is plausible as a secondary benefit but lacks documentary support, and the engineering explanations above are sufficient on their own. A color that doubles as a reminder of the engine’s efficiency claims costs the manufacturer nothing, which may be why no one has felt a need to change it.

The green interior of the GTF is a small example of a larger trend in which material properties are doing more of the work that markings once did. As engines move toward larger, slower fans housed in shorter nacelles, liners will have to absorb more sound from less surface area, which pushes designers toward more sophisticated core geometries and multilayer constructions. Pratt & Whitney’s improved GTF Advantage variant retains the same gearbox architecture, so the existing liner conventions should carry forward into the newer engines.

Inspection practice is also changing. Airlines and maintenance providers are adopting borescope automation, drone-assisted visual checks, and machine-vision software that compares images against a reference baseline. A controlled, repeatable color simplifies that comparison, because software can flag deviations in hue or texture more reliably when the underlying surface is uniform. Should manufacturers publish color tolerances for liners and rub strips, the green interior could evolve from an informal convention into a formal measurement reference, with deviations scored automatically before a technician reaches the engine.

Material choices will also respond to environmental scrutiny. Chromate-based primers are under regulatory pressure in several jurisdictions because of worker exposure and disposal concerns, and the industry is moving toward alternatives. Any substitute for current coatings will need to preserve acoustic openness, bonding strength, and the visual contrast that crews rely on, which may lead suppliers to add deliberate pigments where natural color once sufficed.

For the existing fleet, the near-term picture is straightforward. With a large and growing fleet in service, the teal ring is likely to remain a recognizable feature for decades, and its meaning will rest on data as much as on appearance. Operators who record inspection images consistently over an engine’s life will build a visual history of wear that could support condition-based maintenance, replacing fixed intervals with decisions informed by measured trends in clearance and liner condition. In that sense, the color’s greatest value may lie ahead of it, as a standardized backdrop for the analytics that will govern how these engines are maintained.

#6278. Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?

The Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card launched in March 2026. On the surface, the card sounds rather uncompetitive — it has a $295 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers “just” 2% cash back on everyday spending, with limited bonus categories.

However, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee. If your business spends a lot, you value having an Amex, and you just want to earn simple cash back without a complex rewards structure, this could be a good option.

This post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review. Is the card worth it, and if so, under what circumstances? And what are the best alternatives?

Link: Learn more about the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card

Before I get into my Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:

Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited:

With the above out of the way, let’s look at the various aspects of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, from the welcome offer, to the fees, to the rewards structure, to the other perks. This card is fairly straightforward, so there’s not all that much to understand, for better or worse.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited currently has a welcome offer where you can earn as high as $2,000 cash back after spending $50,000 within the first six months on eligible purchases. Reward Dollars can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases.

Given that the card ordinarily offers at least 2% cash back, that means spending $50,000 could earn you a minimum of $3,000 (if offered the full bonus amount), equivalent to 6% cash back on that amount of spending, which is solid.

Admittedly the spending requirement is big (it averages out to $8,333 per month over the course of six months), but I do think businesses that spend a lot might find this to be achievable. Furthermore, it’s nice that you have six months to complete the spending requirement, while many other cards give you only three months to reach the spending requirement.

If you’re applying for the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, be aware of Amex’s general restrictions on applying for cards, including the “once in a lifetime rule.” That means you’re not eligible for the welcome offer on the card if you’ve already had this card, though you are potentially eligible for the bonus if you’ve had other Amex cards.

Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to be quite easy to get approved for. I also love how with Amex, you can know if you’ll be approved with no credit score impact — the hard pull only happens after you’re told if you’re approved, and you accept the offer.

Also keep in mind that if you’re concerned about staying under Chase’s 5/24 limit, applying for an Amex business card won’t count toward that, since it doesn’t show up on your personal credit report in that way.

When it comes to credit score, there’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the card, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility. Personally, I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an annual fee of $295 (Rates & Fees), which is definitely on the steep side, especially given the relatively narrow appeal of the credits offered on the card, which require a lot of spending.

With the card’s 2% cash back rewards structure, you’d essentially recoup the annual fee (in terms of rewards) after $14,750 in spending.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an authorized user fee of $95 for the first 5 cards, and a $95 annual fee for each thereafter (Rates & Fees), though you can also get a no annual fee Employee Business Expense Card with no additional fee. Still, that’s a rather steep authorized user fee for a card that doesn’t actually offer many incremental perks. You can add up to 99 employee cards to your account.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has no preset spending limit. The idea is that this gives you flexibility in ways that traditional credit cards don’t. The amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history. Rather than having a set limit, you could grow your purchasing power the more you consistently use your card and regularly make payments.

In fairness, it is also worth mentioning that not having a preset spending limit can also lead to some declines if the amount you can charge decreases, so it’s a little less predictable than a regular credit card. However, I find that more often than not, it works in the favor of cardmembers.

No Preset Spending Limit means your spending limit is flexible. Unlike a traditional card with a set limit, the amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history

In terms of its rewards structure, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers 2% cash back on eligible purchases. On top of that, the card offers 5% cash back on flights and prepaid hotels booked through American Express Travel® Online. Just to do some very basic math:

All cash back on the card is earned as Reward Dollars, which can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases. Unfortunately there are no other redemption options, so you couldn’t directly deposit the cash back into a business checking account, or anything like that.

2% cash back on credit card spending is the “gold standard,” as I see it, so that’s excellent, and what everyone should be aiming for, at a minimum.

Meanwhile the 5% cash back on Amex Travel might sound appealing, but there are some catches. If you can route travel spending that way, it’s a good option, but the catch is that you may sometimes find lower rates elsewhere, so there could be an opportunity cost to booking that way.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year. Statement credits will be applied to the monthly bill charged to the card for Amex’s accounts payable solution, One AP, for the following calendar year, and this includes an auto-renewing platform access fee.

American Express One AP® is an accounts payable solution that can help transform the way your business pays suppliers. With One AP, you can streamline your supplier invoice payments on a single platform and pay by virtual card, check, and ACH. Enrollment is required.

This program charges a $200 monthly fee to pay vendors with non-cards, plus has a fee for checks and ACHs over a certain limit. So the $2,400 annual credit can potentially fully cover your monthly fee. While this is potentially a nice feature, keep in mind that many platforms already offer this as a built in feature at no extra cost, so it’s not really that special.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers the Pay Over Time feature, whereby cardmembers can carry a balance with interest on eligible charges, up to the Pay Over Time limit. The way this works, eligible charges will automatically be added to a Pay Over Time balance, up to the Pay Over Time limit.

You can choose to pay for these charges over time with interest, or you can pay your full balance each month, whichever is best for your business. You must pay in full any charge or a portion of a charge that is not added to a Pay Over Time balance.

Personally, I recommend paying the balance in full each billing cycle if possible, to avoid interest charges, especially given how high they can be. However, I think it’s worth clarifying that the Pay Over Time option is possible, given that this isn’t a traditional credit card.

It’s also worth emphasizing the difference between the Pay Over Time and the Pay In Full Limit. The latter could be an amount that has to be paid in full, and there’s no option to pay that over time with interest charges.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card earns 2% cash back, and I consider that to be the minimum “gold standard” of credit card rewards. So the card’s rewards structure is perfectly fine. The 5% cash back on travel is also pretty limiting, given that you have to book through Amex.

I think the issue is the steep annual fee, given that there are also much more affordable (and even no annual fee) cards with that kind of a rewards structure. In fairness, Amex doesn’t have another business card earning unlimited 2% cash back. It’s just not a new concept more broadly, and there are lots of competing cards that I’d consider to be superior.

So who should consider the card? As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is targeted at a specific demographic. This card could make sense for the following types of customers:

I do truly think this is a niche product. But the idea is that if you’re a small business owner charging hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars on credit cards per year, that annual fee won’t make much of a difference.

Still, I’d like to compare this to some other popular products, as I think there are other cards that may be a better fit for some other people.

Perhaps the best direct comparison to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1% cash back thereafter).

The upside here is obvious, as you’re earning 2% cash back with no fee. The downside is that the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

For a small business mostly spending money domestically, the Amex Blue Business Cash is a great alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash.

Another potential alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1x points thereafter).

If you’re good at redeeming points, that’s a pretty incredible return, since based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, for a return of up to 3.4%. The downsides to the Amex Blue Business Plus are otherwise identical to those on the Amex Blue Business Cash — the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2x points on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

So the card is either useful if $50,000 covers your annual business spending, or you’re willing to use another card after you hit that initial $50,000 spending cap.

Speaking of premium Amex business cards, it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the American Express® Business Gold Card (learn more). The Amex Business Gold has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers an incredible rewards structure (with up to 4x Membership Rewards points in select categories), plus statement credits that can greatly help offset the annual fee.

As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is the better option if you value cash back and a straightforward rewards structure, while the Amex Business Gold is the better option if you can take advantage of the bonus categories, and are willing to put in the effort to maximize points.

While the above comparisons are all to Amex cards, I think it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Capital One Spark Cash Plus (learn more), as it’s perhaps the most direct competitor.

The card has a massive welcome offer of $2,000 cash back after spending $30,000 within the first three months (plus an additional $2,000 cash back bonus for every $500,000 spent during the first year), offers 5% cash back on select Capital One Business Travel purchases and 2% cash back with no caps and no foreign transaction fees on other purchases, and it has a $150 annual fee. Furthermore, the card offers an annual bonus of $150 if you spend at least $150,000 on the card in a calendar year, essentially rebating the annual fee.

I do think the Capital One Spark Cash Plus is more compelling than the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card on balance, unless you specifically have a reason you’d like an Amex, or value the statement credits tied to spending $250,000 per year.

I’d also like to compare the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (learn more), as it’s another potentially lucrative cash back card.

In addition to a big welcome offer of $1,000 cash back after spending $10,000 within the first three months, the card offers 5% cash back on Chase Travel purchases, 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more, and 2% cash back on all other purchases, with no foreign transaction fees, and it has a $195 annual fee. So if you have a business that frequently makes large purchases, the Chase Ink Business Premier could be a great alternative.

The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card has a $295 annual fee, and offers unlimited 2% cash back, with no preset spending limit, plus a large welcome offer. The card also offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year.

Ultimately I’d consider this to be a niche card. The card could be worth getting for the excellent welcome offer, and it could be worth it if you have a business that spends a huge amount, and values the lack of a preset spending limit, the card’s Amex branding, and/or the statement credits.

Beyond that, though, I tend to think there are better options. If you’re not a huge spender, the Amex Blue Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Plus are excellent options. If you’re willing to maximize points and bonus categories, consider the Amex Business Gold. And if you’re looking for the best direct alternative that’s arguably more lucrative, consider the Capital One Spark Cash Plus.

#6276. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6275. Buy Avianca Lifemiles With 145% Bonus (1.35 Cents Each): Worth It?

The avianca lifemiles program is currently offering a limited time 145% bonus on purchased miles. With this, lifemiles members can purchase miles for as little as 1.35 cents each. Is this a good deal?

I find lifemiles to be one of the more useful frequent flyer programs for redeeming miles, thanks to the ability to redeem for long haul premium cabin Star Alliance awards. However, let me emphasize that the program doesn’t always have access to the same award space as other Star Alliance programs, so you’ll want to do your own research, based on the travel you’re trying to plan.

I’d only consider buying miles with a very specific use in mind. For what it’s worth, I don’t get any sort of kickback if you buy miles — I just want to make OMAAT readers aware of the deals that are available.

Link: Buy avianca lifemiles with this promotion with a 145% bonus

Between November 18 and November 21, 2026, the avianca lifemiles program is offering a bonus on purchased miles. While different members may be targeted for different offers, the standard offer that I see across accounts is for a bonus of up to 145%, structured as follows:

You’ll of course want to check your account to see what offer you’re targeted for, as it could be different. It’s common for lifemiles to promote one amount, and then actually offer a bigger bonus. Note that nowadays lifemiles promotions are generally targeted, so different members may see different offers, and on top of that, some members may not see any offers at all.

Ordinarily you can buy avianca lifemiles for 3.3 cents each, before any discounts or bonuses. That means that if you purchased 200,000 lifemiles (pre-bonus) with a 145% bonus (assuming you’re eligible for that), you’d receive a total of 490,000 lifemiles for $6,600, which is a cost of 1.35 cents per mile. That’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

If you wanted to buy as few miles as possible at the possible price, you’d want to buy exactly 51,000 miles at a cost of $1,683, and that would get you 122,500 lifemiles.

Unfortunately this isn’t quite the best promotion we’ve seen from the program, as we’ve seen bigger percentage bonuses in the past. However, it’s anyone’s guess when we see a bigger offer again.

The lifemiles program lets members purchase up to 500,000 miles per account per calendar year, before factoring in any bonuses. However, the limit per transaction is 200,000 miles, so if you really wanted to max out the number of miles you can buy, you’d need to make multiple transactions.

When members purchase lifemiles, they typically post nearly instantly. However, in rare cases it can take up to 72 hours for them to post. Mileage purchases are non-refundable, so once you make the purchase, it’s final.

When the lifemiles program does offer a promotion on purchased miles, it’s typically in the range of 120-130%. So this is within that range. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 120% bonus vs. 125% bonus vs. 130% bonus doesn’t differ that much.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

Mileage purchases are processed directly by avianca lifemiles, which means the purchase of miles does qualify as airfare spending. Therefore you’ll want to consider using one of the below cards for your purchase, since you’d earn bonus points for airfare purchases.

For context, avianca is in the Star Alliance, which means you can redeem lifemiles on all Star Alliance airlines without any fuel surcharges. Really this is the core value proposition of buying lifemiles, since this is a great way to book Star Alliance premium cabin seats at a huge discount. Check out my guide on how to redeem lifemiles for ideas on how to redeem these miles.

With a specific use in mind, this lifemiles promotion can be a great value, whether you’re looking at traveling in first class on All Nippon Airways, or are looking at traveling in business class on a countless number of airlines.

Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves and decide whether this makes sense or not.

Let me again emphasize that in some cases, lifemiles doesn’t have access to the same award availability as Star Alliance partners, for better or worse. Sometimes lifemiles doesn’t have access to partner awards that other programs do have access to, and other times the inverse is true.

That’s why I always recommend doing some “dummy” award searches before buying miles, so you can get a sense of how award availability lines up with your needs. Keep in mind that you can get even more value from the program with a lifemiles+ subscription, and lifemiles’ credit cards offer a discount on that.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider avianca lifemiles to be worth 1.3 cents each. That’s based on the redemption values on Star Alliance partners, as there’s tons of value to be had. I tend to value miles very conservatively, so if you’re maximizing miles you should be able to get way more value than that.

Miles with the lifemiles program don’t expire as long as you accrue some miles at least once every 12 months. Any mileage earning activity, including buying miles, will extend the expiration of your miles. However, redeeming miles as such doesn’t extend the expiration of your miles.

If you’re looking to earn lifemiles, the good news is that there are lots of options beyond outright buying them. Specifically, avianca lifemiles is partners with several bank currencies, including Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so there are lots of ways to pick up these miles.

For purchases through November 21, 2026, the avianca lifemiles program is offering a promotion on purchased miles. Different members may be eligible for different offers, though it appears that the standard offer is for up to a 145% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire miles for 1.35 cents each. This has the potential to represent a solid value, though I’d only recommend buying miles with a specific, short term use in mind.

#6274. Why Virgin Atlantic Is Targeting The 40 RAF Pilots Keeping Britain's F-35 Fleet Flyable

jremes84 & Ian Cramman | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The United Kingdom only has around four dozen trained F-35B fighter jet pilots and around 150 Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet pilots. Losing even a handful of these hard-to-replace pilots to commercial airlines is painful. They are targeted by British airlines, with Virgin Atlantic directly targeting them in its recruitment ads in 2024.

As the Royal Air Force is so much smaller than the United States Air Force (and Marines/Navy), it lacks depth in pilots. Training an F-35 fighter jet pilot can cost around $10 million, and new pilots graduating annually in the UK are often measured in the single digits.

With that being said, airlines will typically focus more on military transport pilots, such as those flying A330 MRTTs and A400Ms. Let's examine how Virgin Atlantic seeks to attract ex-RAF pilots and why this is a major problem for the Royal Air Force (and Royal Navy).

In 2024, the publication London Loves Business wrote that "RAF pilots who have operated on F-35 B Lightning II and Typhoon FGR4 are being offered double their annual salary to join Virgin." It adds that those pilots would be given routes to Barbados and New York to quit the RAF and fly with Virgin Atlantic.

The report stated that the pilots were being offered around double the money that they would typically earn flying for the Royal Air Force. At the time, the Virgin Atlantic advert was reported to read as follows:

"In order to be suitable, you must be operating, or have operated in the last three years on one of the following RAF Aircraft: F-35 B Lightning II, Typhoon FGR4. As a member of our Flight Crew, you will be joining the UK’s only exclusively long-haul airline. Flying out of London Heathrow to exciting destinations such as New York, San Francisco, Las Vegas, Delhi, Barbados, Antigua, and many more."

The advert went on to say that Virgin Atlantic operates the "youngest, cleanest, and most technologically sophisticated" widebody aircraft. Virgin is unusual in exclusively operating a fleet of widebody aircraft. Airlines poaching trained fighter jet pilots is common in many countries, including the United States. For air forces, this can be devastating as it costs around ten million dollars to train a frontline fighter jet pilot and takes years to replace them.

In a typical Western air force, there should be around 1.3 to 1.5 trained pilots for every fast jet. That said, Britain (and other air forces) have struggled to maintain this figure. While the US military has around 37,000 military pilots, including in the USAF, Army (helicopters), Marines, Navy, and Coast Guard, the British military likely has around 2,500.

Of these, around 1,500 are in the RAF and 500 are each in the Royal Navy and British Army. In 2014, the British Government revealed that there were 1,760 trained regular pilots in the RAF (excluding reserves and other aircrew), although that number has likely declined somewhat over the last decade. However, fighter jet pilots are a small subset of the overall group of pilots.

In late 2022, former Defense Secretary Ben Wallace revealed there were only 30 qualified British F-35 pilots, plus three exchange pilots. By 2023, that number had risen to 34, with seven more soon to graduate. By mid-2026, the RAF had received all of its initially ordered 48 F-38Bs, minus one that fell off an aircraft carrier.

Ideally, the RAF should have around 60–70 or so trained F-35B pilots, but it is unclear how many there are. There have been reports that the ratio may be closer to one pilot per jet, suggesting the RAF may now have somewhere around 45 to 50 trained F-35B pilots. Headlines will often talk about the fighter jets, how many there are, and how ready they are, but pilot availability is often a more pressing bottleneck.

The RAF procured a total of 137 Eurofighter Typhoons. Of these, 26 of the Tranche 1 fighter jets have now been retired, leaving a fleet of four remaining. These are stationed at RAF Mount Pleasant in the Falkland Islands as the UK's farthest air base with a permanent fighter jet presence. They are tasked with defending the islands from Argentina and are supported by A400Ms and A330 MRTTs.

The remaining Typhoons include 67 Tranche 2 and 40 Tranche 3 fighter jets. In January 2026, the British Government stated it would upgrade 40 of them with new radars and other systems. In July 2026, the budget was significantly increased, and it was reported that all would be upgraded. Britain had previously said the remaining four Tranche 1 fighter jets would retire in 2027, but now it is unclear.

Select aircraft of the Royal Air Force (per RAF)

There has not been an equivalent public disclosure for how many Typhoon fighter jet pilots are serving in the RAF. A reasonable range would be 140-160 trained Typhoon pilots. This would give the RAF a group of up to 200 fast jet pilots in total. Additionally, as of June 2026, the Royal Air Force had 119 trainee fast-jet pilots progressing through the training pipeline, from RAF Cranwell to the point of starting an Operational Conversion Unit.

Beginning around 2015 and then accelerating after COVID-19, the US airline industry has faced an unprecedented pilot shortage. This has affected regional airlines in particular and is made worse by retiring baby boomers. In response, the industry moved to attract former US military helicopter pilots; previously, the focus had been on fixed-wing pilots.

One of the most famous examples was that of Frontier Airlines, which launched its Rotor Transition Program to help military helicopter pilots transition and receive their fixed-wing qualifications. The program ended up being so successful that, Frontier's website said:

"Due to the overwhelmingly positive response and large number of applications we received for our Rotor Transition Program, we have temporarily closed the application window. Keep an eye out for more information regarding the application window opening and future recruitment events."

Meanwhile, there has not been the same recruitment drive in the UK, as the UK airline industry is much smaller, the military is much smaller (only a few hundred helicopter pilots), and converting is less straightforward. Instead, British industry focuses on recruiting former RAF transport pilots, fast jet pilots, airline cadets, and airline pilots from other airlines.

Why do airlines pay A350 and Boeing 777 Captains the same, even though no US carrier operates both of the aircraft types?

In both the United States and the United Kingdom, it is relatively straightforward for fighter jet pilots to transition from flying fixed-wing military aircraft to flying commercial passenger jets. With that being said, the United States has built a considerably more mature and streamlined process.

For ex-British fast-jet pilots, the primary challenge is obtaining the civilian licenses, certifications, and experience required by the UK Civil Aviation Authority. The CAA does recognize military flying experience through its Military Aircrew Accreditation Scheme, meaning that transitioning pilots do not need to start from scratch.

They can get credits toward their Commercial Pilot License, but still generally need to complete their ATPL theoretical knowledge tests, civilian flight tests, and so on. The entire process of converting from military to commercial jets often takes six to twelve months, depending on how much training credit is granted and the airline course start date.

In the US, the process typically takes around three to nine months. For comparison, for those starting from scratch in the UK, it typically takes three to over eight years for a pilot to fly with a major airline. It's between two and over six years in the United States, depending on various factors.

According to Planespotters.net, Virgin Atlantic currently operates an all-widebody fleet of 44 aircraft with an average age of 8.4 years. These include 14 Airbus A330s (six A330-300s and nine A330neos), 12 Airbus A350-1000s, and 17 Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. This makes it one of the largest all-widebody fleets in the world, although, for comparison, this total would only represent around 15% of Emirates' giant all-widebody fleet.

Virgin Atlantic's outstanding A330-900 orders will replace its remaining fleet of legacy A330-300s by 2027 while growing the overall fleet. The airline was established in 1984 and serves around 29 destinations, mostly from its hubs at London Heathrow and Manchester. The airline is also a member of SkyTeam and is 49% owned by Delta Air Lines. Virgin Atlantic has evolved into a mixed network carrier that serves both leisure-heavy destinations and business-heavy routes.

It offers flights to Caribbean destinations like Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Grenada, Jamaica (Montego Bay), Mexico's Cancun, St. Lucia, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines. Its US destinations include Las Vegas, Orlando, Miami, Tampa, as well as some other less leisure-heavy destinations, such as Boston. #6273. Buy JetBlue TrueBlue Points With 125% Bonus (1.43 Cents Each): Worth It?

JetBlue is currently offering a limited time 125% bonus on purchased points. With this, TrueBlue members can purchase points for as little as 1.43 cents each. Is this a good deal?

Let’s take a look at the details — so that I don’t bury the lede, let me say that I’d only recommend taking advantage of this JetBlue buy points offer with a specific use in mind, and primarily if you intend to redeem on partner airlines.

Link: Buy JetBlue TrueBlue points with this promotion with a 125% bonus

Between 12AM ET on November 18 and 11:59PM ET on December 31, 2026, JetBlue TrueBlue is offering a bonus on purchased points, which is close to being in line with the best offers from the program.

JetBlue TrueBlue is offering up to a 125% bonus on purchasing points. The offer is structured as follows, with three tiers of bonuses:

Let me emphasize that this appears to be the standard offer, though sometimes different members are targeted for different offers. You’ll want to log into your TrueBlue account to see what you’re eligible for.

JetBlue ordinarily allows TrueBlue members to purchase up to 200,000 points per calendar year. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 300,000 points.

JetBlue ordinarily charges 3.0 cents per purchased point, before the 7.5% federal excise tax. After factoring in the federal excise tax, the standard cost is 3.225 cents per purchased point.

With this JetBlue points sale, you’d pay the following amounts per purchased point, factoring in the bonus:

If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to purchase a total of 45,000 points (20,000 points plus 25,000 bonus points) at a cost of $645, which gets you the cost of 1.43 cents per point, including all taxes.

Meanwhile if you wanted to purchase the most possible points, you’d want to purchase a total of 675,000 points (300,000 points plus 375,000 bonus points) at a cost of $9,675, which gets you the same cost per point.

Officially, JetBlue states that it can take up to 72 hours for purchased points to post. However, in practice (based on my test experience of buying points), they’ll typically post almost instantly. There’s no guarantee of that, though.

Note that the purchase of JetBlue points is non-refundable, so only make a purchase if you have a specific use in mind. Furthermore, the purchase of JetBlue points doesn’t count toward Mosaic elite status, in case that’s a consideration.

When JetBlue does offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically in the range of 120-130%. So this is within that range. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 120% bonus vs. 125% bonus vs. 130% bonus doesn’t differ that much.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

JetBlue TrueBlue points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you use a JetBlue credit card to pay for your purchase, it wouldn’t code as a JetBlue purchase.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See my guide to the best credit cards for buying points.

JetBlue TrueBlue has become more interesting on the redemption front in recent years, and there are definitely some ways to get outsized value. For that matter, in some cases people may find value in topping off their points balance, in order to have enough points for a redemption.

Let’s look at the opportunities to redeem TrueBlue points, first for travel on JetBlue, and then for travel on partner airlines. For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider TrueBlue points to be worth 1.3 cents each.

When it comes to redeeming on JetBlue, TrueBlue is a revenue based frequent flyer program. That means the cost of an award redemption is correlated to how much a ticket would cost in cash, though it’s not always a consistent cent per point value.

In my experience, you’ll typically get around 1.3-1.5 cents per TrueBlue point toward the cost of a ticket on JetBlue in economy.

Just as an example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, which costs $334 if paying cash. If redeeming TrueBlue points, you’d pay 22,500 points plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.46 cents of value per point.

As another example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to San Francisco, which has both economy and Mint business class. If paying cash, you’d pay $198 or $676. If redeeming points, you’d pay 14,200 points or 47,300 points, plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.35-1.42 cents of value per point.

As you can see, these are situations where you probably shouldn’t buy TrueBlue points. For example, there’s no reason to acquire 14,200 points for 1.43 cents each, for a total cost of $203 (plus the $5.60 in taxes & fees), when you could instead just outright buy the ticket for $198.

One thing to keep in mind is that if you have JetBlue’s most premium card, you can get a 15% award rebate, so maybe there is a little upside there.

JetBlue TrueBlue has gotten better about adding redemptions on partner airlines in recent times, including on Qatar Airways, Condor, and United Airlines. We’re also now seeing redemptions added on China Airlines. There’s definitely some value to be had here.

For example, you could redeem just 47,400 points for Condor business class one-way from Frankfurt to Toronto. That’s an amazing opportunity to buy points and immediately get outsized value.

As another example, you could redeem 29,600 points for Qatar Airways business class one-way from Munich to Doha. Given the points acquisition costs we’re talking about, that’s an amazing value.

One caveat I’d just like to add is that partner award availability can be really tough to come by, so only buy points if you have an understanding of what that availability is like.

As I see it, the decision of whether to buy points from a particular loyalty program comes down both to how valuable that currency is, and it also comes down to how many ways there are to acquire the currency. So that’s why it’s worth mentioning that JetBlue TrueBlue points are really easy to acquire.

At this point, JetBlue partners with virtually all transferable points currencies, so you can earn TrueBlue points through Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One Rewards, Chase Ultimate Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Wells Fargo, etc. Bilt, Chase, Citi, and Wells Fargo, have 1:1 transfer ratios, while Amex has a 5:4 ratio, and Capital One has a 5:3 ratio.

Another option is to apply for JetBlue’s co-branded credit cards, which often have large welcome bonuses. Those points of course won’t post anywhere close to instantly, but it’s a good strategy for building up your TrueBlue points balance over time.

So there’s no shortage of opportunities to earn TrueBlue points — it’s just a function of whether you’d rather part with cash or a points currency.

Through December 31, 2026, JetBlue is selling TrueBlue points with up to a 125% bonus, an opportunity to buy points for as little as 1.43 cents each. I’d only buy JetBlue points with a specific use in mind. There’s value to be had in some situations, such as if you have a particular Qatar Airways or Condor award you want to book, and there’s availability.

Anyone plan on buying JetBlue TrueBlue points with a bonus?

#6271. Most Airports Cap Concession Prices… But The System Is A Total Joke

Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.

However, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced? Well, or perhaps more accurately, they are enforced, but using very dishonest math. The backstory of this is interesting.

Airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal. An airport is like a shopping mall with a very captive audience, and as you’d expect, rent for businesses in airports is absolutely through the roof, as a result of that.

But in order to balance things out and prevent retailers from exploiting consumers, over 80% of airports in the United States specifically stipulate the maximum prices that airports can charge consumers. These terms are typically baked into the contracts that airport retailers sign, and failure to adhere to the rules can lead to consequences, at least in theory.

The airports with pricing caps for airport businesses generally fall into one of two categories:

If there are supposed to be rules in place capping airport pricing, then why is this such a widespread issue? More Perfect Union recently published a great video investigating this issue, and it’s a fascinating watch. First they actually analyze airport pricing, and then they confront airport authorities about the lack of enforcement.

Here’s what’s interesting — airport retailers do have to submit comparisons for benchmark pricing, to prove that they’re not violating rules and exploiting customers. The issue is what kind of businesses are considered comparable for the purposes of “street pricing.”

For example, 9NEWS recently investigated this at Denver Airport, finding that a basic Starbucks coffee cost $4.55 in the airport, compared to $2.95 outside the airport (a 54% markup), and a bag of cashews cost $9.99 in the airport, compared to $4.74 outside the airport (a 110% markup).

The airport’s VP of Concessions agreed to sit down with the reporter to discuss this, and she said the results of his investigation were great news — she suggested that 93% of the prices were compliant, and said “that’s pretty darn good.” How could that be, given the high markups compared to nearby businesses?

The issue boils down to how much latitude businesses have to submit pricing comparisons:

What’s wild is how the airport official responds to Starbucks just having consistent pricing, and violating the rules:

VP of Concessions: “What I get from that is, they’re looking for consistency, across the board, across the nation, across the world.”Reporter: “I can’t help but think that travelers may be looking for consistency, but if they see a cheaper cup of coffee, they’ll probably be okay with it.”VP of Concessions: “I don’t know the answer to that. This is how we take care of our passengers, by ensuring that they are paying fair and transparent pricing, while supporting our business partners.”

Back to the original story, the More Perfect Union reporter confronted the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey about pricing like $6.89 for one liter of Smart Water, compared to closer to $3.50 at nearby bodegas.

The response was that “comparing a Hudson to a bodega isn’t appropriate,” because “Hudson is a specialty market.” The approved price comparison was reportedly based on the price of water at Tablet Works, a “wellness & concierge pharmacy” in a high-end mall.

The other thing to keep in mind is that a large percentage of airport retailers and restaurants are run by the same few companies, like HMSHost, which is a subsidiary of Avolta. So clearly they have a centralized approach to submitting pricing comparisons, and know exactly what they’re doing. Interestingly, the few independent businesses in some airports were found to have the most honest pricing.

So to sum it up, the system is designed to be rigged. Airport authorities can technically pretend they’re looking out for consumers by setting a cap. Retailers can submit pricing comparisons to the highest prices they can find anywhere. Then airport authorities verify those prices to pretend they’re doing their jobs.

Airports are obviously complicit in all of this. They make money by charging sky high rent, and the reason they can do that is because retailers can charge hugely inflated prices. The more profits retailers make, the more airports can charge in rent. And they know that no consumer is going to avoid an airport because of high concession costs.

Around 80% of airports in the United States cap the prices that retailers can charge, so in most cases, you’re not supposed to be paying more than 15% above “street pricing.” The issue is the liberties that businesses can take with what constitutes “street pricing.”

The price of the bottle of water or smoothie you’re buying isn’t compared to what you’d pay at a nearby gas station and smoothie shop, but instead, is being compared to what you’d pay at Erewhon. Talk about a very broken system, with no incentives for any party to actually be honest…

What do you make of this airport pricing situation?
