Many of us have been there: You book a flight through an airline's major hub, but your first segment is delayed and you miss your connecting flight, only to find out the next available flight with an open seat is hours away (or even the next morning). Or maybe you're trying to get home, but your flight is canceled, and you're stuck at your destination an extra night.

And when things go really wrong, it could be days before you can reach your destination.

There's no way to get that lost time back, but trip delay protection can come to the rescue if you used the right credit card to pay for your trip.

Trip delay protection reimburses reasonable out-of-pocket costs (lodging, meals, toiletries and local transportation) when a trip you paid for with an eligible card is delayed past a set threshold for a covered reason. You’ll pay these costs upfront, then file a claim for reimbursement so you're not left to cover those expenses yourself.

This coverage is secondary — meaning it only kicks in after you receive any other compensation. So if an airline provides food vouchers, you can't also request reimbursement for those meals. Even if the airline covers some expenses, you can still file a claim for any remaining expenses, like if you book a hotel at your own expense.

Importantly, a canceled flight is not automatically a covered trip delay. The cancellation generally must leave you stranded long enough to meet the policy's time requirement, result from a covered reason and involve a trip booked according to the card's payment rules.

Related: The best credit cards that offer trip cancellation and interruption insurance

While numerous travel rewards credit cards include trip delay protection, each policy is a little different.

*Eligibility and benefit level varies by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Can I get flight delay compensation? These are the ways you qualify

The $500 headline makes these policies look more alike than they are. In practice, they differ on how soon coverage begins, whether the cap scales with each traveler or ticket and whether the way you paid actually activates the benefit.

Being reimbursed per traveler means you actually have a much higher limit to work with. For example, if you're traveling as a family of four and spend a total of $800 on two hotel rooms, meals and transportation, you'd be reimbursed for all $800 if the policy is "per traveler", assuming everyone qualifies and all expenses are eligible. But if the card is capped at $500 per trip, you'll only get a $500 payout, regardless of how many people are traveling, leaving you to foot the rest of the bill.

For your travel to be covered, you must have paid for the original trip with the credit card that provides coverage. Some cards, like those issued by Capital One or Chase, include award travel if you paid for the taxes and fees on your flight with an eligible card.

However, other issuers, including American Express, require you to pay for the full cost of the trip with the card (or with reward points from the program). Amex also requires cardholders to pay for round-trip travel with their eligible card, though it's not as limiting as it sounds. Two separate one-ways still count, as long as both were purchased with the same card.

The also requires round-trip travel purchased on the card.

Before counting on coverage, read your card’s Guide to Benefits before you book.

Related: Times your credit card's travel insurance might not cover you

Trip delay coverage is only set up to cover expenses from lengthy delays rather than minor inconveniences. A minimum six-hour delay is required before coverage kicks in, and some cards require longer.

Some cards also allow for reimbursement of expenses during a forced overnight stay. That overnight provision makes some 12-hour policies more useful than they first appear because a flight that was supposed to take off at 10 p.m. and is now at 6 a.m. would qualify.

Every card in our table covers bad weather and equipment failure. Beyond that, the lists differ. Capital One and Chase also cover strikes. Amex and Citi don't, but they do cover lost or stolen passports.

Traffic or arriving late at the airport will not turn a missed flight into a covered delay. A previously announced or "known" disruption may also be excluded, so don't book a flight during a hurricane that's already started and expect to be covered.

Capital One has a pretty minimal umbrella of coverage when it comes to who's eligible. Trip delay protection usually only covers you, your spouse and your dependent children under the age of 22.

Chase has a more inclusive definition of family, including children (of any age), as well as parents, siblings, grandparents and more. Covered Chase family members also do not necessarily need to be traveling with the cardholder, as long as an eligible ticket was purchased with a qualifying card.

But Amex cards with this benefit generally cover companions who are traveling with you, even if they're unrelated, as well as tickets you purchased with your card on behalf of your spouse/domestic partner or unmarried dependent children up to age 19 (or under age 26 if a full-time student at an accredited college or university) even when they aren't traveling with you.

Chase doesn't list a maximum number of claims anyone can file, but American Express restricts you to two claims per eligible card per 12-month period. That distinction matters for frequent travelers.

Two claims may sound sufficient, but a frequent traveler could use both during one rough round-trip. For someone who flies regularly, an unlimited annual claim cap can be a meaningful advantage.

Claims can take weeks to be processed and paid out, which can make other card benefits you have useful in the meantime. Airport lounge access might cover the cost of food and drinks while you're waiting out a delay rather than having to collect and submit restaurant receipts, for example.

The exception is the : If your Alaska Airlines flight booked directly with Alaska on the card is delayed two hours or more, or canceled within 24 hours of departure, the primary cardholder automatically gets a $50 credit. It expires in 48 hours, so use it during the delay.

Though it's a modest credit, it can help cover your meal or transportation in real time, no paperwork required (and doesn't preclude you from filing a trip delay claim for other expenses later).

Related: Who is covered by your credit card travel insurance?

The most convenient way to file a claim is online through your card issuer's benefits website. You'll find the link within your online account or benefits guide. You can also initiate a claim by calling the phone number on the back of your card.

Usually, you must initiate a claim within 30 to 60 days of the event. I recommend opening the claim as soon as possible, even if you don't have all the receipts and paperwork yet. You'll typically have an additional grace period to submit all documentation after the claim has been formally opened.

Expect to provide four types of documentation:

Take screenshots of delay notifications, canceled segments and rebooking options before they disappear from the airline's app. Most airlines allow you to request statements confirming the delay and its reason through online customer service.

Related: Flight delayed? 4 things to do to get trip delay reimbursement from your credit card

When deciding between earning slightly more rewards and activating stronger insurance, the insurance may be the better trade on an expensive, complicated or disruption-prone itinerary. You'll also want to double-check that your trip delay coverage rules match how you actually booked.

Before travel, save your card's current benefits guide, use the card in the required way and keep every receipt. You certainly hope to never use this benefit, but it can be extremely valuable if you do.

#6269. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6268. The Manufacturing Decision Boeing Was Forced To Make When It Developed The 737 MAX

In August 2011, Boeing officially launched its 737 MAX program after American Airlines made the historic decision to split its once all-Boeing fleet and buy 50% of its next-generation narrowbodies from Airbus. AA was facing rising fuel expenses and operating an aging fleet of roughly 300 McDonnell Douglas MD-80 jets. Thus, in July of that same year, AA revealed that of the 460 jets it planned to procure to modernize its fleet, 260 would be from the A320 family.

By mid-2011, Airbus had accumulated more than 1,000 orders for its re-engined A320neo. The airline chose to award more than half of its future fleet slots to Airbus because it already had a production-ready jet. In the aftermath, Boeing leadership abandoned plans for an all-new composite narrowbody within hours. Developing a new mainline jet would have required an estimated $10 billion to $12 billion and up to a decade of research. Instead, it committed to developing a re-engined 737 to retain its portion of the order.

Modifying the legacy 737 airframe was estimated to cost a third as much, with initial deliveries expected in 2017. Boeing also pursued certification as a derivative of the original 1967 type to entice operators with a cheap transition, even earning a $1 million per-aircraft rebate from launch customer Southwest Airlines. However, preserving grandfathered handling characteristics while integrating larger, higher-bypass turbofans onto the low-slung 1960s airframe imposed engineering constraints that forced Boeing to make a fateful compromise: the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System.

At first, Boeing executives James Albaugh and Jim McNerney placed a wager on the Yellowstone Project, believing that airlines would wait for a 2020 clean-sheet composite plane instead of using the Airbus A320neo. Instead, to immediately save 15% on fuel consumption, operators quickly acquired more than 1,000 European narrowbodies. McNerney was then forced to abandon the Yellowstone study over the course of one weekend after American Airlines CEO Gerard Arpey threatened to terminate the airline's exclusive purchase agreement unless Boeing promptly supplied a re-engined 737.

Following the 737 MAX's formal debut on August 30, 2011, commercial contracts obliged Boeing to follow an accelerated derivative timetable. Southwest Airlines, the first client, ordered 150 aircraft in December 2011 under an arrangement that called for a $1 million rebate per plane if regulators imposed pilot simulator training. With Southwest eventually buying over 240 airframes, avoiding hundreds of millions of dollars in penalties necessitated certifying the 737 MAX using its original 1967 type certificate on a tight timetable.

Aerodynamic concessions were necessary to meet that deadline while mounting larger CFM International LEAP-1B engines onto the low-slung 1960s airframe. At high angles of attack, an uncontrollable nose-up pitching tendency was produced by cantilevering the nacelles forward and upward. Engineers used the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System software to digitally mask the pitch anomaly, accelerating delivery while introducing a single-sensor flight control vulnerability, instead of implementing structural wing modifications that would cause certification delays and simulator training.

Boeing engineers had to extend the nose landing gear on the 737 MAX by 8 inches (20 cm) more than the Next Generation series, as well as cantilever the nacelles forward and upward using structural titanium pylons in order to fit 69-inch (175 cm) CFM International LEAP-1B engines onto the low-slung 1967 737 airframe. These larger engine cowls, which were positioned above the wing chord, produced excess aerodynamic lift ahead of the center of gravity at high angles of attack, creating an uncontrollable nose-up pitching tendency that went against federal regulations for linear control column force progression toward an aerodynamic stall.

Rather than executing costly structural wing redesigns or installing mechanical counterweights, Boeing relied on the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System software to automatically command nose-down horizontal stabilizer trim without pilot input. To preserve grandfathered type-certificate commonality and avoid simulator training penalties, program officials positioned the software as a minor modification to the existing speed trim system and obtained Federal Aviation Administration approval to strip all references to the system from flight crew manuals, leaving operators and pilots unaware of its existence.

During certification flight testing, Boeing engineers increased the software's ability at lower airspeeds to push the horizontal stabilizer by 2.5 degrees based on input from a single angle-of-attack sensor, without reassessing single-point failure dangers. Boeing withheld internal simulator data from the Federal Aviation Administration, demonstrating that a company test pilot took more than 10 seconds to diagnose and counter an uncommanded activation, a delay classified as catastrophic internally when compared to the four-second federal response standard.

How the 767 is bridging the gap to a new generation of widebody twinjets in its twilight.

Boeing's Yellowstone Project originally divided commercial fleet renewal into three clean-sheet phases: Y1 for narrowbodies, Y2 for mid-sized jets, and Y3 for widebodies. While Y2 materialized as the composite 787 Dreamliner, severe delays and cost overruns on that program exhausted Boeing's engineering capacity and capital for Y1 and Y3. Simultaneously, Y1 studies stalled when engine manufacturers elected to frame their next-generation turbofans around the A320neo and air carriers ran out of patience, turning to the European planemaker.

Abandoning Y1 for a modified 737 forced engineers to integrate modern high-bypass engines on a fuselage created for 1960s crashworthiness and operating regulations. Grandfathering the type certificate allowed the 737 MAX to use older mechanical flight controls rather than adopt modern fly-by-wire. Thus, engineers could only use software-driven flight controls to a limited extent in compensating for the aircraft's size and weight. Instead, they modified the existing mechanical Speed Trim System with MCAS, using its jackscrew to move the horizontal stabilizer.

This reliance on grandfathered systems created direct performance gaps that a clean-sheet Y1 design would have eliminated through new systems and certification criteria. Unlike the 787, which features a digital alert system, the 737 MAX retained legacy warning lights and its AOA disagree alert. Disastrously, Boeing engineers discovered in August 2017 that the AOA alert was inoperable on more than 80% of delivered aircraft. Management deferred an MCAS software patch until 2020 and withheld the defect from operators and regulators until after the fatal crash in October 2018 of Lion Air Flight 610.

Shareholders have some serious questions for the manufacturer.

To reclaim narrowbody market share lost to the Airbus A320neo, Boeing structured the 737 MAX around minimizing airline transition costs and preserving existing fleet infrastructure. The high-bypass turbofans of the A320neo achieved 15% better fuel efficiency than the 737 NG thanks to large volumes of air around the engine core. Boeing required a very wide front fan diameter on its 737 MAX to match that, a design criterion that clashed with the 737's low ground clearance.

Boeing commercial leadership recognized that any derivative aircraft requiring full-flight simulator sessions would forfeit sales to legacy 737 operators. These commercial imperatives were codified directly into customer purchase agreements, most notably SWA's 240-strong order that included a $1 million rebate per delivered aircraft. Consequently, Boeing set minimal difference training as a core program objective. That meant pilot transition instruction from the 737 NG would be just a computer-based course, avoiding the expense of building and certifying new full-flight simulators before service entry.

Thus, to preserve the 1967 type certificate and avoid costly landing gear and wing-box redesigns, CFM International constrained the LEAP-1B to a 69-inch fan (175 cm) and a 9:1 bypass ratio, using 18 carbon-fiber composite blades to reduce rotational mass. Even with a flattened nacelle bottom, fitting the 6,129-pound (2,780 kg) engines required lengthening the nose gear by 8 inches (20 cm) and cantilevering the powerplants forward and upward on titanium pylons.

Positioned ahead of and above the wing chord, these enlarged cowls generated excess aerodynamic lift at high angles of attack, inducing an uncommanded nose-up pitching tendency that violated federal stall-recovery handling standards. Because extensive wing modifications would have invalidated the standing type certificate and triggered mandatory simulator retraining, Boeing engineers compensated digitally through MCAS to command 2.5 degrees of nose-down trim using data from a single external angle-of-attack vane.

The software enabled the airframe to meet certification handling rules on paper, but leadership went on to lobby the FAA to omit the software from flight crew manuals and differences tables, so Boeing could secure Level B training approval to win back airline orders. A conventional runaway stabilizer shows trim wheel rotation that pilots can recognize and disable. Meanwhile, MCAS was in discrete increments, and omitting the system deprived flight crews of the diagnostic knowledge to distinguish it as the source of a malfunction.

The families of those who perished continue to seek justice.

That software reliance was predetermined by 737 sales contracts negotiated years before the prototype flew. Southwest Airlines, the first customer, ordered 150 737 MAX aircraft in December 2011, with the agreement that Boeing would pay a $1 million rebate per jet if the Federal Aviation Administration permitted simple, simulator-based training for pilots migrating from the 737 NG to the MAX. With Southwest eventually buying over 240 airframes, avoiding hundreds of millions of dollars in penalties forced leadership to maintain common type ratings and remove system references from manuals.

During the initial 737 MAX 8 flight test campaign starting in January 2016, Boeing originally designed the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System to operate exclusively during high-speed, flaps-up wind-up turns. Lift generated by the forward-mounted CFM International LEAP-1B28 nacelles lightened control column forces as angle of attack increased, violating FAA stall characteristic parameters. Subsequently, software authority was extended to lower airspeeds by developers, allowing 2.5 degrees of nose-down horizontal stabilizer trim based on single-sensor AOA input.

In 2017, 737 Chief Technical Pilot Mark Forkner emailed the FAA Seattle Aircraft Evaluation Group requesting permission to remove references to the MCAS from the Flight Crew Operations Manual, unaware of the extended speed range of MCAS authority. In November 2016, Forkner discovered the system activating aggressively at lower airspeeds in simulator testing, claiming he had unknowingly misled regulators. Yet, Boeing officials never briefed the Seattle Aircraft Evaluation Group on the expanded low-speed authority or corrected their earlier operational representations.

#6267. Emirates Finally Revamping Dubai Lounges: Temporary New First Class Lounge Now Open

Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

While I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

Well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has announced plans to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a new global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

As is the case for any airline, rolling out a new lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:

Emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:

“Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This new First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”

We’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary new first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:

Featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

When it comes to the temporary new first class lounge, here are the details:

As much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉

But when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

Emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s new lounge aesthetic.

We’ve just seen the opening of a new temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

The new design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

What do you make of Emirates’ new lounge concept?

#6266. FAA Technician Only Unlocked The Door: Inside The Oversight Gap Behind The Nationwide Ground Stop

Last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We quickly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:

So, what’s actually going on here? A new report sheds some more light on this…

CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

According to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications issues across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”

Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

This type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”

With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

While the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

It also has to be pointed out that the March 2025 memo about a reduction in oversight came just weeks after Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.

That’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

We have to be honest, in general, politicians are really bad at accountability, and being honest when things go wrong. But whether you like Trump’s policies or not, there’s no denying that he takes lack of accountability to new levels. Everything good that happens is immediately his doing, and everything bad is Biden’s fault.

It would be nice if one Trump administration official actually had the introspection to say “hey, let’s make sure this doesn’t happen again,” rather than just yelling “give me $50 billion” and “Biden, Buttigieg, Biden, Buttigieg.”

We’re getting a clearer picture of the circumstances that caused the nationwide ground stop last Friday, the biggest disruption to US air travel since 9/11. A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

While the FAA claims that there’s supposed to be oversight of contractor work, in this case the FAA employee was reportedly just tasked with unlocking the door. The approach to overseeing contractor work is reportedly a new system as of March 2025, where contractor work went from being viewed as “requests” to being viewed as “notifications,” with just a handful of people to oversee these requests. This came just weeks after hundreds of employees were laid off from the FAA, thanks to Musk’s DOGE.

What do you make of this FAA contractor oversight situation?

#6264. Atmos Rewards Business Card Changes: Higher(ish) Fee, New Benefits

Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian, and that includes three co-branded credit cards. There’s only one business credit card in the portfolio, and that’s the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

Along those lines, there’s a major update, as the card has just undergone a full refresh. The bad news is that the card’s annual fee has gone up considerably (at least for most people), and the benefits have also changed. Let’s take a look, because as you’d expect, the changes are a mixed bag.

The good news is that there’s a huge incentive to apply for the card, given the massive limited-time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is undergoing some major updates. This includes a higher annual fee, new rewards structure, and new set of perks. However, these changes only apply to new card members, as existing card members will keep the old benefits (and fee).

Let me emphasize that the card has a huge limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. So that’s a major incentive to apply for the card, if you’re eligible. I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so to me, that’s worth $1,350.

With that out of the way, let’s go over the details…

The Atmos Rewards Business Card now has a flat $195 annual fee, which covers the primary card member and any employee cards. Previously, the card had an annual fee of $70 per company, plus $25 per employee, so the minimum annual fee you’d pay would be $95.

It goes without saying that this change represents a significant increase in the annual fee, unless you had more than four employee credit cards on your account.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card also has a new rewards structure. The card now offers:

What has changed here is the new 10x points for booking through Atmos for Business (great for those who can use it), as well as a full overhaul of the 2x points categories. Previously the card offered 2x points on eligible gas, EV charging stations, shipping, and local transit purchases (including rideshare), while now it just offers 2x points on dining. As before, the card offers one status point for every $3 spent, with no cap.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card is picking up quite a few new benefits that it didn’t previously offer:

The refreshed card also keeps a first checked bag free and preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian flights for the card member and up to six guests on the same reservation when the trip is paid with the card, a 20% rebate on eligible inflight purchases, a 10% rewards bonus for cardholders with an eligible Bank of America small business account, and no foreign transaction fees.

Let me emphasize that the card will no longer offer a $99 companion fare, so that’s being replaced by the new 50% off vouchers that can be earned with spending.

As of November 18, 2026, customers who apply for a new Atmos Rewards Business Card will be receiving the refreshed card, with the new benefits and fee.

Applications submitted before November 18 will continue under the prior card offering. What’s interesting is that current cardholders will keep their existing benefits, and will not be automatically moved over. However, you can call up Bank of America if you’d like to see about the opportunity of switching.

As of now, it sounds like there are no plans to transition people to the new system, so existing card members shouldn’t be negatively impacted by this.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card changes are a mixed bag. First, I want to once again emphasize that since existing card members aren’t impacted by these changes, I don’t think there should be too much frustration here.

In the past, the Atmos Rewards Business Card basically felt like the business version of the $95 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more), while now the card feels more like a hybrid between that and the $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more), in terms of both cost and benefits.

Admittedly it’s hard to do an apples-to-apples comparison between personal and business cards, because at least in theory, they’re supposed to serve different purposes. So here’s my take:

So I don’t have a terribly strong take here, other than wishing that spending on the card were a bit more lucrative, and more competitive with what’s offered by the Atmos Rewards Summit Card. The Summit Card will continue to be my go-to card for Atmos Rewards.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has just undergone some major changes, though they don’t impact existing card members. For new applicants, the card now has a $195 annual fee, compared to the old fee of $70 for the company, and $25 per person.

The card is also getting a new set of benefits, including a new rewards structure, additional perks, and new incentives for spending. People will have varying takes as to whether these changes are positive or negative, depending on their consumer patterns.

My biggest takeaway is that the bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending is excellent, and a great incentive to apply for the card.

What do you make of these Atmos Rewards Business Card changes?

I'd heard rumblings about CardPointers for years before I finally started using it early last year. I've found it to be a very useful tool for auto-enrolling me in credit offers and helping me track my savings over time. It also helps me keep track of my various credit card perks (I have some 27 credit cards, so this is vital).

Special TPG deal for 50% off CardPointers: Use this special TPG link: cardpointers.com/partner/tpg

CardPointers is an app for both iOS and Android phones and a browser extension that automatically adds offers across your credit cards, including American Express, Chase and Citi cards.

It has everything from location-based reminders for nearby offers to alerts that tell you the best credit card to use for each store. It can also flag when a statement credit is available for a particular brand.

Best of all, it auto-enrolls my credit cards in all offers, so I never have to go hunting for specific credit card offers. In fact, I just shop normally and consider it a special occasion when a surprise statement credit hits my account.

I have all my Citi cards linked to CardPointers. Whenever I open up the Citi website on my computer, CardPointers automatically enrolls all my cards with any new offers. As you can see from this screenshot, CardPointers worked in the background to add 841 new merchant offers to my eligible cards.

A CardPointers extension sits in my browser and keeps a current tally of all the offers I'm enrolled in, in alphabetical order.

Just one example: I got a $5 statement credit for buying a $10 dinner at Burger King back in September. That was an offer I'd been auto-enrolled in by Cardpointers.

Here's another surprise credit I got on my American Express account after a stay at the Grand Hyatt Resort & Spa in Kauai, Hawaii, earlier this year.

And in another more recent example, I was looking to buy an Oura ring (currently on sale for Black Friday), and it showed me I had a $200 credit available that I hadn't used yet.

I'd conservatively say that Cardpointers has saved me several hundred dollars this year.

As I mentioned, there is a free version of Cardpointers, but I recommend upgrading to the paid version, which usually costs $100 per year. You can easily get that much value from the tool, especially if you have multiple credit cards to keep track of. But right now, it's 50% off through a special TPG offer.

The free version allows you to add and track your credit cards, but only one card of each brand. The paid version is CardPointers+ and includes:

And right now, during a special sale, you can get 50% off a CardPointers+ membership, so it's a great time to buy. In fact, I'm going to use the sale to buy a lifetime membership at half off. (Regular price is $300).

To get the special offer, use this special TPG link: cardpointers.com/partner/tpg

It's fairly straightforward to use CardPointers, but you'll need to input some data along the way. To start, download the mobile app, then you'll be prompted to create an account. Once you've been verified via email, you'll be able to input your credit card data. You won't need to input credit card numbers, but CardPointers will ask you for the card name and the date you opened it (to better track available offers).

You'll be prompted to input your cards. It's pretty straightforward, though a bit time-consuming.

I've only scratched the surface of everything CardPointers can do, but after using it for nearly two years, I'm a convert. With some 27 credit cards in my wallet, keeping track of all the available offers, statement credits and other benefits can feel like a full-time job. CardPointers takes much of that work off my plate.

What I love most is that I don't have to spend hours scrolling through my credit card accounts looking for offers to activate. CardPointers does the heavy lifting for me, automatically adding eligible offers and helping me take advantage of savings I might otherwise miss. There's nothing quite like getting a surprise statement credit for a purchase you were going to make anyway.

I've conservatively saved several hundred dollars this year alone, including credits on everything from fast food to luxury hotel stays. And it's not just about the money. The time I've saved and the peace of mind that I'm not leaving valuable credit card benefits on the table make the service even more worthwhile.

While the free version is a good place to start, I think the premium CardPointers+ membership is well worth the $100 annual price, particularly for anyone juggling multiple rewards credit cards. And with the current 50% off promotion, it's an even more compelling deal. In fact, I like the service so much that I'm planning to upgrade to a lifetime membership.

If you're serious about maximizing your credit card rewards, benefits and statement credits, CardPointers is one of those tools that can quickly pay for itself. It's become an essential part of my credit card strategy, and I can't imagine managing my growing collection of cards without it.

#6262. Can Rocky Save the World?

Anthony Ippolito (Sylvester Stallone) in I Play Rocky

Sylvester Stallone has been a Hollywood institution for so long — his breakthrough movie Rocky premiered 50 years ago — that his previous underdog status as a struggling actor seems perfectly mythic in the new behind-the-scenes biographical drama I Play Rocky.

The fairy-tale aspect of I Play Rocky comes from its background story. In this, young Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) is a virtually homeless outsider, working at a movie theater, who after spending 16 months on writing eight screenplays, joins the creative zeitgeist of 1970s Hollywood, also known as the American Renaissance. It is this personal journey that illuminates the Stallone legend that climaxes with Rocky winning the Academy Award for best picture over such esteemed movies as Taxi Driver, Network, Bound for Glory, and All the President’s Men.

Starting with Stallone practicing elocution (using Walt Whitman’s “I Sing the Body Electric”) to soften his rough New York accent, the film then places him against odds in an era of cultural ferment that included such films as Altman’s The Long Goodbye and Coppola’s The Conversation. (Stallone pays particular attention to the intonation of Coppola’s actors repeating the line “He’d kill us if he found out.”) Screenwriter Peter Gamble doesn’t make that detail ominous but simplifies the life-or-death aspect of Stallone’s career and artistic ambition as part of the wannabe actor’s desperate, working-class consciousness — inspired by viewing the heavyweight championship boxing match between Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner. It’s easier to take than the sociological theme in Green Book, the egregious previous film of director Peter Farrelly. I Play Rocky regains the genial humanism of such Farrelly brothers’ movies as Me, Myself and Irene, Stuck on You, and The Ringer, and especially the Farrelly brothers’ script for Outside Providence.

Kiki Seto (Talia Shire) and Anthony Ippolito (Sylvester Stallone) in I Play Rocky

Stallone’s ambition is epitomized by his insistence that the Rocky screenplay he wrote in four days and sold to producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff can be filmed only starring himself. He demands, “I play Rocky.” That’s not a playground taunt in the milieu of financial bargaining and egotism that’s gleefully depicted by a series of Hollywood types — P. J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell as Winkler and Chartoff, Rob Demery as Joe Frazier, and a standout cameo by Trevor St. John as a self-serious fight coordinator.

In Hollywood’s gladiatorial circus, Stallone’s striving and eventual success become a credible moral victory. He must claim his own identity and career path separately from his worldly father Frank (Matt Dillon gives a moving characterization of a parent’s cynicism, affection, and personal regret). His wife Sasha (AnnaSophie Robb) encourages him: “I’d rather be optimistic and be wrong than pessimistic and be right.” These backstage details (including a hostile producer who dismisses Stallone as “a droopy-eyed hack actor”) make I Play Rocky a credible and appealing saga of Stallone’s indefatigable confidence. The movie rejects the sort of dark, objectionable narcissism that we saw in the Springsteen hagiography Deliver Me from Nowhere.

It is important that the filmmakers accurately measure Rocky’s significance. Farrelly and Gamble mix film history with good sense and humor when portraying wild-eyed director John Avildsen (Jay Duplass) deep in his own world of pragmatic professionalism (“Great art never comes through compromise”). They also capture Stallone’s own, uncanny sense of achieving the proper effect — not so much when Rocky emotes to his manager Mickey as when, in a startling shot, he points to details in a big-screen image of Kirk Douglas in Champion, from 1948.

Putting Rocky in proper perspective is a curatorial feat. It recognizes Stallone’s film as a work of pop lore. Its popularity gave Hollywood the opportunity to ignore scary powerful art like Scorsese’s Taxi Driver in favor of the folk and commercial elements that are easily enjoyed in American culture — although missing from Millennial film culture. Remember: In 1976, Rocky seemed an artificial retread of old boxing films, pilfering the ethnic sentimentality of Marty, On the Waterfront, and Requiem for a Heavyweight as if Muhammad Ali had never happened.

But I Play Rocky works differently. It recalls Stallone’s response to Wepner (“This guy won’t go down!”) to achieve the authentic Millennial pop lore of Better Man, Song Sung Blue, Back 2 America, Power Ballad, and the upcoming Madden. (These restorative myths correct the disappointing Creed sequels that failed to live up to Rocky.) I Play Rocky channels Stallone’s personal perseverance to enlighten our current demoralized sensibilities.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

#6261. Buy Air Canada Aeroplan Points With 100% Bonus (1.31 Cents Each): Worth It?

The Air Canada Aeroplan program is currently offering a bonus on purchased points. While this is a mystery bonus, where different members may be eligible for different offers, it seems the best version is for up to a 100% bonus.

Is there value with this offer? With a specific use in mind, absolutely, in my opinion. Aeroplan is one of my all-around favorite frequent flyer programs, thanks to the huge variety of airline partners, the ability to have stopovers on one-way awards for 5,000 points, and the generally great online booking experience.

Link: Buy Air Canada Aeroplan points with this promotion with up to a 100% bonus

Between 12AM PT on November 19 and 11:50PM PT on December 10, 2026, the Air Canada Aeroplan program is offering a promotion on purchased points.

Different members may be eligible for different offers, so you’ll want to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for. However, it appears that the best version of the offer is for up to a 100% bonus, structured as follows:

I should emphasize that other members seem to be eligible for offers of 85%, 90%, or 95%, so it’s no guarantee that everyone will see the 100% offer.

Ordinarily, Air Canada Aeroplan charges $0.0375 CAD (~0.026 USD) per point. Any purchases made with US credit cards and US billing addresses aren’t subject to sales tax either.

If you purchased 500,000 Aeroplan points with a 100% bonus, you’d receive a total of 1,000,000 Aeroplan points at a cost of $18,750 CAD (~$13,101 USD), which is a rate of 1.31 cents (USD) per Aeroplan point.

If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to buy exactly 90,000 points at a cost of $3,375 CAD (~$2,358 USD), which would potentially get you 180,000 points, for the same cost per point.

While you can purchase up to one million Aeroplan points per account per calendar year, there’s ordinarily a per-transaction limit of 250,000 points pre-bonus. However, during this promotion that has been doubled, to 500,000 points.

Aeroplan points purchases typically post pretty close to instantly, though in some situations, it could take up to 72 hours for points to post. Note that the purchase of Aeroplan points is non-refundable, and Aeroplan points purchases also don’t count toward elite status.

When Air Canada Aeroplan offer a promotion on purchased points, we most commonly see a bonus in the range of 90-110%, but the exact offers do vary. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 100% bonus vs. a 110% bonus isn’t vastly different.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the Aeroplan program, before this one.

Air Canada Aeroplan points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Since the purchase of Aeroplan points is billed in CAD, there is one other great option. The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) offers 3x points on foreign purchases, so that’s a fantastic card for this kind of purchase. Beyond that, the best options would be cards that offer 2x transferable points, while having no foreign transaction fees.

Aeroplan is one of my favorite frequent flyer programs out there. To cover a few of the basics:

There are lots of phenomenal uses of Aeroplan points, and this is a program that I redeem through regularly. Just keep in mind that Aeroplan now has dynamic award pricing on select partners, including Emirates, Etihad, FlyDubai, and United, among others.

One of my favorite things about Air Canada Aeroplan is that the program has more airline partners than any other frequent flyer program, and you can redeem points on over 45 airlines. In addition to Air Canada belonging to the Star Alliance, Aeroplan also partners with airlines that include Etihad, Azul, Air Serbia, Virgin Australia, Air Dolomiti, Eurowings, Gulf Air, Oman Air, Air Mauritius, and Emirates.

Always look up award availability before buying points, to get a sense of what you can expect.

Many consumers are frustrated by the practice of airlines adding carrier imposed surcharges to award tickets. In the case of Aeroplan, there are no fuel surcharges on award tickets, meaning you shouldn’t expect to pay big fees when redeeming points.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Aeroplan points to be worth 1.4 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from Aeroplan points than that.

Air Canada Aeroplan points only expire after 18 months of inactivity. However, any account activity that leads to earning or redeeming points (including buying them) would reset the expiration.

While buying Aeroplan points could represent a great deal, keep in mind that there are lots of other ways to earn Aeroplan points. Most significantly, Aeroplan is transfer partners with American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, making the currency pretty easy to acquire. From all those currencies, rewards transfer at a 1:1 ratio, and sometimes you’ll even find transfer bonuses.

On top of that, in the United States there’s the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card (learn more), which is pretty lucrative.

Air Canada’s Aeroplan program is offering a bonus on purchased points. While people may be targeted for different offers, it appears the best offer is for up to a 100% bonus, which kicks in as long as you purchase at least 90,000 points in one transaction. This is an opportunity to buy points for 1.31 cents (in USD) each.

This could represent a good deal, and there are plenty of situations under which the math will work out for this promotion. Still, in general I’d only recommend buying points with a short term use in mind, as there’s always risk to holding onto points for longer periods of time.

#6260. Alaska Atmos Rewards Business Card Bonus: 90K Points Welcome Offer

The $195 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card currently has a huge bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. For context, this is the business card of the Atmos Rewards portfolio, the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian. This is a potentially lucrative card that has just undergone a refresh, and you can read my Atmos Rewards Business Card review here.

In this post I’d like to go over the details of the Atmos Rewards Business Card bonus, for anyone who may be considering applying. There are lots of reasons to get this card, particularly the incredible bonus.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card with 90K bonus points

The Atmos Rewards Business Card currently has a welcome offer of 90,000 Atmos Rewards bonus points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, meaning the 90,000 points are worth $1,350 to me, which is among the best bonuses out there. There are lots of great uses of Atmos Rewards points, for travel on Alaska, Hawaiian, oneworld partners, and non-alliance partners.

Atmos Rewards points have all kinds of uses, ranging from booking short haul one-way economy awards on American for 4,500 points, to booking Starlux business class one-way awards from the US to Asia for 75,000 points. Of course capacity controls apply, so patience and flexibility will be required to get the best deal. Still, I find this to be one of the most useful points currencies out there.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card 90,000-point offer is the best publicly available sign-up bonus that we’ve seen on the card since it launched in August 2025 (which is when the Atmos Rewards program formally launched). How do the previous Atmos Rewards Business Card bonuses compare?

As you can see, the Atmos Rewards Business Card sign-up bonus has varied from 70,000 points to 90,000 points, and the current bonus of 90,000 points is the best publicly available offer we’ve seen. So if there has ever been a time to apply for this card, this is it.

When it comes to getting approved for the Atmos Rewards Business Card, what rules should you be aware of? There are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Bank of America policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

This one-time promotion is limited to company level Business Card clients opening a new account in response to this offer and will not apply to requests to convert existing accounts.

The good news is that eligibility for the Atmos Rewards Business Card is considered completely independently of any other cards in the portfolio, so you’re eligible if you have either of the personal Atmos Rewards credit cards. Many people even report being eligible for the Atmos Rewards Business Card (including the bonus) if they’ve had it in the past.

Beyond that, Bank of America doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for business cards. While Bank of America has the 2/3/4 rule and 3/12 rules, those apply to personal cards, and not business cards. Generally those with a Bank of America banking relationship also have the best odds of approval (though it’s by no means a requirement).

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to have to be approved for this card, though personally I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

Applying for this card won’t count as a further card toward Chase’s 5/24 rule, in case that’s a limit you’re trying to stay under.

Beyond the great bonus, there are multiple reasons to consider the $195 annual fee Atmos Rewards Business Card:

If you fly Alaska or Hawaiian with any frequency, then having this card should be a no-brainer. The benefits really add up, between the lounge passes, the first checked bag free, preferred boarding, savings on inflight purchases, and more.

The Atmos Rewards Business Card has introduced a best-ever welcome offer, whereby you can earn 90,000 Atmos Rewards points upon completing minimum spending.

This is an exceptional bonus, and this card is absolutely worth picking up for the points, especially given that eligibility isn’t mutually exclusive with other Atmos Rewards cards. In the long run, the card can be worth it for the perks for travel on Alaska and Hawaiian.

Anecdotally I find Bank of America business cards to be quite easy to get approved for, including if you’ve had the card in the past. Applying for this card also shouldn’t count as a further card toward the Chase 5/24 limit, if that’s of concern to you.

Anyone plan to pick up the Atmos Rewards Business Card with this great offer?

#6259. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”
