The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card is a solid option for travelers who want to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

While it offers access to Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel transfer partners, its earning rate of 1.25 miles per dollar on most purchases and limited travel perks may leave some travelers wanting more.

Still, I think the VentureOne is worth considering if you're new to transferable rewards and aren't ready to commit to a more expensive travel card. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards is a no-annual-fee travel rewards card that earns Capital One miles.

The biggest draw here is the ability to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee. You can get more value from your rewards by transferring miles to airline and hotel partners, or redeem them at a fixed rate toward travel purchases if you'd rather keep things simple.

The card doesn't charge foreign transaction fees and comes with a few travel perks, including complimentary Hertz Gold+ Rewards Five Star status.*

That said, the VentureOne's everyday earning rate is on the lower side. I'd recommend it primarily to travelers who want access to Capital One's transfer partners without paying an annual fee, rather than those looking to earn the most rewards on everyday spending.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: The best Capital One credit cards to add to your wallet

Related: How to choose the best credit card for you

The VentureOne doesn't offer the extensive travel benefits of its higher-tier counterparts, but it still has a handful of perks worth knowing about.

One of the VentureOne's most useful benefits is that it doesn't charge foreign transaction fees.

Some credit cards charge around 3% on purchases made abroad, which can add up over the course of an international trip.

With the VentureOne, you can make international purchases without worrying about additional card fees.

Related: Best credit cards with no foreign transaction fees

VentureOne cardholders can enroll in complimentary Hertz Gold+ Rewards Five Star status.

Normally, earning this status requires completing three rentals or spending $1,000 on eligible rentals in a calendar year.

This status can provide benefits such as vehicle upgrades when available and additional rewards on eligible rentals.

While I wouldn't recommend choosing the VentureOne solely for this perk, it's a nice addition for travelers who occasionally rent cars.

The VentureOne also includes several protections that may come in handy when traveling or making purchases.

These include auto rental insurance, extended warranty protection and travel and emergency assistance.

For coverage details, including terms and exclusions, refer to your card's guide to benefits. These aren't necessarily benefits you'll use regularly, but they can provide some reassurance.

Related: The best credit cards for purchase protection

One of the VentureOne's biggest advantages is that it earns flexible Capital One miles rather than rewards tied to a single airline or hotel program.

That gives you several ways to use your rewards, depending on how much effort you want to put into maximizing them.

The VentureOne earns 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel and 1.25 miles per dollar spent on everyday purchases.

To put that into perspective, spending $1,000 on everyday purchases would earn you 1,250 miles. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuation of 1.85 cents per Capital One mile, those miles would be worth approximately $23 when maximized through transfer partners.

That's not a particularly strong return, especially when other no-annual-fee cards offer higher earning rates.

Still, the VentureOne keeps things simple. You don't have to keep track of rotating bonus categories, and you'll earn miles on every purchase.

If you're more concerned with earning transferable miles without paying an annual fee than maximizing every dollar you spend, that might be enough for you.

Related: How to earn, redeem and transfer Capital One miles

One of the easiest ways to use your Capital One miles is to use them to pay for eligible purchases as a statement credit.

You'll get a fixed value of 1 cent per mile, meaning 20,000 miles would cover a $200 travel purchase. This can be especially useful for expenses that aren't always easy to book with traditional airline or hotel points, such as Airbnb stays or Uber rides.

I like this option for beginners because there's no need to search for award availability or figure out how different loyalty programs work. You can just make an eligible travel purchase with your card and use your miles to cover it afterward.

You can also redeem your miles for Amazon purchases, Capital One entertainment purchases, cash back and gift cards. However, these options generally offer less value than travel redemptions, so I'd stick with using miles for travel whenever possible.

Related: How to get the maximum value when redeeming Capital One miles

If you're willing to put in a little more effort, transferring your Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners can be a great way to get more value from your rewards.

Capital One has more than 15 transfer partners, including programs like Avianca LifeMiles, British Airways Club and Choice Privileges. Most transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, although some partners have different ratios.

Personally, I love transferring Capital One miles to airline partners like Virgin Atlantic Flying Club and Air France-KLM Flying Blue.

For example, I recently transferred 6,400 Capital One miles to Flying Blue to book a Scandinavian Airlines flight from Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN) to Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS). I paid just $10.70 in taxes and fees for a flight that would have otherwise cost $163.95.

That worked out to about 2.39 cents per mile, well above TPG's valuation of Capital One miles. And while I booked through Flying Blue, I actually flew on Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) — a good example of how you can use one airline's miles to book flights on its partners.

Of course, not every transfer will give you that kind of value. I always recommend comparing the cash price of a flight to the number of miles you'd need to transfer.

I'd also avoid transferring miles before you have a specific redemption in mind, since transfers generally can't be reversed. Instead, find the flight you want, confirm award availability and then transfer your miles.

If you're new to points and miles, redeeming miles to cover travel purchases might be an easier place to start. But once you're comfortable with the basics, learning how to use transfer partners can really help you stretch your rewards further.

Related: How to transfer Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners

The VentureOne's biggest drawback is its relatively low everyday earning rate.

Earning 1.25 miles per dollar may be simple, but several competing cards offer higher returns without charging an annual fee — more on that below.

The VentureOne also lacks many of the travel benefits that make premium rewards cards appealing, including airport lounge access and annual travel credits.

If you travel frequently or put a significant amount of spending on your credit cards, you may find that paying an annual fee for a more rewarding card makes sense.

Related: How to decide if a credit card’s annual fee is worth paying

If you're considering the VentureOne, I'd also take a look at the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

Both cards earn transferable Capital One miles, but the Venture Rewards earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases, compared to the VentureOne's 1.25 miles per dollar spent. It also comes with a few additional travel perks, including up to a $120 statement credit every four years for the application fee for either Global Entry or TSA PreCheck

The trade-off is that the Venture Rewards has a $95 annual fee, while the VentureOne doesn't charge one.

Still, depending on how much you spend, that $95 could be worth paying. Based on TPG's valuation of 1.85 cents per Capital One mile, you'd need to spend about $6,850 a year on purchases earning the base rate for the extra miles to offset the Venture Rewards card's annual fee.

That's before factoring in welcome offers or other benefits. And if you typically redeem miles for travel statement credits at 1 cent apiece, you'd need to spend more to make up the difference.

Personally, I'd lean toward the Venture Rewards if you plan to use your card regularly and want to earn miles faster. But if avoiding an annual fee is your priority, the VentureOne still gives you access to the same transfer partners.

Related: Capital One Venture vs. VentureOne: Which card is right for you?

I think the VentureOne is worth considering if your priority is earning transferable travel rewards without paying an annual fee.

However, if you spend heavily on your card or travel frequently, the Venture Rewards or another higher-earning card could provide better long-term value.

There are currently two welcome offers available on the VentureOne, each with a different spending requirement:

Based on TPG's valuations, which peg Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, these bonuses are worth $370 and $740, respectively.

The biggest difference between the two offers, aside from the bonus miles and spending requirements, is that the standard VentureOne offers a 0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers, followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74% (a balance transfer fee applies). The Miles Boost version doesn't offer this benefit.

Compared to the card's offer history, the standard 20,000-mile bonus has been available for most of the past few years, although Capital One briefly added a $100 travel credit to the offer in 2025.

The Miles Boost offer, on the other hand, matches the highest bonus we've seen on the VentureOne. So if you've been considering this card, now could be a particularly good time to apply for that version.

Personally, I'd lean toward the Miles Boost offer if you can comfortably meet the higher spending requirement and don't need the introductory APR benefit. You'll earn twice as many bonus miles for an additional $500 in spending.

Keep in mind that Capital One has a 48-month welcome bonus restriction across its Venture card family. If you've received a new cardmember bonus on the VentureOne, Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card within the past 48 months, you won't be eligible for another VentureOne bonus.

However, earning a VentureOne bonus doesn't, on its own, prevent you from qualifying for a future Venture Rewards or Venture X welcome bonus.

Related: Evaluating the current offer on the Capital One VentureOne

The VentureOne isn't the only option for travelers who want to earn rewards without paying a high annual fee. Depending on your spending habits and travel goals, one of these cards could be a better fit.

For additional options, check out our full list of the best no-annual-fee cards.

The Capital One VentureOne offers something you won't find on every no-annual-fee card: the ability to earn miles that transfer directly to airline and hotel partners.

That makes it a reasonable starting point for travelers who want to explore transferable rewards without committing to an annual fee.

However, its modest earning rate makes it harder to recommend to anyone looking to maximize rewards on everyday spending.

If you're comfortable paying a modest annual fee, I'd consider the Venture Rewards instead. But if avoiding an annual fee is your top priority and you want access to Capital One's transfer partners, the VentureOne is worth a look.

#6256. Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female. Airlines will sometimes have special celebrations with all-female crews, so here’s an interesting twist on that.

Today is (apparently) International Men’s Day. We often see airlines commemorate International Women’s Day, but there aren’t many airlines that celebrate the equivalent for men… well, except Finnair! The airline has today operated its annual flight with an all-male crew. This was the case for Finnair flight AY1331, from Helsinki (HEL) to London (LHR), using an Airbus A350-900.

The crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also all men. So, why is this important? Finnair highlights how only around 10% of cabin crew at the airline are male, but the company hopes to see that number grow in the future.

I think this is a fun concept, and it would be nice to see a closer to 50/50 gender ratio in both the cockpit and cabin, as it would show that everyone is given a fair chance at such a career.

I think it’s worth acknowledging that at many airlines, hiring of flight attendants is still primarily or exclusively based on gender. Now, the policies do vary significantly by airline, but perhaps an extreme example is India’s largest airline, IndiGo, which only hires female flight attendants. It’s literally written on the application, that it’s a job for “Female Indian nationals.”

It’s all so strange, because the airline has this super enthusiastic page about the importance of diversity in the workplace, and says “all employment decisions are made solely on the basis of merit and qualifications, without regard to a candidate’s gender…” You mean except the single largest portion of your workforce, which is cabin crew?

What’s interesting is that while those gender restrictions exist in the cabin, roughly 18% of the carrier’s pilots are female, which is way above the global average of 7%. That’s obviously a conscious effort, so I guess the idea is that women can become pilots but men can’t become flight attendants.

In fairness, I suspect part of the motivation here is that IndiGo flight attendants share hotel rooms on layovers, and that is a bit more complicated with mixed genders. Then again, it seems easy enough to just try to pair male flight attendants on trips, so it’s hardly a hurdle that can’t be overcome.

While we’re used to seeing airlines celebrate International Women’s Day, it’s rare to see an airline celebrating International Men’s Day. Finnair has operated an all-male flight today, intended to highlight how only 10% of flight attendants at the airline are male, and the airline wants to change that. While an unconventional initiative nowadays, I think this is still pretty cool.

What do you make of Finnair’s all-male flight?

#6254. Amex Auto-Enrolling Card Members In Paperless Billing (Sorry, Dad!)

Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)…

With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:

We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

After that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

Now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it says this:

Not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

It’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary says something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress…

As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

What do you make of Amex’s switch to paperless billing?

I'm glad you alerted us to this so I can opt back in.

Chase does this too once in a while. Have to go into the account and undo paperless.

#6253. UBI Breeds Dependence and Restricts Opportunity

The new Democratic Congress should walk away from the destructive path of this policy.

Democrats seized control of Congress, in part by focusing on affordability and the economy. An AP-NORC survey conducted just before the election found that both were ranked top issues for registered voters, outpacing the next most important issue, health care, by about 15 percentage points.

The new Democratic Congress will presumably pursue policies that are advertised as ways to reduce the cost of living. One idea they should reject is universal basic income (UBI). Leftists have long pushed for UBI, and the idea is gaining stream among tech leaders. It’s a policy that would backfire by reigniting inflation and ultimately harming those it attempts to help.

Joshua Bandoch is a research fellow with the Competitive Enterprise Institute, a free-market public-policy organization based in Washington, D.C.

Kevin Corinth is the Daniel C. Searle Chair and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

#6252. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#6250. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

Aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's new premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a new product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#6249. Hah: Emirates Puts Auditors On Flights To “Provide Support & Guidance” To Crew

Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service issues at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a new initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants…

Emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a new initiative involving this small group of employees:

On 3 November, Emirates introduced a new initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers…

A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha)

Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

It goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

When it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”

As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”

I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”

There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

Why would an auditor on board create stress? If you are doing what you are supposed to be doing, then there would not be a problem. That auditor that write up how wonderfully well you performed your duties and are ready for promotion.

I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. On those flights I wear a uniform and am additional to the crew complement and my role is to support and to a lesser degree assess member of my flying team. I find it really beneficial as airline crew are typically remote workers and rarely have access to their ground manager. It also gives me the ability to see first hand lots of the pain points my team complain to me about - service routines, galley layouts etc. I don't think these kind of roles are that unusual in the airline world. We just aren't called 'Standard Pursers' ouch.

If they're not "working" the flight, I could perceive this not going well with customers as well in a way: if you see people constantly passing by you and never checking on you, or if you ask that person for help and they direct it to another person, then it could come across the wrong way. Imagine you press the call attendant button and the Standard Purser just walks right by you. You'd probably think that you're being ignored by staff / they're slacking off.

If only all airlines had in-flight service auditors, the skies would be a better place.

Amanda Seyfried and then-husband Thomas Sadoski attend the TIME100 Gala at Jazz at Lincoln Center in New York City June 08, 2022.

#6247. Bilt Rent Day Promotion December 2026: JetBlue Mosaic Status Challenge

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus new ways that housing rewards are offered.

There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With a new month being right around the corner, I’d like to cover the details of the December 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a JetBlue Mosaic elite status challenge, as well as an up to 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions (which isn’t a very good deal). It’s interesting to see a second month in a row with no transfer bonus…

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

On the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:

Let me cut to the chase — don’t redeem your points this way. It’s a bad value. Ordinarily you get 0.55 cents per Bilt point for statement credit redemptions, so even with a 100% bonus, you’re looking at getting 1.1 cents per point. Hard pass.

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:

The status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:

Regardless of which tier you initially match to, the status you get to keep is based on the activity over the course of those three months. As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $100 spent on JetBlue, or every $1,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

This of course comes at a generally useful time for JetBlue elite status, given that the airline is introducing first class, with space available upgrades being an elite perk. However, it’s worth emphasizing that this really isn’t such a special offer, as it’s basically just JetBlue’s standard status match challenge offer. Except in this case, you can unlock it with Bilt elite status rather than airline elite status.

On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for December 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions, which can get you at most 1.1 cents per point of value. Please don’t redeem your points that way. JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

#6246. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#6244. Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

However, I quickly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:

After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”

So they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

Airline loyalty is really important to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day…

Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

That feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

Even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that…

Have the rules changed, or have air France not worked out how to bypass the queue?

LATAM is no better. I had to fight tooth and nail with them at AEP over baggage allowances. I finally got a stupervisor and quoted actual tariff rules. She was a bit shocked and quickly backed off. @Daniel--Welcome to OMAAT. I can understand your disappointment with AR. We value loyalty program status for what it takes to achieve it as well as its promised benefits. When those benefits are not delivered, one has a right to complain. However, I agree that your complaint likely should be with the FlyingBlue program, which issued your ticket. I haven't been to Argentina recently but years ago, I liked how convenient AEP was as compared to EZE, at least for domestic flights. Sorry to hear that the security lines are so long. My most recent foray into South America was to Chile, where I flew 4 domestic segments on LAN as a SkyTeam Elite+ member. All of the expected elite benefits were available to me and a companion on the same itineraries, i.e., I had none of the issues you described. So, your characterization of AR may be correct.

Hi Daniel! Great review but I’m afraid I might have to disagree a little with you here based on my personal experiences with AR this April and November. It is a shame that FB sent you an email that conflicted with AR’s policy. I suspect that it might be FB’s fault and not AR because it’s a standard email template. I flew with AR 4 times this year both domestically within Argentina and internationally. Their unconventional luggage allowance was stated quite clearly at online check-in. Unless you did not check in online or missed it ;). As for the checked luggage allowance in practice, I’ve found that it’s a YMMV situation. On 3 of my 4 legs with AR this year, the check-in agents accepted all the bags that I had paid for and the cabin bags that I had not. On my fourth leg AEP-IGR about two weeks ago (early Nov 2026), the agent told me that I had exceeded my allowance by one entire piece that weighed 8kg, which was unfortunate but fair. I had to pay the fee outside and it came up to US$10. Unlike you however, I did not have to go back in to show my EMD as proof of payment. It was automatically dispatched. I had some time at AEP and a chatty agent with whom I could practice my imperfect Argentine Spanish. She clarified with a few shrugs that there is no clear formula for calculating the fee. It seems to be a combination of fare class, date of booking mixed in with some Argentine chaos and charm. The maintenance issues, delays and their handling of irregular ops are two other stories altogether though.

Glad to always hear more about AR, even if it is not always positive news, and welcome to the blog ^^

#6243. Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum

The museum needs to ditch its proposed expansion, an unneeded temple to therapy culture.

Joel Sternfeld, McLean, Virginia, December 4, 1978, printed 2005, dye transfer print.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, © Joel Sternfeld

‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement. New boulevards, new, fancy neighborhoods, hundreds of fountains, and much more were in the works. The sparkle of a new art museum was in the civic eye, too. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art didn’t open its doors until 1933, but better late than never. It’s an essential visit for art lovers.

I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today. It presents Joel Sternfeld’s lovely, often sad, wry, late-1970s and early-1980s landscape photographs in the context of the American landscape-photography genre. I love Sternfeld’s work. Born in 1944, he was the cutting-edge photographer who took color landscape photography mainstream, mostly through American Prospects, his portfolio of photographs published in book form in 1987. Color? Cutting-edge in the ’80s? Well, 1987 is about to be 40 years ago, so it qualifies as days of yore, and what has became American Prospects started in the late ’70s, when Sternfeld started an epic road trip to make art about Americans and the land. Landscape photography was, à la Ansel Adams, commonly in black and white, thought to evoke grandeur and mystery. What pushed Sternfeld to color was the advent of Kodak Vericolor III film in the 1970s. It delivered accurate, vibrant color and was good for various lighting and especially skin tones.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”

#6242. End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with new cabins, including the new business class.

Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

Specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between New York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

#6240. Why International First Class Has Failed At US Airlines (But Shouldn’t)

We’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

Airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:

What’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

The US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

When they fly first class, they want this…

It’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

What explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:

Call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest issue:

If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):

I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:

At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The issue is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service…

What’s your take on the possible merit of US carriers offering first class?

#6239. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

#6238. Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

However, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

It’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and said she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

In the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time…

I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

#6236. Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

The plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then quickly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

After the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

Once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

What explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

In other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

In this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety issue. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

While this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety issue, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?
