#6235. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

#6234. Mexico’s President Flew 21 Hours To China In Economy (In A Middle Seat!)

I’ve gotta say, huge kudos to Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, for setting quite the example in terms of how she recently traveled to China, as flagged by View from the Wing…

World leaders have just met in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting. As you’d expect, most leaders flew on their government planes. There were some exceptions, though I can’t imagine anyone else flew the same way as Mexico’s 64-year-old president.

Viajamos hacia Shenzhen para representar a México en el Foro de Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC) China 2026; la agenda de actividades incluye reunión con empresarios de países miembros. Además, participaré en la conferencia de prensa matutina para informar avances de… pic.twitter.com/F9UqRLjFlb

Media reports suggest she flew to China on China Southern. Specifically, she traveled on Sunday, November 15, 2026, on CZ8032, from Mexico City (MEX) to Shenzhen (SZX), with a refueling stop in Tijuana (TIJ), and the journey covering a distance of 8,803 miles.

The Airbus A350-900 took off from Mexico City at 12:49AM, arriving in Tijuana at 2:02AM, after a flight time of 3hr13min. Then it took off again at 4:34AM, and landed in Shenzhen the following morning at 11:31AM, after a flight time of 14hr56min. All-in-all, the flight took around 21 hours, including the refueling stop.

The shocking thing here isn’t that she traveled commercial, but instead, that she reportedly flew in economy! Reports suggest she was in seat 33B, which would be a middle seat in economy, no less!

Llegamos a la Ciudad de México en el vuelo CZ8031 desde Shenzhen, China. Agradecemos a toda la tripulación por su apoyo. pic.twitter.com/DSC83CpnDQ

I think a head of state should reasonably be able to fly business class on a flight of this length, for two reasons:

That being said, I absolutely commend her for the example she is setting. It’s certainly quite a contrast to what we’ve seen here, where President Trump accepted a Boeing 747-8 as a gift from Qatar, and talked about how he has done it to make Americans be proud, because “our country has to be represented properly.” Heck, just this week he talked about “China was very impressed” and “Russia was very impressed” of his new plane. Lovely, I’m happy we’re impressing Putin, that makes me proud to be an American!

"Russia was very impressed" — Trump leads his press conference by bragging about taking the longest flight in Air Force One history, in case you were worried that he actually accomplished something useful on his trip pic.twitter.com/dDIHg8wb1w

Keep in mind that Mexico has an interesting history when it comes to how leaders fly. In 2016, Mexico’s government took control of a private Boeing 787, which flew around former President Enrique Pena Nieto. The purchase of the plane had actually been arranged under the previous president, Felipe Calderón, in 2012.

Then in 2018, when Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador took charge in Mexico, he fulfilled a campaign promise of selling that 787, which turned out to be pretty challenging, given that demand for a secondhand VIP 787 isn’t exactly that high (the plane ended up going to Tajikistan). Sheinbaum has kept that general legacy going, by flying commercial.

Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, traveled to the recent summit in China differently than virtually all other government leaders. Not only did she fly commercial, but she traveled in economy, and reportedly even in a middle seat.

There’s no denying that this is more about optics than anything, but I very much respect that. It’s nice to see heads of state who lead by example, as it’s pretty rare to see nowadays.

What do you make of Sheinbaum’s travel style?

#6233. Why JSX Just Bought New Pacific Airlines, The Strange, Failed 757 Startup

Public charter air carrier JSX has just acquired New Pacific Airlines, and with this, New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights, with Embraer E145 aircraft.

If you’re not familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “huh?” If you are familiar with New Pacific Airlines, you’re probably thinking “WTF?” There’s a sneaky and logical explanation here, so let me explain.

Let’s start with a little context. JSX is a public charter air carrier, which operates a fleet of nearly 60 planes, most of which are Embraer E135s and E145s.

It operates as a Part 135 operator, meaning it’s not technically an airline, as it’s using a loophole that allows it to not use standard TSA security screening, hire pilots with fewer than 1,500 hours, etc. Basically what’s happening is that one subsidiary sells the tickets, and then another subsidiary operates the flights, so it’s technically a “charter” (with 30 people who don’t know one another).

Then there’s New Pacific Airlines, one of the strangest airline startups we’ve ever seen, and which I’ve covered extensively. The airline acquired some Boeing 757s, and the business plan was to connect North America and Asia via Anchorage (ANC).

The business model made zero sense in the first place, though there was some funding there, and they even invested in constructing a lounge in Anchorage, even though those flights never did happen. The airline did briefly fly from (ONT) to Nashville (BNA) — as one does — before ultimately going out of business.

That brings us to the news. New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with Embraer E145s that are leased from JSX, as reported by IshrionA. According to a Department of Transportation filing, the airline intends to resume flights with planes featuring 42 seats, which is higher than the 30-seat limit you’ll find on current JSX planes.

JSX acquires New Pacific Airlines.New Pacific Airlines intends to resume flights with ERJ 145 leased from JSX. pic.twitter.com/uMMS0J2fZy

On the surface, this of course makes absolutely no sense. New Pacific Airlines was out of business, and the business model made no sense. So why would JSX buy an airline and then lease planes to it?

Long story short, this seems to be a play to acquire a cheap Part 121 certificate. A Part 121 operator is a company that’s allowed to operate scheduled air transport… in other words, a “real” airline. As I mentioned above, JSX has historically been a Part 135 operator, and that explicitly means it’s not an airline. It’s a public charter air carrier, so it’s not a “real” airline.

Going back a couple of years, we know that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) was considering cracking down on carriers like JSX, since they definitely don’t operate within the spirit of the rules. That’s not to say that JSX did anything wrong, because by the letter of the law, they’re following it exactly. It’s just that the letter of the law makes no sense, and clearly doesn’t reflect the intent behind distinguishing between Part 121 and Part 135 operators.

Under Trump, there was no scrutiny of this. However, with Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, I imagine JSX leaders may be worried that there could again be more scrutiny. If nothing else, buying a cheap Part 121 certificate is a good insurance policy, in case the government does crack down. After all, these can basically be “sold,” while acquiring one from scratch can be grueling process.

I wouldn’t assume that anything will really operate with New Pacific Airlines branding, or based on a New Pacific Airlines business model. Instead, I imagine the idea is that JSX will start dabbling in Part 121 operations, which is why these planes will have more seats (above the 30-seat cap that’s allowed), since that’s no longer a factor.

If the government were to crack down on Part 135 operators, JSX could move to Part 121 operations. However, they’d have to make lots of changes, from their pilot hiring, to the way passengers are screened.

JSX has just bought New Pacific, the airline with an absurd business model that went bankrupt. No, JSX isn’t inspired by the concept of flying Boeing 757s to Asia. Instead, this is clearly the cheapest way for JSX to acquire a Part 121 certificate, which would be required for the carrier to continue operations in the event that the government were to crack down on the Part 135 operator loophole.

It’s going to be interesting to see how this evolves, both since JSX seems to have plans to operate Part 121 operations in the near future, and also to see how JSX’s business model would evolve if the Part 135 concept were blocked.

What do you make of this JSX Part 121 play?

Citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

Citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

But Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

Like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

Generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points

Unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi says statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

In many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT."

If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

Citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

#6230. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

#6228. Bilt Seeks An $18 Billion Valuation — The Business Behind Its Jennifer Lopez Concert Goes Far Beyond Rent

Bilt is reportedly seeking to raise $500 million at an $18 billion valuation. That would be roughly two-thirds higher than the $10.75 billion valuation from its last funding round in 2025. They’re asking investors to back a company that wants to influence where people eat, shop, travel and spend their time, starting with the relationship it built through paying rent. Last week Bilt held a dinner for 400 people in the two thousand year old Egyptian Temple of Dendur inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art, with food led by Thomas Keller and Daniel Boulud and a private Jennifer Lopez concert. Ken Chenault, Roger Goodell and Barry Sternlicht were some of the business leaders speaking. The event launched their ‘NeighborhoodOS’ platform. And that provides real insight into the actual Bilt business, where rewards are just one piece of it. Jennifer Lopez’s video from the Met performance Consumers see the side of the business that’s relevant to them. Most people won’t ever view it as anything other than rewards for rent, or a credit card, and that’s fine. The merchant side doesn’t need to understand the travel rewards piece, either. But in case you want a window into what’s really going on, here’s an attempt at an explanation. J. Lo held a private concert at this dinner. I often see remarks on Reddit about how Bilt spends money each month on celebrities hosting its Rent Day, basically seeing that transaction as payment to market Bilt to them (or as just wasted money). That misses half of it. Bilt’s CEO explained the J. Lo relationship, “We agreed to help do the relaunch of her new album.” There’s huge value to the celebrity in being featured in front of Bilt’s audience. The financial terms probably vary with each one, but Bilt gains attention from the celebrity and the celebrity gains access to Bilt’s audience. You often see celebrities with something to promote, like J. Lo’s new album. We naturally see ourselves as the customers being rewarded. Our attention and spending are also what Bilt brings to its partners. That’s how it can negotiate rewards for us. Businesses spend money trying to reach customers, and a rewards program returns some of that money to the people whose business they’re trying to attract. The scale of Bilt’s ambitions are pretty massive. Bilt is trying to eat the world. Or at least a meaningful share of the $6.6 trillion in annual U.S. retail and food services spending it says happens in person. Their business began with a really insightful way to find good customers – reach into their homes, process their rent and get them signed up. Bilt’s latest company announcement says its platform reaches approximately one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. They report more than 8.2 million members and over $12 billion in rewarded spending at local merchants over the past year. Rewarded spending isn’t necessarily spending Bilt caused, but it’s a substantial base of transactions to build their platform off us. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is a particularly valuable moment. Someone needs a coffee shop, gym, pharmacy and regular place for dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. Acquiring that relationship through their home gives Bilt a chance to influence years of spending. The early audience was especially attractive. In a 2024 interview, its head of loyalty Dave Canty (ex-Starwood, IHG, JetBlue) described core customers aged 24–34, a median age around 29 and average income around $147,000. That made it easier to sign on initial partners who wanted access to the young professionals Bilt was reaching. Airlines start with people who want their miles already sitting on their planes. An independent rewards program has to find its own reason for customers to join. Bilt found one in an expense nearly everyone has, and where there wasn’t competition in offering rewards for their transactions. They offered property owners stickiness as well as a better payment processing platform. American Express’s Plenti had big merchants and their customers, but never established a compelling enough new relationship to change spending. It closed in 2018. Coalition rewards have achieved some scale abroad, including Air Miles in Canada and Nectar in Britain. The challenge is making the common program worth choosing over whatever customers already do. Bilt has better tools for that than a small rebate. I consider its points the most valuable transferable currency. A restaurant’s standalone rewards might never accumulate into anything I care about. Combine them with points from housing and other spending, and they can contribute to a Hyatt stay or an international business class award. A restaurant wants nearby customers who spend well and return. It also needs to handle reservations, remember guests, deliver good service and get paid without wasting staff time. Neighborhood OS connects systems the restaurant already uses. OpenTable’s new partnership puts guest information into its table management system and brings personalized offers into the OpenTable app. The restaurant can send an offers to people who’ve just moved nearby and manage offers for regulars – their own loyalty platform. OpenTable reports that participating restaurants have seen: Average checks up to 18% higher among Bilt members than other guests. Table turns reduced by up to 11 minutes on average. Higher average bills may be Bilt’s customer base being higher spending, or they may be encouraging higher spend. That’s not clear. But their technology does seem to speed up paying and leaving, which means serving more guests per table. Bilt’s mobile checkout lets diners tap or scan a receipt card, view the check, split it and pay in a browser. You can leave when you’re finished without waiting for someone to take your credit card and bring it back. Removing dead time after a meal gives the guest back their evening and makes the table available sooner. When there’s demand for another seating, a restaurant can generate more revenue from the same space. Keller and Boulud’s involvement extends beyond preparing food for a launch dinner. In Bilt’s March hospitality announcement, Keller described learning who guests are before they arrive. Boulud talked about inviting wine enthusiasts to wine events and cocktail enthusiasts to cocktail events. Connecting reservations, preferences, past visits and payments helps a restaurant recognize more people than an owner can personally remember. The restaurant can also deliver an experience through other Bilt partners. At Block’s investor day last year, Bilt’s President and Chief Revenue Officer Brandt Smallwood described automating drinks after a third visit, as well as benefits such as dessert or a free Lyft ride at the end of the meal. A ride home can be part of the restaurant’s hospitality, with Bilt doing the work connecting the businesses. The customer doesn’t need to understand the systems behind it. They get recognized, something arrives at their table, and their ride is arranged. That’s different from getting an email with a coupon code to remember next time. There’s also less work for employees. A Google Cloud case study describes Bilt’s concierge moving a reservation and adjusting party size through the underlying systems. It reports about 95% of member conversations handled without a human handoff, up from 86% six months earlier. More partners also means more ways to fund the benefits. Bilt’s acquisition of Banyan brought technology for reading individual items on receipts. A consumer brand can reward the purchase of its product rather than merely knowing someone spent $80 at a store or restaurant. A restaurant supplies a complimentary appetizer, a brand funds a product promotion, a landlord, hotel chain or sports partner funds a member benefit – Bilt connects the offer, the targeted customer and the transaction, and does so in a way no small merchant could accomplish on their own. It can reach consumers through organizations they already belong to and merchants through suppliers they already work with. Bilt earns money from housing and resident technology, merchant commissions, its card business and now additional software subscriptions. Its restaurant pricing is $495 a month for Neighborhood OS plus $195 for Neighborhood Marketplace ($690 combined). Software income from merchant tools gives it another way to make money. I don’t use all their partners but I do use Lyft and Grubhub, and I redeem with Blacklane and BLADE. I book travel through their portal. And their Palladium card is my daily driver. Palladium gets most of my spending and I’ve chosen to preserve 4% Bilt Cash earning. They’ll pry that option from my cold dead hands. (The option offering up to 1.25 points per dollar on housing is what most people choose anyway and still leaves a very good card once 4% back in Bilt Cash goes away for new cardmembers.) Still, my experience isn’t the experience of every member. Bilt told Thrifty Traveler that fewer than 10% of members have its credit card. Last week Bilt held a dinner for 400 people in the two thousand year old Egyptian Temple of Dendur inside the Metropolitan Museum of Art, with food led by Thomas Keller and Daniel Boulud and a private Jennifer Lopez concert. Ken Chenault, Roger Goodell and Barry Sternlicht were some of the business leaders speaking. The event launched their ‘NeighborhoodOS’ platform. And that provides real insight into the actual Bilt business, where rewards are just one piece of it.

Jennifer Lopez’s video from the Met performance

Consumers see the side of the business that’s relevant to them. Most people won’t ever view it as anything other than rewards for rent, or a credit card, and that’s fine. The merchant side doesn’t need to understand the travel rewards piece, either. But in case you want a window into what’s really going on, here’s an attempt at an explanation.

J. Lo held a private concert at this dinner. I often see remarks on Reddit about how Bilt spends money each month on celebrities hosting its Rent Day, basically seeing that transaction as payment to market Bilt to them (or as just wasted money). That misses half of it.

Bilt’s CEO explained the J. Lo relationship, “We agreed to help do the relaunch of her new album.” There’s huge value to the celebrity in being featured in front of Bilt’s audience. The financial terms probably vary with each one, but Bilt gains attention from the celebrity and the celebrity gains access to Bilt’s audience. You often see celebrities with something to promote, like J. Lo’s new album.

We naturally see ourselves as the customers being rewarded. Our attention and spending are also what Bilt brings to its partners. That’s how it can negotiate rewards for us. Businesses spend money trying to reach customers, and a rewards program returns some of that money to the people whose business they’re trying to attract.

The scale of Bilt’s ambitions are pretty massive. Bilt is trying to eat the world. Or at least a meaningful share of the $6.6 trillion in annual U.S. retail and food services spending it says happens in person.

Their business began with a really insightful way to find good customers – reach into their homes, process their rent and get them signed up. Bilt’s latest company announcement says its platform reaches approximately one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year.

They report more than 8.2 million members and over $12 billion in rewarded spending at local merchants over the past year. Rewarded spending isn’t necessarily spending Bilt caused, but it’s a substantial base of transactions to build their platform off us.

As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is a particularly valuable moment. Someone needs a coffee shop, gym, pharmacy and regular place for dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. Acquiring that relationship through their home gives Bilt a chance to influence years of spending.

The early audience was especially attractive. In a 2024 interview, its head of loyalty Dave Canty (ex-Starwood, IHG, JetBlue) described core customers aged 24–34, a median age around 29 and average income around $147,000. That made it easier to sign on initial partners who wanted access to the young professionals Bilt was reaching.

Airlines start with people who want their miles already sitting on their planes. An independent rewards program has to find its own reason for customers to join. Bilt found one in an expense nearly everyone has, and where there wasn’t competition in offering rewards for their transactions. They offered property owners stickiness as well as a better payment processing platform.

American Express’s Plenti had big merchants and their customers, but never established a compelling enough new relationship to change spending. It closed in 2018. Coalition rewards have achieved some scale abroad, including Air Miles in Canada and Nectar in Britain. The challenge is making the common program worth choosing over whatever customers already do.

Bilt has better tools for that than a small rebate. I consider its points the most valuable transferable currency. A restaurant’s standalone rewards might never accumulate into anything I care about. Combine them with points from housing and other spending, and they can contribute to a Hyatt stay or an international business class award.

A restaurant wants nearby customers who spend well and return. It also needs to handle reservations, remember guests, deliver good service and get paid without wasting staff time.

Neighborhood OS connects systems the restaurant already uses. OpenTable’s new partnership puts guest information into its table management system and brings personalized offers into the OpenTable app. The restaurant can send an offers to people who’ve just moved nearby and manage offers for regulars – their own loyalty platform.

OpenTable reports that participating restaurants have seen:

Higher average bills may be Bilt’s customer base being higher spending, or they may be encouraging higher spend. That’s not clear. But their technology does seem to speed up paying and leaving, which means serving more guests per table. Bilt’s mobile checkout lets diners tap or scan a receipt card, view the check, split it and pay in a browser. You can leave when you’re finished without waiting for someone to take your credit card and bring it back.

Removing dead time after a meal gives the guest back their evening and makes the table available sooner. When there’s demand for another seating, a restaurant can generate more revenue from the same space.

Keller and Boulud’s involvement extends beyond preparing food for a launch dinner. In Bilt’s March hospitality announcement, Keller described learning who guests are before they arrive. Boulud talked about inviting wine enthusiasts to wine events and cocktail enthusiasts to cocktail events. Connecting reservations, preferences, past visits and payments helps a restaurant recognize more people than an owner can personally remember.

The restaurant can also deliver an experience through other Bilt partners. At Block’s investor day last year, Bilt’s President and Chief Revenue Officer Brandt Smallwood described automating drinks after a third visit, as well as benefits such as dessert or a free Lyft ride at the end of the meal. A ride home can be part of the restaurant’s hospitality, with Bilt doing the work connecting the businesses.

The customer doesn’t need to understand the systems behind it. They get recognized, something arrives at their table, and their ride is arranged. That’s different from getting an email with a coupon code to remember next time.

There’s also less work for employees. A Google Cloud case study describes Bilt’s concierge moving a reservation and adjusting party size through the underlying systems. It reports about 95% of member conversations handled without a human handoff, up from 86% six months earlier.

More partners also means more ways to fund the benefits. Bilt’s acquisition of Banyan brought technology for reading individual items on receipts. A consumer brand can reward the purchase of its product rather than merely knowing someone spent $80 at a store or restaurant.

A restaurant supplies a complimentary appetizer, a brand funds a product promotion, a landlord, hotel chain or sports partner funds a member benefit – Bilt connects the offer, the targeted customer and the transaction, and does so in a way no small merchant could accomplish on their own.

Constellation Brands is participating, bringing Modelo Especial and Corona Extra benefits to customers across sports fandoms, residential communities, offices and local businesses. A national brand’s marketing budget can help make a neighborhood membership more valuable.

An appetizer can cost less to provide than the guest values it. An empty table on Tuesday has different economics from the last table on Saturday. Bilt can help direct incentives to the places and times where they create more business, then show the merchant which offers led to visits and spending. That’s not surprising. But it means that there are also likely a lot of members who don’t transact with Bilt frequently, outside of paying rent. An on-time housing payment earns a reward with Bilt or a partner, as does one qualifying neighborhood activity per day. Points, Bilt Cash and collectibles toward larger prizes are available. Bilt is also white labeling its membership technology. A sports team can reward fans between games and a hotel program can be useful when a member is home. The organization keeps its customer relationship while Bilt supplies connections to businesses where those customers spend.

Some of the expansion is already being bought or distributed through partners:

Capillary’s planned integration offers a route to clients of an established loyalty provider serving more than 450 brands, including Hertz, Shell and PUMA.

Kastle’s partnership would let 60,000 business building access customers offer employee memberships combining office access with neighborhood benefits, like a nearby dry cleaning credit or a team happy hour.

Marriott, Hyatt, the Phoenix Suns, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans and Sacramento Kings have been announced as membership partners. Broader integrations roll out starting next year. Verifone, Fiserv, Adyen and OpenTable provide another route into businesses through systems they already use.

That gives Bilt distribution on both sides. It can reach consumers through organizations they already belong to and merchants through suppliers they already work with. A competing program would have to assemble enough of both in the same places. And each of these pieces is hard on their own.

Bilt earns money from housing and resident technology, merchant commissions, its card business and now additional software subscriptions. Its restaurant pricing is $495 a month for Neighborhood OS plus $195 for Neighborhood Marketplace ($690 combined). Software income from merchant tools gives it another way to make money.

I don’t use all their partners but I do use Lyft and Grubhub, and I redeem with Blacklane and BLADE. I book travel through their portal. And their Palladium card is my daily driver. Palladium gets most of my spending and I’ve chosen to preserve 4% Bilt Cash earning. They’ll pry that option from my cold dead hands. (The option offering up to 1.25 points per dollar on housing is what most people choose anyway and still leaves a very good card once 4% back in Bilt Cash goes away for new cardmembers.)

Still, my experience isn’t the experience of every member. Bilt told Thrifty Traveler that fewer than 10% of members have its credit card. Someone whose landlord uses Bilt may pay rent through it and do little else. Founder Ankur Jain has called the card “less than 11%” of Bilt’s business (without defining the denominator).

That’s not surprising. Delta says roughly one-third of active SkyMiles members carry a cobrand card (without defining ‘active’), while its American Express relationship is on track to generate more than $9 billion this year.

But it means that there are also likely a lot of members who don’t transact with Bilt frequently, outside of paying rent. Daily Rewards launches January 15 and looks designed to develop more of that engagement. An on-time housing payment earns a reward with Bilt or a partner, as does one qualifying neighborhood activity per day. Points, Bilt Cash and collectibles toward larger prizes are available.

What they’re attempting hasn’t already been done well because it’s hard. Restaurant software is hard. Housing payments are hard. Banking, travel, sports loyalty and customer service are each businesses with their own difficult problems. Putting them together is even more complicated. Jain’s March letter acknowledged that simultaneous integrations, the card transition and mortgage launch strained then and their support suffered. In my experience they ironed out the kinks.

They don’t need every category to succeed. There’s a tension for merchants, too: Bilt can make a customer more loyal to a restaurant, but it can also send that customer to the restaurant down the street. The merchant needs enough additional profit to make sharing the customer relationship worthwhile.

The scale of ambition here is huge, they’re executing along a lot of different fronts simultaneously. It’s all expensive. If it works, this is – apparently – at least an $18 billion business, holding aside things like liquidation preferences or other undisclosed elements of a financing deal. Will it work? No one else has really done it before…

After a failure of a credit card launch they are trying to pivot. Throwing a splashy launch party at the Met is part of the pivot. Folks like free food paid for by marketing dollars, but they like money even more. And while this is a lovely word salad, other than being a payment processor for landlords, the Neighborhood OS is about as relevant as the new Resy Rewards. Small potatoes.

Whether Bilt is able to raise any money will be very telling.

Not having rent to pay, I’m clearly of no interest to them, and vice versa.

I’ve been really hard on them, on here, and elsewhere, but, I must say, they’ve taken the feedback, implemented good improvements (specifically Bilt Cash expiration and additional redemption options), and I’m actually considering renewing my Palladium. At this point, I just hope they keep their transfer partners, continue the Alaska Atmos Summit rent option, and don’t go under. A little consistency and a few decent transfer bonuses would be nice, too.

@Kirk Benson – they reward mortgage payments as well, and have plenty of partners if you don’t have a housing payment .. they aren’t just rent anymore is the idea.

Half a billion dollars to buy a nebulous ‘platform’ that works primarily with B and C level sports franchises offering people free drinks and food…founder of it a billionaire who could have financed going further himself unless he got someone to pay a ridiculous valuation.

I wonder if Gary has a financial interest in Bilt.

t’s still gratuitously complicated. I use Bilt to pay my mortgage and my kid’s rent, and I use the card. The restaurant and local promo layer solves a problem I don’t have. I have other cards linked to it, but I have no idea whether I’m earning extra points on those transactions. I’ve redeemed for Blacklane and Blade, which I associate, appropriately, with the credit card. The local stuff is just too much. I live, eat and breathe this stuff, and I still can’t explain it well to people who ask. That’s not on me. It’s a communications and product failure.

Sorry, but I don’t believe the J.Lo concert was anything more than Bilt paying a performer who does corporate events with some regularity. I understand Bilt leadership wants to portray it as “synergistic” or “mutually beneficial,” but J.Lo needs Bilt like a hole in the head. If she wanted a distribution partnership, it would be with Target, Walmart or someone with far broader reach.

Ultimately, these are guys trying to raise money at a massive valuation. I hope it works, since I’m sitting on a heavy inventory of points and find the card basics lucrative. Perhaps they exit to AmEx or Chase, or more likely to an aspiring incumbent trying to build out its ecosystem, like Wells Fargo, Capital One or Citi.

More likely, they’re way out over their skis, trying to be much more than they need to be or are capable of being. If they want to raise at such a lofty valuation, the public markets may be the only option for the next round. At that point we’ll see what their real numbers are, or in my opinion, aren’t.

Any investor should look closely at the Glassdoor reviews from employees. Very negative quantitative and qualitative feedback, even by Glassdoor standards.

@BC – WF just poached JPM’s credit card chief to become their COO. WF just very publicly exited their relationship with Bilt, and is clearly much more interested in building out its own ecosystem than revisiting their time with a failure. The reality is no bank will touch Bilt ever again. It’s purely a creature of PE and Fintech now. Bilt is a payment processor that really would like to be more than it is, because that’s how you attempt to justify hockey stick valuations.

Think we’re circling around the same square and saying the same thing, though. These guys are on the next mountain over, let alone over the edge of their skis. The idea of Bilt going public is hilarious – these are numbers that are clearly far from ready for prime time. In the meantime, some folks can listen to a 57 year old singer perform a short set. Yippee.

@Peter — If we’re throwing-shade at JLo, I’d like to add, she doesn’t think you’re a ‘real New Yorker’ unless you were literally born here, so… (yeah, doesn’t she live in LA, anyway?)

Understanding their business plan doesn’t mean believing in it.

Bilt believes they can drive high margin incremental business to their partners (think fill an empty table at a restaurant) and because those sales are highly profitable, get a good chunk of the action.

Remember the discount books and more recently Groupon and Restaurants.com? That’s Bilt only with the promise the supplier is only discounting business they wouldn’t have otherwise gotten.

Is that a compelling sell? It might be and if this was coming from Facebook or Google whose sites have millions of eyeballs and are run by very smart people looking for the next big dollar business they can build because of them we’d be taking the idea seriously. But pure play startups need a now that I’ve seen it I can’t live without it product whereas existing players can are happy just finding new streams of revenue.

It comes down to whether Bilt is going to really be able to 1) drive demand for goods that would otherwise go unsold and 2) reap significant rewards for making the match with a buyer.

@1990 – it was not her best ‘take’. But no shade, she’s from the block and all. It’s just not that impressive to get someone like that to perform at a NYC gala. That happens literally every night here at the parties for the “millionaires and billionaires”.

It just potentially sounds impressive – which is pretty much a perfect encapsulation of Bilt – something that might sound impressive, but is just another pleasant valley Sunday here in status symbol land. Oh, don’t mind me, I’m just Monkees-ing around.

Meanwhile I connected my Amex card to Resy Rewards and it did not delink it from Rakuten Dining? So there may be a stacking opportunity there… I do see restaurants that are on Resy with the bonus that are also on Rakuten dining, etc.

@Peter — If that double (triple?) stacking works out, that’s epic!

#6226. The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

North Carolina Electoral College representatives sign the Certificates of Vote after they all cast their ballots for President-elect Donald Trump at the State Capitol building in Raleigh, N.D., December 19, 2016.

Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president. Alexander Hamilton marveled at the time, in Federalist No. 68, that it was “almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents.” The core of that process is that the members of the Electoral College are selected in each state. With only the Twelfth Amendment’s modification in 1804 to adjust how the vice president is selected, this same system has been in continuous use for 238 years. It is how George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, and Barack Obama were elected. Now, a nefarious plot aims to overthrow the American system.

Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote. These partisan sour grapes have often been dismissed as empty talk because the Electoral College is established by the Constitution, so only an amendment could abolish it. An amendment requires a two-thirds vote of Congress and the consent of 38 states, both of which are out of reach on a party-line vote.

A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The theory is that these states would award their electors not to the winner of the popular vote in their own state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. It may be that a state can decide on its own to do this. States have not always picked electors by statewide popular vote. Many states at the Founding had their state legislatures choose electors. South Carolina did so all the way to the Civil War. Colorado in 1876 was the last state to do so, but only because it had just been admitted to statehood and claimed not to have time to organize a statewide vote. Other states have awarded electors to the winners of each House district, as Maine and Nebraska do today; this system was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1892.

But the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is not just a unilateral decision by individual states about how to award their electors. If it had been, it would already have been effective in 2024, and Donald Trump would have won the Electoral College 530–8 with 49.7 percent of the popular vote. Instead, it is styled as an agreement that goes into effect only if states composing a majority of the Electoral College approve it. At present, the signatories control 222 electoral votes. With Democrats gaining trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona, they conceivably could pass the compact in states controlling 283 electoral votes. They also now control the New Hampshire state legislature, although with a veto-proof majority only in one of its two chambers, they would have to get through Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte.

Passage is not certain. Michigan Democrats have previously rejected the compact in 2023 and 2024, and in Nevada (a smaller state that would be swamped under the compact), the Democratic governor vetoed it in 2019. Some of the small-state signatories, such as Delaware, Vermont, Rhode Island, or New Mexico, might yet have second thoughts now that they are playing with live ammunition.

Moreover, under Article I, Section 10, interstate compacts require the consent of Congress. Even if Democrats passed it in the next two years with the aim of changing the rules for the 2028 election, Trump would surely veto it. After the 2030 Census, a number of the signatory states are expected to lose House seats, which will further narrow the margin for keeping it in effect. Then, there’s the question of whether the Supreme Court would allow individual states to gang up and effectively nullify the entire constitutional design of our presidential election system.

Legal obstacles aside, this is a bad idea. To start with, the very durability of our system over such a long period is an argument in its favor. No other nation has used the same system for choosing its head of state and government for so long. Leaving aside the dubious precedents of 1824 (when popular vote records were not kept in the most populous state) and 1876 (when fraud was rampant in both parties and Southern Democrats engaged in mass violence against Republican voters), the Electoral College has only delivered a different outcome from the national popular vote three times in our history. In each case, the national vote was fairly close and neither candidate got a popular majority, so the Electoral College provided the legitimacy of a majority result that the popular vote could not. This may have frustrated Californians, but it was not just the tyranny of a few small places with no people in them. In 2016, Trump won the popular vote in seven of the ten largest states. It is nearly impossible to win a national popular majority without carrying the Electoral College.

We have an Electoral College because we are a nation of diverse and distinct states. The American people are long accustomed to this system. The people ratified the Constitution and its amendments state-by-state. The Senate is elected by the people in states, the House by people in districts. Both political parties choose their presidential nominees by primary elections in each state. Americans have never before held a nationwide popular vote for any purpose. Our election systems, run by state and local officials with a variety of rules for the timing of casting and counting ballots and for confirming the qualifications of voters, are not designed for such a vote.

Our campaigns today still prioritize appeals to the most closely divided states. This encourages presidential candidates to pitch at least some of their message to voters in the center, and also to travel the country in order to garner coverage in statewide media and the support of state and local power brokers. A national popular vote campaign would drive us even further down the road of nationalizing the campaign media environment and encouraging candidates to rally voters in their party’s strongholds. It would also exacerbate the divide between urban and rural or small-town America, given how the largest cities could effectively ally themselves against their own in-state neighbors.

Few of the world’s democracies conduct a nationwide vote for the chief executive. In France, which is one of those, the first man to win such a vote seized power in a coup before his first term ended. National popular plebiscites are far more common in dictatorial systems, where the president has more control over who counts the votes. One of the reasons why the January 6 mob was never a serious threat to overturn the 2020 election was that the state-by-state winners had already been publicly certified in 50 separate state capitals. This was a deliberate feature of the system: As Hamilton wrote, “as the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments . . . than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.”

We would inevitably need to overhaul our entire election system to accommodate a nationwide vote. It is not a coincidence that such a nationalization of elections is favored by many of the same people who want to do away with the Electoral College. As things stand today, the whole country would have to wait on California, which not only takes weeks to count votes, but does so in order to count late-arriving ballots and to “cure” defective ballots — a process bound to erode confidence in a close election. That matters little when nobody doubts the outcome in California. But by making elections turn on the margins of victory in the deepest-blue or deepest-red jurisdictions, whose election officials are uniformly of the same party, the incentives for all manner of electoral malfeasance would be supercharged.

The 1888 election provides a vivid, if extreme, example of how the Electoral College limits the scope of mischief done by the corruption of voting systems in particular states. The eleven states of the former Confederacy were then well into the post-Reconstruction suppression of the black vote in their states. As a result, the Democratic nominee, Grover Cleveland, won those states by almost 25 points, with over 60 percent of the vote. This propelled Cleveland to a narrow plurality in the national popular vote even though his Republican opponent, Benjamin Harrison, won a popular majority in the rest of the country. Yet the Electoral College gave Harrison the victory because his support was not as concentrated in an unrepresentative handful of states in which the vote was compromised.

If a nationwide vote would be a headache, a nationwide recount would be a nightmare. Nobody who lived through the 2000 and 2020 post-election controversies should have any illusions that such a thing could be conducted in a civil and orderly fashion in today’s America. Rather than wait to learn that lesson the hard way, we should step back from the brink of overthrowing the system that has chosen our nation’s leader from the beginning.

The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

#6225. Rove Launches Shopping Offers Of Up To 25 Miles Per Dollar—Why Brands Will Pay So Much To Win Your Business

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Rove is launching personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar on November 20. Connect your card accounts, activate an offer, and the program can give you a higher earning rate based on your shopping history.

If you buy from Nike, Adidas may be willing to spend real money to win your next purchase. That’s the example I reported from Rove’s presentation at the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September. CEO Max Morganroth described targeted merchant commissions reaching 40%. This puts that pitch in front of consumers, with an established advertising company helping supply the offers.

Rove says members will find personalized offers in the ‘For You’ section of its website and app after connecting their card accounts. Enhanced offers will display the standard earning rate alongside the higher rate.

They’re also expanding in-store earning to hundreds of participating physical retailers. Activate an eligible offer before buying, pay with the connected card, and the purchase gets tracked when the charge clears. Rove says miles will typically post within seven days.

These are selected offers reaching up to 25x, and Rove tells me merchants can change from month to month, and the same merchant might offer one person 5x and another 20x depending on whom it wants to reach.

Rove began rolling out in-store shopping alongside its app, dining program and instant gift card rewards in August. The new pieces are the personalized enhanced rates and broader retail coverage.

A shopping portal generally earns a commission for sending a merchant a sale. Better targeting can make that referral worth more.

Someone who regularly spends money in a category, but buys from a competitor, is a prospect worth reaching. So is someone who used to shop at a store and stopped. A merchant might pay to bring that person back, get an occasional customer to make another visit, or encourage a larger purchase.

The best prospect isn’t necessarily the biggest spender. It’s the person whose spending the offer can profitably change. Adidas gains little from paying a committed Adidas customer a huge rebate on shoes they were already going to buy. And it doesn’t much from showing a Nike loyalist an offer they’ll never use.

Rewards provider Valuedynamx describes a retailer campaign that gave new shoppers stronger incentives, lapsed shoppers offers to bring them back, and loyal customers smaller rewards. Its case study reports a 20.2% incremental sales lift among lapsed customers and 13.3% among new ones.

Targeting also lets a brand offer a substantial rebate without cutting the public price for everyone. It can spend more to win a customer it wants while avoiding an expensive storewide sale.

Cardlytics announced its Rove partnership on October 6, giving Rove access to its offers program. Rove brings an audience motivated by travel rewards. Cardlytics brings merchant campaigns and purchase-based targeting.

Rove’s program terms name Cardlytics and Plaid. Members can connect eligible debit or credit accounts through Plaid, and Cardlytics uses account transactions for targeting, reporting and measurement. Rove tells me its partners process the last 24 months of transaction history so merchants can target offers. Rove itself says it neither stores nor interacts with that history.

That history can reveal which merchants you use, how recently you’ve shopped, how often you return and how much you spend.

The policy also says Rove’s browser extension matches participating stores locally and doesn’t transmit your browsing history.

For the Cardlytics offers, personal identifiers are removed, but permit aggregated marketing insights, transaction-level validation and licensing transaction data to partners. There Are Already Several Versions Of This Chase Media Solutions uses purchase history to select offers for new, lapsed and existing customers through Chase Offers. Amex Offers is another familiar way to receive targeted rewards for qualifying purchases on an enrolled card. Capital One Shopping can use browsing, product and purchase information to personalize offers. Its rewards redeem for gift cards. The separate Capital One Offers available through Capital One accounts includes online and in-store offers, with payouts that can be miles, cash back or statement credits. Bilt’s neighborhood rewards and airline dining programs are other familiar ways to earn from merchant relationships using cards you already have. SimplyMiles is also activated offers that then earn American Airlines miles and Loyalty Points. Rove‘s appeal is the combination of earning rates, transferable miles and travel redemption options. I’ve written about redeeming its miles for Loyalty Eligible hotel stays while still earning hotel points and elite credit. Washingtonians have a new option to Portugal next summer.

TAP Air Portugal will launch a new thrice-weekly service from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Porto Airport (OPO) on March 30, 2027. Westbound flights will operate on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays through the summer, and on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays beginning in October.

TAP, a Star Alliance partner of United Airlines, will fly an Airbus A321LR on the new IAD-OPO route. The long-range, single-aisle aircraft is fitted with 16 lie-flat business-class seats and 155 economy seats.

The new Portugal route is the latest international addition at IAD. United plans to launch new service to Toulouse, France, in April and to Milan in May, using its new long-range A321XLR on the former route.

International seats from IAD will increase nearly 7% in the first six months of 2027 compared to this year, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

IAD is undergoing a massive, $22 billion redevelopment to bring its infrastructure up to modern standards. The first piece — a 14-gate section of the new Concourse E that includes a new, large United Club — opened earlier in November. Future phases include a new international arrivals facility that would support additional long-haul growth.

And if the redevelopment plan stays on schedule, IAD could retire its jet-age mobile lounges by the mid-2030s.

TAP’s new OPO route complements its existing service to IAD from Lisbon Airport (LIS).

The state-owned Portuguese airline is in the process of being privatized as part of the Lufthansa Group. The German airline conglomerate plans to buy an initial 44.9% stake in TAP, aiming to close the deal by the first quarter of 2028.

Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx said in October that once the TAP deal is done, Lufthansa intends to integrate the Portuguese airline into its transatlantic joint venture with Air Canada and United.

#6222. Southwest Airlines Passenger Was Kicked Off When Her Husband Didn’t Board The Plane—Even Though She Offered To Pay

A Southwest Airlines passenger says she was settled into an exit row window seat in Las Vegas, pleased about the empty middle seat beside her, when the crew began looking for her husband. He wasn’t coming—and she was traveling on his Companion Pass. Angie Batis says she offered to buy her own ticket, using a credit card or points, but was told it was too late. Instead, she was escorted off the roughly 9 p.m. flight to Boise and quoted about $400 for a departure the next morning. Southwest was right about the Companion Pass rule. Surely though it shouldn’t take materially longer to sell a ticket than to remove a passenger. She’d spent four days in Las Vegas, checked two 50 pound bags, and was ready to get home. Sitting in row 14, she’d already given the flight attendant her verbal agreement to help with the emergency exit. Her headphones were on. She was listening to an audiobook and playing a game on her phone. Then came the announcement asking Mr. Batis to identify himself. She told the crew he wasn’t on board and wouldn’t be joining them. That’s when she realized why the middle seat was empty. An employee came back to her row and explained that her free ticket depended on her husband actually taking the flight. Well, can I just pay with a credit card? … I’ve been a Southwest card member for 20 plus years. I have my own points. Can I just book it, you know, pay for it now? She says he told her they were ready to push back. He left, returned about three minutes later, and told her she’d have to get off. She gathered her things and went with him. I think he was expecting, like, some complete chaos. @angiebatis — Her account of being removed from the Southwest flight Companion Pass Requires The Passholder To Travel I’ve been a Companion Pass holder, including through promotions, and it’s still an extraordinary deal. Book your own Southwest flight with money or points, then add your designated companion for taxes and fees starting at $5.60 each way, as long as there’s a seat available. The free travel is tied to accompanying the passholder. Her husband paid for a ticket, which then supports the companion’s ticket. The rules though are very clear: If the Companion is not traveling with the Member, the Companion’s reservation will be canceled. I’ve covered almost this exact situation before. In June 2024, a companion boarded Southwest flight 2097 from Savannah to Baltimore. The passholder canceled his own ticket just before departure. Southwest removed the companion, conducting a manual boarding pass check to find her in the days before assigned seating. That case involved a cancellation and an apparent attempt to get the companion transported while refunding the underlying ticket. Here the passenger was fully willing to pay. I don’t think she was actually trying to scam the airline, though she’d be traveling free (and if her husband did cancel in time prior to departure he’d still have his flight credit to use). The requirement to fly together isn’t one of the changes Southwest is making to Companion Pass in 2027. It’s been a longstanding requirement. She Offered To Pay For The Seat Comments on the woman’s video between people who think a longtime Southwest customer should know how the pass works and people who think the airline should have found a way to get her home. It’s probably just best that she got off without making a scene. Several viewers ask why this wasn’t caught at check-in or at the gate. But checking in isn’t the same as boarding. If her husband wasn’t checked in though it should get caught at the check-in deadline. He may have been checked in and just didn’t board. There’s an interesting bit of history here. This same woman went viral in 2024 praising a Southwest gate agent in Phoenix. She filmed herself thanking an employee named Krista for her kindness. In this video, she also thanks the gate agent and tells her it isn’t her fault. Her host at the Venetian arranged a chauffeur, another room, dinner and a car back to the airport. She was still separated from her checked bags, without a phone charging cord or a brush. I bet her casino host could manage that… So this was day old hair yesterday. Today it’s two day old hair. …I was embarrassed, I was humiliated, I was mad at my husband, the whole thing. If her husband wasn’t checked in though it should get caught at the check-in deadline. He may have been checked in and just didn’t board. There’s an interesting bit of history here. This same woman went viral in 2024 praising a Southwest gate agent in Phoenix. She filmed herself thanking an employee named Krista for her kindness. In this video, she also thanks the gate agent and tells her it isn’t her fault. Her host at the Venetian arranged a chauffeur, another room, dinner and a car back to the airport. She was still separated from her checked bags, without a phone charging cord or a brush. I bet her casino host could manage that… So this was day old hair yesterday. Today it’s two day old hair. …I was embarrassed, I was humiliated, I was mad at my husband, the whole thing. (HT: Paddle Your Own Kanoo) Topics on this pageAirline PassengerSouthwest AirlinesBaltimoreBoiseLas VegasPhoenixThe Venetian+5 more More From View from the Wing

Comments on the woman’s video between people who think a longtime Southwest customer should know how the pass works and people who think the airline should have found a way to get her home. It’s probably just best that she got off without making a scene.

Several viewers ask why this wasn’t caught at check-in or at the gate. But checking in isn’t the same as boarding. If her husband wasn’t checked in though it should get caught at the check-in deadline. He may have been checked in and just didn’t board.

There’s an interesting bit of history here. This same woman went viral in 2024 praising a Southwest gate agent in Phoenix. She filmed herself thanking an employee named Krista for her kindness. In this video, she also thanks the gate agent and tells her it isn’t her fault.

Her host at the Venetian arranged a chauffeur, another room, dinner and a car back to the airport. She was still separated from her checked bags, without a phone charging cord or a brush. I bet her casino host could manage that…

So this was day old hair yesterday. Today it’s two day old hair.

…I was embarrassed, I was humiliated, I was mad at my husband, the whole thing.

Someone always trying to cheat the system. Even more.

She knew the system and the rules. She tried to scam the system to get the free flight. I would say she got caught and frankly I have no sympathy. She wouldn’t have volunteered to pay properly if they didn’t kick her off.

She should have had a full fare and cancelation of the companion pass as repercussions.

Can’t travel as a free companion without the person who earned the companion pass. They know this. The time to rectify the situation is not when the plane is boarded. It’s before you board. Just like when people want to upgrade seats after they board. They could have done it when they booked. They could have done it in the app. They could have done it at the ticket counter. They could have done it in the gate area. But suddenly it is an emergency once they have boarded because they didn’t plan ahead?

Compared to the other stories about passengers getting kicked off Southwest flights, I much prefer Carolina from June 5, 2026…. But, unfortunately, I think she made her profile private, so the pics are down from that ‘article’ (sad face, Gary…)

When you try to cheat the system…you can lose!

“A Southwest Airlines passenger says she was settled into an exit row window seat in Las Vegas, pleased about the empty middle seat beside her…”

“Then came the announcement asking Mr. Batis to identify himself. She told the crew he wasn’t on board and wouldn’t be joining them. That’s when she realized why the middle seat was empty.”

She knew her husband wasn’t traveling and THAT’S when she realized why the seat next to her was empty?

Noseatforu: I first read your username as an anagram of Nosferatu.

So how did she get to LAS in the first place ? Same Companion Pass or separate paid ticket. I am curious. If the outbound was Companion it evidently did not get caught then,

The rules are the rules, especially when something is a perk, not a payment. She should’ve known the rules, and if she and her husband knew he wasn’t going to be on the flight should’ve called SWA to switch it over to paid or points before heading to the airport.

Finally rules are being enforced, she knew she was in the wrong. Should have just got off the plane and went to nearest ticket counter to buy a ticket and not expected airline to accommodate her an “already” on the plane ticket.
