But the airport’s general counsel Everett Martinez says city officials retaliated against him for raising legal objections to their improper dealings and for refusing to help push out airport CEO Phil Washington. The city says he violated his professional obligations and wants to stop paying someone who can’t perform the job.

Meanwhile, Denver has authorized up to $970,000 for outside lawyers handling his case and a separate employment lawsuit. The $470,000 budget for the first phase of his case is quite an expense for a fight between the city and its own airport lawyer.

I’ve called Denver the worst airport in the country. It can work reasonably well as a connecting hub. Actually getting to and from Denver, through the terminal and out to a gate is another matter. This latest fight brings together several of the reasons the place inspires so little confidence: political interference, weak financial oversight, and executives spending their time fighting each other.

The city’s November 10 filing argues keeping Martinez on leave is harming Denver during a budget crisis. Martinez wants paid leave to continue while he litigates, potentially for years. At approximately $225,000 annually, eight months works out to about $150,000 in salary, before benefits. That’s arithmetic, rather than a payroll accounting.

The distinction between airport money and city money matters here.

The outside defense contract is budgeted to city money. The council’s contract worksheet identifies the general fund as its funding source. So it’s actually the city that’s draining funds amidst a budget crisis, although it’s possible they try to bill it back to the airport.

The $970,000 covers two cases. The city’s budget presentation allocates $470,000 to the first phase of Martinez’s case and $500,000 to a separate case. They’re authorizing spending ‘up to’ this amount at this stage.

The amended agreement sets rates of $800 an hour for attorneys and $375 for paralegals. The firm is Wheeler Trigg O’Donnell, where city attorney Miko Brown previously worked. Funny that. Brown says a five-person panel considered four firms and unanimously selected this one, which Denver had used since 2011. She says she cast her vote for her former firm last.

Martinez alleges he was punished after objecting to the Park Hill Golf Course land swap, warning against withholding information from federal aviation officials, and resisting pressure to help remove Washington. He also alleges discriminatory treatment and an ugly remark from Brown suggesting he get a noose. The city denies his allegations.

The city didn’t want to lease airport space to a carrier involved in ICE deportation flights and Martinez wasn’t helpful in covering this up (it’s against the law). I coverde the Key Lime Air affair last year.

Then I covered a memo supporting Martinez’s account that officials subsequently sought to manufacture a safety justification for the decision. The memo was written before his lawsuit, and another airport executive endorsed its accuracy. The Federal Aviation Administration opened a formal investigation into the lease denial with $90 million in federal grants at risk.

Additionally, the city wanted airport property for a park. There are federal restrictions involved in transferrin ghte land. Martinez appears to have stood in the way (likely as he was obligated to).

But the city has counterclaimed for breach of fiduciary duty, conversion and civil theft. Martinez may have a legitimate employment claim but that doesn’t give him the right to remain on the payroll throughout the litigation. He says his first amendment rights are being violated, but the Supreme Court generally doesn’t treat speech made pursuant to an employee’s official duties as protected citizen speech and giving the city legal advice was his job. And while he ostensibly also helped protect then-airport CEO Phil Washington, it’s not at all clear that Washington was doing a good job. (He retired August 1.) I covered Washington’s nomination to lead the Federal Aviation Administration and its collapse. He’d spent less than two years running an airport after a career in the military and public transit. During his confirmation hearing, he couldn’t answer a series of seven aviation questions from Senator Ted Budd. And his actual airport record is spotty. Construction oversight. A 2023 audit of the Great Hall project identified inadequate contractor oversight, procurement concerns and overcharges. The January 2025 follow-up found only two of ten recommendations for improvement fully implemented, and no corrective action on seven items. The construction debacle predated Washington, but I view his record as overall quite bad on accountability. Concession revenue. After an audit found weaknesses in rent collection and monitoring concessionaire deductions, the airport accepted 13 recommendations. By October 2025, only three were fully implemented. Accounting problems continued. Executive travel. I wrote about the extraordinary airfare bills for a Madrid conference. His ‘need to be ready-to-work-on-arrival’ justification looked weak when he arrived three days before being on the program. The trains remain a good illustration of the airport’s deeper problem. Denver is finally planning pedestrian routes through existing baggage tunnels, estimated at $300 million to $700 million, with completion expected in 2028 or 2029. That’s where I’d like to see the airport’s management attention go. The is the premium card for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines loyalists, but look beneath the surface and you'll find a trove of rewards for Oneworld and other flyers, too.

Take it from me: I live in the southeastern U.S. (outside Alaska and Hawaiian’s core markets), but I highly value Atmos Rewards points because I can use them to book tickets on American Airlines, the carrier I fly most often, for excellent value. Of course, the Atmos Rewards Summit is a stellar option for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flyers and those based in the Pacific Northwest as well.

That broad appeal helped the Atmos Summit win TPG's 2026 award for Best New Personal Credit Card. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

The is a cobranded airline card for Atmos Rewards, the joint loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. The card earns Atmos Rewards points, which TPG's November 2026 valuations place at 1.6 cents apiece — one of the highest airline currency valuations.

Its headline perk is an annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award, but its suite of benefits also includes a free first checked bag and preferred boarding (when you purchase your Alaska or Hawaiian flight with your card).

Cardholders also have a faster path to Atmos Rewards elite status, as they earn 1 status point for every $2 spent (with no spending cap) and receive an anniversary status points boost.

One of my favorite card perks is the Atmos Rewards Summit's standout earning rates, which are especially impressive compared to other airline cobranded cards. Cardholders earn 3 points per dollar spent on all foreign transactions, an unusual (and potentially quite rewarding) bonus category.

One of the best ways to redeem Atmos Rewards points is for flights on Alaska, Hawaiian, Oneworld and other partner airlines.

Related: 10 best ways to redeem 100,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points

Related: Why this is the most rewarding airline card for international travelers

The provides multiple benefits when you fly Alaska and Hawaiian, but there are perks to enjoy in other parts of the travel journey as well.

These benefits kick in when you purchase a fare on Alaska or Hawaiian with your Atmos Rewards Summit:

The following perks are exclusive to Alaska Airlines flights, though they are expected to eventually be extended to Hawaiian Airlines flights as well:

Additionally, cardholders can share points with up to 10 other Atmos Rewards members at no additional charge.

The Atmos Rewards Summit provides an annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award that offers a discount on a second award ticket on Alaska, Hawaiian or a partner airline in any cabin class. This perk is worth $400 per TPG's valuations.

High-spenders who put $60,000 or more on their Atmos Rewards Summit every anniversary year can earn a second 100,000-point Global Companion Award, which TPG values at $1,600. If you already spend a lot on your credit cards, it may be worth re-routing those purchases to your Atmos Summit card.

Related: Atmos Rewards elite status: What it is and how to earn it

Cardholders receive two Alaska Lounge passes each quarter. These passes can be shared with friends and family.

You must be traveling on a same-day ticketed flight on Alaska, Hawaiian, Oneworld or a partner airline to receive access with your lounge pass. A standard day pass costs $70 per person.

While these perks certainly help offset the Atmos Rewards Summit's $395 annual fee, this card doesn't offer a full Alaska Lounge membership or the broad collection of lifestyle credits found on some competing premium cards. This could be a downside for cardholders looking for more comprehensive benefits.

However, if you redeem the full 25,000-point Global Companion Award at TPG’s valuation, its estimated $400 value slightly exceeds the card’s $395 annual fee.

Related: Is the Atmos Rewards Summit worth the annual fee?

Cardholders who have an eligible Bank of America account also earn a 10% rewards bonus on all points earned from card purchases.

The foreign transaction category stands out at 3 points per dollar spent, or an estimated 4.8% return on purchases abroad (5.3% with the Bank of America bonus). The earning rate for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases is standard for an airline cobranded card.

You'll generally get the most value by using your Atmos points for award flights.

TPG staffer Gabrielle Bernardini recently used her points to snag American Airlines flights from Florida to Philadelphia. With holiday fares being so expensive, redeeming 7,500 points saved her about $200 per person one-way. Plus, since she has the Atmos Summit Card, the $20 per-person partner booking fee was waived.

If an international flight in luxury is more your speed, you can fly from the West Coast to Tokyo in Japan Airlines' business class or to Taipei, Taiwan, in Starlux Airlines' ultramodern business class from 75,000 points. Atmos Rewards allows you to book stopovers and/or multicity award itineraries at no additional cost, so you can combine destinations in one trip.

Related: Beginner's guide to finding award space with ExpertFlyer

The Atmos Rewards Summit offers an unusual benefit for a cobranded airline card: Primary cardholders can transfer Atmos Rewards points to participating hotel programs, which include:

However, you may not want to use your points this way unless you have a specific hotel redemption you're ready to book and need to top off your balance.

The may not be the best fit for all types of travelers. Here are some downsides to consider:

If you're interested in an Atmos Rewards card but don't want to pay a $395 annual fee for premium perks, I recommend considering the instead.

The Atmos Rewards Ascent charges a $95 annual fee and offers perks similar to those of the Atmos Rewards Summit when flying on Alaska or Hawaiian, including free checked bags and preferred boarding.

Atmos Rewards Ascent cardholders can earn an annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) upon each account anniversary after spending $6,000 or more within the prior anniversary year.

The Atmos Rewards Summit doesn't include this perk, and the two variations aren't direct substitutes. The Ascent’s benefit lets you add a companion to an eligible paid Main Cabin itinerary within North America for $99 (plus taxes and fees), while the Summit’s award discounts award travel to any destination in any cabin by up to 25,000 points.

To learn more, read our showdown of the Atmos Rewards Ascent versus the Atmos Rewards Summit.

The currently offers new cardholders the chance to earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

Per TPG's valuations, the points and the Global Companion Award included in this bonus are worth $1,680.

We've seen this identical offer come around a few times in the Atmos Rewards Summit's offer history. It's neither the highest or lowest offer the card has, so you'll need to determine if it lines up with when you can meet the spending requirements and have a use in mind for the bonus points and Companion Award.

Since Bank of America issues the Atmos Rewards Summit, you'll most likely be subject to the 2/3/4 rule. This means you can only get approved for two new Bank of America cards in a 30-day period, three cards in 12 months and four cards in two years.

In addition, datapoints suggest Bank of America is inquiry-sensitive, so it may be worth waiting several months from your last hard inquiry before applying. TPG staffers have also found that holding Bank of America checking or savings accounts may increase your odds of approval.

However, if you're more of a casual traveler and aren't chasing Atmos Rewards elite status, you may be better off with the mid-tier .

Overall, Atmos Rewards points are a standout currency that can unlock redemptions across the Oneworld alliance, so the Atmos Rewards Summit is worth a look regardless of where you're flying from.

#6210. Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

In a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in her statement.

Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

“We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

“I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges

Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

Earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

#6209. Trump Says His Private Pilot Used To Use Foreign Air Traffic Control Because The American System Is So Bad

Donald Trump says his private pilot used another country’s air traffic control because the American system was so bad. He wouldn’t identify the country, as though his pilot had discovered a better provider for approaches into Teterboro and didn’t want everyone else signing up. Pilots don’t get that choice. And this isn’t just an ambiguous reference to flying overseas. Trump has made this claim before and described landing in New York, Florida and Tennessee. At his Friday press conference, Trump said his “pilot would use the air traffic control from a totally different country.” This was supposedly before his first term, 11 or 12 years ago. Then he declared, “I know a lot about air traffic control.” Watch Trump describe his pilot using another country’s air traffic control — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar), November 20, 2026 Air traffic control assigns clearances and separates aircraft sharing the same airspace. The controller responsible for your flight changes as you move between sectors and facilities. Your pilot can request a different route or altitude. They can reject an unsafe instruction. They can’t decide to use a different country’s air traffic control service because they like it better. And there’s a clear division of responsibilities. Pilots fly the aircraft and request changes to clearances when needed. Controllers coordinate the traffic. Could There Be A Real Story Behind This? I’ve tried to come up with something plausible, to create the most generous interpretation of these remarks. The best I can do is that Trump is confusing navigation equipment with air traffic control. Perhaps his pilot told him about a preferred navigation system, approach procedure or a piece of equipment he liked from overseas, and that became a story about choosing another country’s controllers. There are also real circumstances where an American flight uses foreign air traffic services: Crossing the North Atlantic. A flight to Scotland could pass through airspace handled by Nav Canada’s Gander operation and Britain’s Shanwick operation. Taking a route through Canada. A pilot could request a route that avoids congested U.S. sectors and spends more time in Canadian airspace (but it doesn’t give Canadian controllers responsibility for a landing in Tennessee). Flying in U.S. airspace assigned to Canadian controllers. “American airspace means American controllers” isn’t always true. Under a 1963 agreement, the United States delegates control of certain portions of its airspace within 50 nautical miles of the Canadian border. But the government assigned that responsibility, the pilot doesn’t choose their preferred controller. None of this would reconcile his comments with what he claimed on May 8, 2025. So, if I’m landing in New York or Florida or Tennessee, they’re using a system from another country. He repeated the story on June 27, 2025, too. So this is a recurring explanation of how he thinks flying works. The U.S. System Really Does Need Fixing I’ve been writing about the FAA’s antiquated technology and failed modernization efforts for years. Last week’s nationwide ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation that disrupted communications and radar information across much of the country. I’ve also pushed back when Trump claimed credit for the 2017 aviation safety record, when he blamed diversity hiring after the Washington crash without evidence, and when he suggested departing air traffic controllers could be quickly replaced. Training qualified controllers takes years. In fact, I supported the direction of Trump’s 2017 air traffic control proposal. He wanted to move operations into a separate nonprofit, with the FAA retaining safety regulation. A Canadian-style organization could finance upgrades without depending on annual congressional appropriations, and the FAA would stop regulating its own service. This year I challenged FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford’s attempt to rewrite that history as though airlines had hijacked Trump’s modernization plan and turned it into a debate over spinning off the system. Trump had announced the separate nonprofit himself. Maybe he think it actually existed, before he was President. Flying in U.S. airspace assigned to Canadian controllers. “American airspace means American controllers” isn’t always true. Under a 1963 agreement, the United States delegates control of certain portions of its airspace within 50 nautical miles of the Canadian border. But the government assigned that responsibility, the pilot doesn’t choose their preferred controller. None of this would reconcile his comments with what he claimed on May 8, 2025. So, if I’m landing in New York or Florida or Tennessee, they’re using a system from another country. He repeated the story on June 27, 2025, too. So this is a recurring explanation of how he thinks flying works. The U.S. System Really Does Need Fixing I’ve been writing about the FAA’s antiquated technology and failed modernization efforts for years. Last week’s nationwide ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation that disrupted communications and radar information across much of the country. I’ve also pushed back when Trump claimed credit for the 2017 aviation safety record, when he blamed diversity hiring after the Washington crash without evidence, and when he suggested departing air traffic controllers could be quickly replaced. Training qualified controllers takes years. In fact, I supported the direction of Trump’s 2017 air traffic control proposal. He wanted to move operations into a separate nonprofit, with the FAA retaining safety regulation. A Canadian-style organization could finance upgrades without depending on annual congressional appropriations, and the FAA would stop regulating its own service. This year I challenged FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford’s attempt to rewrite that history as though airlines had hijacked Trump’s modernization plan and turned it into a debate over spinning off the system. Trump had announced the separate nonprofit himself. Maybe he think it actually existed, before he was President. I’ve tried to come up with something plausible, to create the most generous interpretation of these remarks. The best I can do is that Trump is confusing navigation equipment with air traffic control. Perhaps his pilot told him about a preferred navigation system, approach procedure or a piece of equipment he liked from overseas, and that became a story about choosing another country’s controllers.

There are also real circumstances where an American flight uses foreign air traffic services:

Taking a route through Canada. A pilot could request a route that avoids congested U.S. sectors and spends more time in Canadian airspace (but it doesn’t give Canadian controllers responsibility for a landing in Tennessee).

Flying in U.S. airspace assigned to Canadian controllers. “American airspace means American controllers” isn’t always true. Under a 1963 agreement, the United States delegates control of certain portions of its airspace within 50 nautical miles of the Canadian border. But the government assigned that responsibility, the pilot doesn’t choose their preferred controller.

None of this would reconcile his comments with what he claimed on May 8, 2025.

So, if I’m landing in New York or Florida or Tennessee, they’re using a system from another country.

He repeated the story on June 27, 2025, too. So this is a recurring explanation of how he thinks flying works.

#6208. Mexico’s President Spent 21 Hours In Coach Getting To China—And Sat In A Middle Seat

Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum spent about 21 hours getting to China in economy on China Southern Airlines. She reportedly sat in 33B. A middle seat, on a trip across the Pacific, to represent her country at a summit of world leaders. That’s quite a contrast with Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for accepting a Boeing 747 in royal configuration from Qatar. But while Sheinbaum is winning praise for saving taxpayers money, she should have flown business class. The 64 year old president traveled from Mexico City through Tijuana to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Here’s her departure update: Claudia Sheinbaum’s update on her trip to Shenzhen, November 15, 2026 21 Hours Includes The Stop In Tijuana She left Mexico City early Sunday, November 15, on China Southern flight CZ8032 and arrived in Shenzhen on Monday. The Airbus A350-900 made its scheduled technical stop in Tijuana along the way. The first flight took 3 hours 12 minutes and the transpacific segment clocked in at 14 hours 56 minutes, with about two and a half hours on the ground between them. China Southern operates the route nonstop from Shenzhen to Mexico City, with the Tijuana stop in the other direction. Several stories report that seat 33B is in the back of the aircraft. In fact, it’s the front of standard economy. On arrival she posted video of her welcome in Shenzhen. An airport bus brought her to the red carpet, where an honor guard and performers waited. She received a presidential welcome. Which reminds me a little bit of when I’ve booked first class awards on Lufthansa, but the intra-European segment was only available in coach. Nobody ever could quite figure out how a coach passenger had a vehicle waiting for them on the tarmac. She returned on China Southern flight CZ8031 and shared a photo with the crew: Claudia Sheinbaum thanks the crew of flight CZ8031 on her return from Shenzhen Mexico Sold Its Presidential 787 Sheinbaum is continuing a practice established by Andrés Manuel López Obrador. In July 2020, I wrote about Mexico’s president flying Delta coach and connecting in Atlanta to meet Trump. He had an exit row aisle seat on a Delta flight from Mexico City. Delta was blocking middle seats at the time, too, due to the pandemic. Reforma’s video of López Obrador boarding Delta for his Washington trip, July 7, 2020 López Obrador refused to use Mexico’s presidential Boeing 787-8. After years of trying to find a buyer, Mexico sold it to Tajikistan for about $92 million in 2023. He said the proceeds would fund two hospitals. This isn’t Sheinbaum’s first long trip in coach, either. In April I covered her economy trip to Europe, flying through Madrid to Barcelona and returning to Mexico City on Aeromexico. She posted a photo of herself working at her coach seat: Claudia Sheinbaum working during her April 2026 trip to Barcelona I thought that was performative then. A president’s time has value, and so does being rested for the work the country is sending her to do. Aeromexico business class would have provided better rest and opportunity to work. Pringles, Princes, And A Qatari 747 I’ve covered plenty of politicians and royals flying coach. Prince William flew American Airlines economy from Memphis to Dallas in 2014, in a bulkhead window seat on an Airbus A319. He’s also flown Ryanair and taken the family on Flybe, carrying their hand luggage. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle flew British Airways coach to Nice for New Year’s in 2017. They and three bodyguards occupied the last three rows, with empty seats around them. T Argentina’s Javier Milei flew coach on his trip to Davos in January 2024. Given Argentina’s finances and the spending cuts he wanted the public to accept, there was a political purpose for the symbolism. David Cameron was photographed eating Pringles and working on his iPad aboard easyJet in 2015, while traveling to Portugal. I liked that one. William and Harry’s grandfather Prince Philip, though, described the improvements in air travel over his lifetime with the qualification, “provided you don’t travel in something called economy class, which sounds ghastly.” Meanwhile, thhe Pentagon accepted Qatar’s Boeing 747-8 in May 2025 for Trump’s use as Air Force One. It was widely described as a $400 million gift. I covered the Qatari jet’s conversion this summer, including the decision to preserve its luxury interior and the plan for it eventually to go to Trump’s presidential library. The U.S. president needs secure communications, protection, and the ability to keep working while traveling. That can justify dedicated aircraft. Sheinbaum’s coach trip earned publicity, including favorable attention in China while she was there to meet its leaders. But saving the difference between coach and business class is simply a poor value tradeoff when the cost is productive time and sleep for someone with a high opportunity cost. #6207. JSX Buys New Pacific Airlines—42 Seat Jets Could Bring Its Private Terminal Flights To More Travelers

JSX has acquired New Pacific Airlines, and plans to bring the failed airline back with 42 seat Embraer regional jets. That’s 12 more seats than JSX sells on its planes today, and it gives them a way to grow beyond the limits of their current operation. I think this fits a company that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them. They brought turboprops to Santa Monica’s shortened runway and used a free membership program to gain access to Teterboro in order to serve New York. JSX isn’t laying out the New Pacific strategy yet. Asked about the deal, they tell me: JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities. As part of that work, we are pursuing additional pathways that could provide even more ways to deliver our award-winning service in the future. Our focus remains on the exceptional experience, convenience, and hospitality our Customers have come to expect from JSX. New Pacific has filed its intent to resume flying and requested a waiver of the usual 45 day advance filing requirement. An operating projection calls for: Embraer ERJ145-LR aircraft with 42 seats. Two aircraft initially, growing to six by the fifth month. 10,106 flights and roughly 309,000 passenger boardings in the first year. Flights averaging about 1.2 hours gate to gate, with staffing growing to 104 employees. New Pacific used to be Northern Pacific, the startup that wanted to connect the mainland U.S. and Asia through Anchorage using Boeing 757s. It seemed unlikely to work anyway but the closure of Russian airspace to U.S. carriers kept them from even trying. It pivoted to short domestic routes and then sports and corporate charters. I reported its shutdown last November, just two weeks after it announced an all-business class venture with beOnd. The bankruptcy process disposed of its 757s. What it has instead is Part 121 certification allowing operations beyond the 30 passenger limit of JSX’s current Part 135 public charter model. I first flew JSX home from Southwest Airlines Media Day in late 2022. JSX’s 4 p.m. departure got me home for dinner, an hour ahead of the Southwest flight I would have taken. I reached the terminal 19 minutes before departure. In Austin, I was in a Lyft less than ten minutes after touchdown. The plane was comfortable, with a seat on each side of the aisle and a side table next to mine. But getting my time back was what made it worth paying more (but honestly, not much more). I didn’t need a bigger airport lounge. I needed to spend less time at the airport. By my March 2023 visit to JSX’s headquarters, they’d fixed my one real complaint: no internet. JSX was the first carrier with Starlink, and the first to finish equipping its full fleet. Notably United Airlines owns a stake in JSX. The early JSX adoption is likely related to United’s head start with Starlink among major airlines. JSX’s business depended on putting several things together: inexpensive used aircraft, a comfortable cabin, friendly service and airports that let customers avoid wasting time. At the time, airport real estate was their biggest constraint. Finding another city with people willing to buy a ticket wasn’t enough. They needed somewhere to put the operation. Look at Santa Monica. The city is literally closing the airport and shortened its runway to 3,500 feet. JSX brought in ATR 42-600 turboprops configured with 30 seats. They found an aircraft suited to an airport that’s convenient for customers on the west side of Los Angeles, and obtained permission to operate despite the local politics. At Teterboro, the solution involved how they sold tickets. The airport prohibits publicly advertised scheduled passenger service. JSX put the flights behind a Club JSX login, limited bookings to members, and marketed the destination publicly as New York City. Joining the program is free, but joining is how they gain access to the airport. Those are different solutions to different problems. With New Pacific, JSX gains the ability to operate with more than 30 seats. My guess is that they see markets where a different version of their product could work, with more passengers sharing the cost of each departure. There is a regulatory insurance benefit. American Airlines, Southwest and the big pilots union have pushed to restrict JSX’s business model. I anticipated that sort of campaign in my first review. Having a Part 121 operation would be useful if the rules change. But the Federal Aviation Administration’s current agenda lists its public charter rulemaking as a long-term action with the next step undetermined. They never closed the rulemaking effort. But I think it’s possible to overread the regulatory risk insurance strategy here. They could still use private terminals with a part 121 operation and 42 seats. Federal security rules provide for scheduled and public charter flights with 31 to 60 seats outside the usual secure terminal area. This wouldn’t work at every airport JSX currently serves due to airport certification requirements. And part 121 means different pilot requirements, including mandatory age 65 retirement (they couldn’t use their ex-American and Southwest senior captains). If they do plan 42 seats that a different product – still more generous than a 50-seat sardine can but not nearly as spacious as the current 30-seat setup JSX appears to have a plan to add 40% more seats to some of the regional jets they own, and operate them under a scheduled airline. They haven’t said what they’re actually planning, but it may be a different niche than their current model rather than the assumed ‘buy a scheduled airline in case the next administration capitulates to lobbyists and puts them out of business’ the way ALPA, Southwest and American sought to do under the last administration. New Pacific used to be Northern Pacific, the startup that wanted to connect the mainland U.S. and Asia through Anchorage using Boeing 757s. It seemed unlikely to work anyway but the closure of Russian airspace to U.S. carriers kept them from even trying. It pivoted to short domestic routes and then sports and corporate charters. I reported its shutdown last November, just two weeks after it announced an all-business class venture with beOnd.

The bankruptcy process disposed of its 757s. What it has instead is Part 121 certification allowing operations beyond the 30 passenger limit of JSX’s current Part 135 public charter model.

I first flew JSX home from Southwest Airlines Media Day in late 2022. JSX’s 4 p.m. departure got me home for dinner, an hour ahead of the Southwest flight I would have taken. I reached the terminal 19 minutes before departure. In Austin, I was in a Lyft less than ten minutes after touchdown.

The plane was comfortable, with a seat on each side of the aisle and a side table next to mine. But getting my time back was what made it worth paying more (but honestly, not much more). I didn’t need a bigger airport lounge. I needed to spend less time at the airport.

By my March 2023 visit to JSX’s headquarters, they’d fixed my one real complaint: no internet. JSX was the first carrier with Starlink, and the first to finish equipping its full fleet. Notably United Airlines owns a stake in JSX. The early JSX adoption is likely related to United’s head start with Starlink among major airlines.

JSX’s business depended on putting several things together: inexpensive used aircraft, a comfortable cabin, friendly service and airports that let customers avoid wasting time. At the time, airport real estate was their biggest constraint. Finding another city with people willing to buy a ticket wasn’t enough. They needed somewhere to put the operation.

Look at Santa Monica. The city is literally closing the airport and shortened its runway to 3,500 feet. JSX brought in ATR 42-600 turboprops configured with 30 seats. They found an aircraft suited to an airport that’s convenient for customers on the west side of Los Angeles, and obtained permission to operate despite the local politics.

At Teterboro, the solution involved how they sold tickets. The airport prohibits publicly advertised scheduled passenger service. JSX put the flights behind a Club JSX login, limited bookings to members, and marketed the destination publicly as New York City. Joining the program is free, but joining is how they gain access to the airport. Those are different solutions to different problems. With New Pacific, JSX gains the ability to operate with more than 30 seats. My guess is that they see markets where a different version of their product could work, with more passengers sharing the cost of each departure. There is a regulatory insurance benefit. American Airlines, Southwest and the big pilots union have pushed to restrict JSX’s business model. I anticipated that sort of campaign in my first review. Having a Part 121 operation would be useful if the rules change. But the Federal Aviation Administration’s current agenda lists its public charter rulemaking as a long-term action with the next step undetermined. They never closed the rulemaking effort. But I think it’s possible to overread the regulatory risk insurance strategy here. They could still use private terminals with a part 121 operation and 42 seats. Federal security rules provide for scheduled and public charter flights with 31 to 60 seats outside the usual secure terminal area. This wouldn’t work at every airport JSX currently serves due to airport certification requirements. And part 121 means different pilot requirements, including mandatory age 65 retirement (they couldn’t use their ex-American and Southwest senior captains). If they do plan 42 seats that a different product – still more generous than a 50-seat sardine can but not nearly as spacious as the current 30-seat setup JSX appears to have a plan to add 40% more seats to some of the regional jets they own, and operate them under a scheduled airline. They haven’t said what they’re actually planning, but it may be a different niche than their current model rather than the assumed ‘buy a scheduled airline in case the next administration capitulates to lobbyists and puts them out of business’ the way ALPA, Southwest and American sought to do under the last administration. #6206. The Complex Reputation of James Burnham

The political theorist was known for his detachment — both in his political views and in his daily life.

James Burnham appears on an episode of Firing Line in 1978.

The British first edition of The Managerial Revolution that I picked up in a Charing Cross Road shop a quarter century ago tells us much about the work itself. I’ve read it four times, conscripted it as an airplane companion, and brought it to the beach. Yet its binding remains strong, its cover quite flexible, and its pages yellowing but intact. We no longer much refer to let alone read such 1941 bestsellers as Clifton Fadiman’s Reading I’ve Liked or Margaret Leech’s Reveille in Washington. But James Burnham, much like my strong and solid copy of his most famous book, endures.

Burnham, who entered the world 121 years ago Sunday and left it nearly 40 years ago, very much remains part of the Great Conversation. The Managerial Revolution, anticipating as it did the ascension of technocrats, specialists, and the bureaucratic elite as a sort of ruling class, surely helped in that regard. Burnham remains read, despite no Burnhamite clique in academia or organized faction among movement conservatives dedicated to advancing his ideas. Kirkians, Straussians, and Randians exist. Why no James Burnham Preservation Society with an accompanying secret handshake?

Daniel J. Flynn, the author of The Man Who Invented Conservatism: The Unlikely Life of Frank S. Meyer, is an American Spectator senior editor, visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution, and YouTuber @RightWingWilderness.

#6205. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

"When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

“The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide said.

King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”

That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”

A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

“We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

#6203. These 14 apps and websites make award redemptions easier to find

See how far your points, miles and dollars go in TPG's first loyalty report.

See how TPG ranks the top US airlines for 2026.

We get it — mastering points and miles is no easy feat. You may have seen our guide to getting started with points and miles, but what happens once you're ready to cash those points in for a trip?

Maximizing points and miles to travel luxuriously without breaking the bank doesn’t need to be laborious and time-consuming. In fact, there are various tools available that make it easier to find hotel and flight award availability.

With these tools, you can use your points to travel where you want, when you want and how you want in 2027 (and beyond) without spending hours searching for availability.

Here are 14 of the best apps and websites that make award travel redemptions easier and less stressful.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: The basic plan is free, but you really unlock the best features with a paid membership. Right now, TPG has a special offer: Roame.travel is offering TPG readers 40% off the Friends of Roame Pro membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY," which brings the regular price down to $94 per year (from $156).

When you sign up for a free Roame account, you can search more than 25 airline programs for instant, real-time award availability.

After clicking a flight option, you can see the points required to book, as well as the available transfer partners and recommended credit cards to help you earn the points you need. You can even add your existing credit cards to your virtual wallet to get recommendations.

With a paid membership, you can also track points pricing with route alerts.

As always, we recommend confirming award availability before transferring points.

Related: The complete guide to searching award space on Roame.travel

What it does: Helps travelers find airline award space.

What it costs: There is a free version that alerts you to seat availability on a specific flight, but you can get additional alerts and better search functions with the Basic ($6.99 per month), Premium ($12.99 per month) or Elite ($19.99 per month) membership options. There are discounts if you choose to pay annually.

And there's an ExpertFlyer discount exclusively for TPG readers: New users can get 30% off any annual subscription.

ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG's parent company, Red Ventures) is a helpful tool for viewing airline schedules, seat maps and flight statuses across more than 400 airlines, as well as award and upgrade availability on select carriers. You can set seat alerts to help snag your preferred seat if it isn't available when you book your flight.

Related: How to use ExpertFlyer alerts to snag a better seat

A free account lets you set one alert at a time, but you will need a Basic, Premium or Elite membership to run an award search. Once you are logged in with a paid account, you can search using the "Awards & Upgrades" tab. When you enter your travel details and select the airline you'd like to fly, you'll see the fare classes that ExpertFlyer can search alongside a description.

When you click the search button at the bottom of the screen, ExpertFlyer presents you with a list of the available flights broken down by date. Once you have the date, flight number and fare class, you can book your flight online or by calling the airline directly. If the flight you're looking to book doesn't have seats available in your preferred fare class, you can set an alert, and ExpertFlyer will email you if a seat is released, taking the legwork out of award searches.

ExpertFlyer's expanded Systemwide Upgrades feature lets American Airlines elite members with systemwide upgrades search availability up to 330 days out across multiple regions. This feature is only available with ExpertFlyer's Elite plan. Basic and Premium members can still search systemwide upgrade space one route at a time through the “Awards & Upgrades” tab.

What it does: Tracks hotel award availability at Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties.

What it costs: Free for basic membership; $3.99 per month for a Gold membership and $7.99 per month for a Platinum membership (though there's a 40% off Thanksgiving promotion if you elect to pay annually).

MaxMyPoint is a website that lets you check award availability for Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties worldwide. It takes the guesswork out of award redemption searches by showing real-time award pricing and availability.

The homepage shows popular properties, but you can filter by hotel brand, location, price and more to narrow down your results. You can also search date-based deals or use the map search feature to search multiple hotels in a single destination.

Once you choose a property, you can view a calendar that displays available points pricing and the lowest cash rate. This allows you to plan your trip around the dates with the best points pricing.

After you select your check-in date, you’ll automatically be redirected to the property’s website to start the booking process. If you can’t find the availability you are looking for, you can register for a free account and set up an alert to receive an email if availability changes.

Paid memberships come with additional features, including more frequent and more detailed alerts.

What it does: Displays award pricing in Google Flights.

What it costs: Free for a standard plan, $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year for a Pro plan. If you want to pay annually, there's also a paid option for alerts only, which costs $34.99 per year.

Points Path is a browser extension that displays award pricing alongside cash prices for select airlines in Google Flights. The free version includes points versus cash pricing for Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue and United Airlines.

It also tells you which transferable points can be used with the airlines it supports, as well as when to book at a paid rate or with points. Once you select an itinerary, you can book it directly with the airline using points or cash, as you would with Google Flights.

Related: How to use the Points Path extension to compare cash and award rates in Google Flights

Points Path simplifies the decision of when to use cash or miles to buy airline tickets. Points Path Pro unlocks additional features such as price alerts, access to additional airline programs and customizable points valuations.

The browser extension is compatible with Chrome, Safari, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Brave and Arc.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: There is a free version, but for real-time availability, you can purchase a Standard ($10.75 per month) or Premium ($21.67 per month) membership. These discounts are available when you pay annually. Concierge services are available starting at $200 per passenger.

TPG readers get seven months free on Standard Annual membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY7."

Point.me's robust interface searches for award flights across more than 30 loyalty programs and more than 150 airlines.

By entering your itinerary details, Point.me will display award availability, including which transfer partner offers the most value for your buck.

In addition to the free and paid versions, you can book one-on-one sessions with one of Point.me's expert consultants who can assist you with flight bookings, points strategies, elite status and mileage runs and more.

American Express cardholders can access a limited version of Point.me for free. As with the full version, you can search for award flight availability, but you will only see results from Amex transfer partners. This is a good way to try Point.me for free if you have Membership Rewards points that you want to transfer to an airline loyalty program to purchase tickets.

What it does: Helps you maximize your points by finding the best flight redemptions.

What it costs: Free for the basic plan; $99 per year for the premium plan (but there's a current promotion for $20 off).

Pointhound takes the guesswork (and hours of searching) out of turning your points and miles into award flights. The site’s search tool helps you find the best deals by displaying preferred booking options for a designated route and date.

For example, if you search for a flight from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), Pointhound will display your flight results alongside all available booking options.

If you know you want to fly Air France but don’t have enough Flying Blue miles, you can see which programs transfer to Air France partners, including those that have current transfer bonuses.

Once you’ve chosen a route and booking option, Pointhound will walk you through the points transfer and booking process. (You still book directly through the airline; Pointhound gives you the instructions on how to do it.)

If you want to stay informed about the latest flight deals, you can sign up to receive flight alerts from specific airports via email.

What it does: Searches for real-time award flight and hotel availability.

What it costs: Free for unlimited basic searches, $19.99 per month or $119.95 per year for Premium (though there are Black Friday promotions).

PointsYeah streamlines hotel and airline award bookings by searching all major credit cards, award programs and booking portals in under 20 seconds. You can view results from more than 20 airline programs and six major hotel programs.

Once you've chosen a flight, PointsYeah will display all available booking options. If you already have enough points, you can book directly with the airline; however, PointsYeah will show the amount of points you'd need to transfer from various credit card programs, including details on current transfer bonuses.

You can create flight and hotel alerts. Basic accounts get up to four flight and hotel price alerts, as well as five multi-region alerts for a 30-day search window.

Premium members get up to 32 flight alerts, 30 hotel alerts and up to 150 multi-region alerts for a 90-day search window. When you upgrade to Premium, you also get access to United Airlines upgrade alerts, expanded date and destination availability when you search and the ability to set custom values for your points currencies.

What it does: Provides real-time search results across multiple airports and travel dates simultaneously.

What it costs: Free for the basic plan; $12.99 per month or $109.99 per year for AwardTool Pro (with Black Friday discounts available).

If your travel dates and destinations are flexible, AwardTool can display results for multiple flights in a single search. If you're extra flexible, you can utilize the Panorama feature to view award pricing by region rather than a specific destination or the Deals feature to see the best award rates from your chosen airport to anywhere in the world.

When you upgrade to AwardTool Pro, you unlock access to additional and expanded search capabilities, up to 100 award alerts, unlimited Panorama alerts and live seat map availability.

What it does: Gondola helps you find the best hotel deals and use your points to book.

Gondola is a free AI-powered hotel booking tool that tracks your points and miles balances to help you maximize your rewards. When you search for your travel dates and destination, the results will display cash and points pricing, along with ratings to help you determine which is the better value.

You'll see results from major hotel groups like Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Accor and more.

Once you've chosen a property, Gondola will direct you to the hotel's website to book award stays directly with the hotel. For paid reservations, Gondola will book the hotel on your behalf, allowing you to earn the usual points and elite benefits, along with between 3% and 7% cash back in the form of Gondola Cashback for every stay.

Gondola will also monitor your bookings and alert you if the price drops, so you can rebook at the lower price.

What it does: Checks flight award availability based on your itinerary and preferred airline.

What it costs: Free for five economy award availability searches per day; $3.39 per month for a Premium subscription or $9.99 per month for a First Class subscription, with discounts for annual payments.

SeatSpy is an easy-to-use website that checks award availability across 10 airlines, most of which are not U.S.-based carriers.

Select your airline, departure and end destination airports, then hit “Search” to see availability across the next 12 months.

SeatSpy is free to use if you’re only searching for economy availability. Where the product really shines, however, is in its premium subscriptions.

The entry-level subscription, Premium, allows unlimited searches across all fares and up to four active alerts sent via email, WhatsApp and Telegram. It also includes AwardWallet integration, so you can track how many points you have to redeem.

First Class includes everything in the Premium plan, plus unlimited alerts sent instantly instead of hourly, along with SMS alerts and "experience alerts."

Both subscriptions offer a “Where Can I Go” search feature that shows all destinations with award availability from your departure airport on the travel dates you select.

It may have few features when compared to other services on this list, but in terms of simplicity, it’s a great site — especially if you’re looking at Europe-based airlines.

What it does: Displays award seat availability on domestic and international flights across fare classes.

What it costs: Free for the basic version and $12.99 monthly for the Pro version, which includes Rooms.aero access for hotel award searches.

Seats.aero regularly refreshes award space across dozens of airline programs and provides results for the next month or two.

The Pro version allows you to search up to a year in advance, set up unlimited alerts (whereas free users get only five) and receive SMS notifications when award availability turns up.

Related: How I use Seats.aero every day to find the best airline award availability in seconds

What it does: Displays hotel award availability across several major hotel brands.

What it costs: Free for the basic version; if you want the paid Pro version, you can get it through your Seats.aero membership.

Rooms.aero works similarly to its counterpart, Seats.aero. Users can search seven major hotel programs — Choice Privileges, Hilton Honors, World of Hyatt, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, I Prefer Hotel Rewards and Wyndham Rewards — for hotel award availability across certain dates or destinations.

Related: How to use Rooms.aero to find the best hotel award availability

Rooms.aero uses a valuation system to indicate whether you are getting good, average or poor value for your points for a given redemption. You can also filter by points program and the maximum number of points per night. When you choose a hotel, you'll see a calendar view with points and cash rates.

You can also use Rooms.aero to set availability alerts to notify you when a specific hotel or destination has points availability. With a Pro account, you get access to advanced search filters, SMS alerts and more.

What it does: Displays points, miles and cash pricing for flights and hotels.

What it costs: Free for a basic membership; $14.99 for a one-time “Trip Pass” valid for three days; and $12.50 per month (or $150 annually) for a premium membership.

Awayz helps you make the most of your hard-earned points and miles by showing when to redeem points and when to pay cash. You can use the Awayz search tool to find specific flight routes or hotels in specific destinations. Awayz will then display live award availability and cash rates so you can make a side-by-side comparison.

You can use the site’s robust filtering system to display certain hotel chains, transferable award programs and even those that qualify for free night certificates.

For flights, you can filter to see only certain airlines, choose the time of day you’d prefer to travel and even indicate which aircraft type you’d prefer. You can also update your “wallet” with the credit cards and reward balances you currently have, so it can tailor your results further.

Related: How to use Awayz to improve your hotel award searches

A free membership includes five hotel and five airline searches per month. An Awayz Trip Pass (great for one-time planning) includes 50 hotel searches, 50 flight searches and 10 award availability alerts for a one-time fee of $14.99. An Awayz Premium membership includes 500 hotel searches, 100 flight searches and 30 award availability alerts, among other perks.

What it does: Finds flight schedules and prices, with several filtering options, for most major airlines.

Google Flights is your one-stop shop for finding the best flight for your schedule and budget.

You can search flight schedules and pricing across most major airlines and sort results based on price, duration, number of stops, fare class and airlines, among other options. You can also set flight price alerts.

One of the best tools within Google Flights is Google Flights Explore.

Google Flights Explore lets you enter only your departure city, then use the interactive map to choose your destination based on current pricing.

Google Flights does not display points pricing (unless you use the Points Path plugin we mentioned earlier in this article), but that doesn’t mean it can’t help you find award space. You’ll still have to book directly through the airline, but you can save valuable search time by narrowing down your options through Google Flights first.

For example, if you have a bank of points and miles with a Star Alliance, Oneworld or SkyTeam partner airline, you can filter search results by alliance to see routing options. Or, you may find a nearby airport with better pricing that you wouldn’t have searched for otherwise.

The great thing about all these tools is that you can use them together to find award flights and free hotel nights.

No matter which combination of sites and apps you use, you’ll find that they take the guesswork out of award redemptions and put you on the fast track to becoming an expert in redeeming points and miles for your 2027 travels.

#6202. The American Genius of Madden

David O. Russell pays tribute to football, folklore, and eccentricity.

Chuck ZlotnickAmazon Content Services LLC

Hang on at the start of David O. Russell’s Madden, as its story of the Oakland Raiders football coach John Madden shifts between semidocumentary and biopic. Russell’s uneven, sketchy narrative steadily turns into a probing human comedy. It’s also a slyly monumental tale of American genius found in an Everyman’s commonplace ambition.

The key to the film’s geniality and surprise is Nicolas Cage’s astounding portrayal of Madden, a former college athlete who blew out his knee but kept his feeling for football. Cage enters the mindset of a sports fanatic who is also an artist, devising plays and strategies that, considering his size and vision, earn him the nickname “Buddha.” But this is not one of those freak-outs that Cage is known for; he seems to transform himself into John Candy — broad-beamed with a tuft of blond hair and a convincing smile. Cage commits to this genial eccentric who, despite his unreachable idiosyncrasy, is harmless, lovable yet tough — an authentic, original American.

Madden became coach for the Raiders, a team known to play with sheer guts and dedication — qualities the burly Buddha shared with team owner Al Davis (Christian Bale), his wiry, sharklike best friend. This thick-and-thin Laurel-and-Hardy pair sustain an unlikely partnership. It’s one of the most remarkable depictions of brotherhood in movies — a friendship that persists over temperamental tensions, even after Madden leaves the team and pursues media entrepreneurship to sustain his love of the sport. Madden the broadcaster converts his playbook ingenuity and follows his father’s advice: “Get away with doing what you love for as long as you possibly can.”

Russell redeems himself with the oddest-yet-normal collection of American eccentrics. Acting on the edge of parody, Cage and Bale, with their uncanny sincerity, reward Russell’s interest in quirkiness. (Madden hears Davis’s voice in his head.) The fascinating scoundrels of Russell’s terrific American Hustle were preoccupied with manipulating one another. Here, friendship, comradeship, teamwork, and family complications are genuinely recognizable. Scenes that emulate a documentary approach — Madden’s wife Virginia (gung ho comedienne Kathryn Hahn) rivals Jennifer Lawrence’s volatility when speaking directly to the camera — satirize realism to fulfill the non-cynical view of national character that Russell fumbled in the bohemian sojourn of Amsterdam. No wonder De Niro is left out of this particular silver-lined playbook.

The patchwork of styles in Madden suggests that Russell investigates American eccentricity as he goes along, finding his way back to the coast-to-coast realness that made his Flirting with Disaster so exhilarating (as in Madden’s surreal, unapologetic pitch for the unique holiday dish the Turducken). Russell adopts Madden’s football-analysis style, such as on-screen telestrator vectors, to humorously examine Madden’s own career shifts and twists of personality (Madden instructing his players, or meeting colleagues Pat Summerall, Howard Cosell, and Bob Costas).

A dull-witted filmmaker, say James Cameron, would choose an “immersive” style for a movie concerned with the gestalt of football. But Russell’s film is also about the phenomenon of a sport that becomes a vanguard of technology and culture. Madden is pursued by Trip Hawkins (John Mulaney), founder of video game company EA (Electronic Arts), who wants to translate Madden’s football theories for a new generation of at-home fans and gamers. Hawkins’s proposal is scored to Beethoven’s Ninth — another example of Russell’s wit, matching the film’s eclectic score from Barry White and Talking Heads to N.W.A. (“You don’t want to know what that means,” Davis says to Madden.)

Through Madden and Hawkins’s acumen, Russell treats the discovery of a new world as an aftereffect of folk intelligence and ingenuity. Genius is kidded when Hawkins’s team of four-eyed computer nerds demonstrate jock potential after applying Madden’s plays to their algorithms. It’s a sweet way of conveying the phenomenon that would turn EA’s Madden NFL video game franchise into a $4 billion enterprise (some estimates raise that into double digits), with annual compensation going to the Madden family estate.

More important, Russell (who co-wrote the script with Cambron Clark) sees Madden as a visionary who proudly summarizes TV sportscasting as “They state the obvious, which is f***ing boring.” My only complaint is that Robert Richardson’s photography tends toward frowzy (perhaps deliberately aping TV docs), not as splendid as Oliver Stone’s Any Given Sunday — the greatest football movie ever made.

Madden itself shares biopic sensibility with John Ford’s The Wings of Eagles, respectfully eschewing its subject’s mortality for an optimistic appreciation of a man’s potential. It is unique to American character and the experience of competition and dreams of the NFL Hall of Fame that Madden shared with Al Davis. Russell’s tribute comes complete with a motto: “You make people feel good and alive and good to be American, and I’m not standing in the way of that.” Thus Russell proves his own resilience and the achievement of a new folkloric genre struggling to emerge.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

#6201. LA-Area Voters Approve Wave of Hotel Tax Hikes Ahead of 2028 Olympics

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Griffith Observatory with downtown Los Angeles in the background. Wikimedia Commons / The Fun Chronicles

A dozen cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties raised or updated lodging taxes in recent elections as cities prepare for a surge in visitors during the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Five months after Los Angeles voters rejected an increase to the city’s lodging tax, the surrounding suburbs hiked their own.

Preliminary results show 12 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties approving changes to lodging taxes on November 3, according to the California Local Government Finance Almanac. Ten created or raised rates, with two cities pushing their hotel rates above Los Angeles’ 14% tax. Two expanded their current tax to cover more types of stays.

The changes come as Los Angeles and the surrounding area prepare for a surge in visitation for the 2028 Olympics, which are expected to draw in roughly 2 million visitors to the greater Los Angeles area, and as local lawmakers work to address widening budget gaps. Skift previously reported that lodging taxes can be an easy sell because the people paying them aren’t usually locals who vote.

In most cities, the increases are "not a huge amount of money compared to other sorts

Five months after Los Angeles voters rejected Measure TT, which would have raised the city's 14% lodging tax to 16%, 12 cities in Los Angeles and Orange counties approved lodging tax changes on November 3, according to preliminary results from the California Local Government Finance Almanac. Ten cities created or raised rates, and two expanded coverage to more types of stays. Hawthorne, which borders Inglewood and its Olympic venues, jumped from 12% to 17% and expects as much as $3.1 million in annual revenue. Lynwood approved its first hotel tax at 12%, and Orange and Placentia each went from 10% to 14%. The revenue goes to general funds rather than tourism-specific uses, and the measures come as the region prepares for roughly 2 million visitors for the 2028 Olympics and as local lawmakers work to address widening budget gaps. Short-term rentals lost some of their tax edge: Alhambra extended its 12% occupancy tax to vacation rentals, Monterey Park will tax short-term rental guests at 16% against 14% for hotels, and Santa Monica's council can now apply the lodging tax to corporate stays over 30 days during "major event periods." Statewide, 29 of 34 lodging tax measures were passing, the second largest wave in a decade. Outside California, results were mixed — Tulsa nearly doubled its rate to 9.9% with hotel association backing and tourism earmarks, while voters in Oklahoma, Oregon, Florida, and Mississippi rejected measures.
